2.6 Category Theory

2.6.1 Categories

Definition 2.6.1 (Category)

A (locally small) category 𝒞︀ consists of

  • a class ob(𝒞︀) of objects
  • for every pair of objects 𝑋,𝑌∈ob(𝒞︀) a set of morphisms Mor(𝑋,𝑌)

  • for every three objects 𝑋,𝑌,𝑍 a law of composition

    Mor(𝑋,𝑌)×Mor(𝑌,𝑍)→Mor(𝑋,𝑍)(𝑔,𝑓)→𝑔∘𝑓

such that the following conditions hold

  • ℎ∘(𝑔∘𝑓)=(ℎ∘𝑔)∘𝑓 (associativity)
  • There exists 1𝑋∈Mor(𝑋,𝑋) such that 1𝑋∘𝑓=𝑓 and 𝑔∘1𝑋=𝑔.
Example 2.6.2
The category of sets is 𝐒𝐞𝐭 with maps in the usual way. Note associativity is automatically satisfied.
Example 2.6.3 (𝑛-pointed category)
Given a category 𝒞︀ where objects are sets, we may consider the pointed category (𝒞︀,⋆𝑛) consisting of pairs (𝐴,𝑎) where 𝐴∈ob(𝒞︀) and 𝑎∈𝐴𝑛. We consider only morphisms 𝑓:𝐴→𝐵 such that 𝑓(𝑎𝑖)=𝑏𝑖.
Definition 2.6.4 (Opposite Category)

Given a category 𝒞︀ the opposite category is denoted 𝒞︀op and given by

  • The same class of objects ob(𝒞︀op)=ob(𝒞︀)

  • For every pair of objects 𝑋,𝑌∈ob(𝒞︀) the morphisms are reversed

    Morop(𝑋,𝑌)≔Mor(𝑌,𝑋)

  • The law of composition is reversed

    Morop(𝑋,𝑌)×Morop(𝑌,𝑍)→Morop(𝑋,𝑍)(𝑔,𝑓)→𝑓∘𝑔
Example 2.6.5
The polynomial ring 𝐴[𝑋] is an initial object in the category of pointed 𝐴-algebras.
Definition 2.6.6 (Isomorphism)

A morphism 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 is an isomorphism if there exists 𝑔:𝑌→𝑋 such that

𝑔∘𝑓=1𝑋and𝑓∘𝑔=1𝑌.
Definition 2.6.7 (Functor)

A covariant functor 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ consists of a mapping of objects

𝐹:ob(𝒞︀)→ob(𝒟︀)

together with a mapping of morphisms

𝐹(−):Mor(𝑋,𝑌)→Mor(𝐹(𝑋),𝐹(𝑌))

which satisfies

  • 𝐹(1𝑋)=1𝐹(𝑋)
  • 𝐹(𝑓∘𝑔)=𝐹(𝑓)∘𝐹(𝑔)

A contravariant functor 𝒞︀→𝒟︀ is equivalent to a covariant functor on the opposite category 𝒞︀op→𝒟︀, namely where arrows are reversed.

Definition 2.6.8 (Full and faithful)

A functor 𝐹 is said to be

  • Faithful if 𝐹(−) is injective.
  • Full if 𝐹(−) is surjective.
Definition 2.6.9 (Concrete Category)
A concrete category is a pair (𝒞︀,𝑈) where 𝒞︀ and a “forgetful functor” 𝑈:𝒞︀→𝐒𝐞𝐭 which is faithful.
Example 2.6.10 (Forgetful Functor)
The category of groups (resp. rings, modules, …) is a concrete category in the obvious way.
Definition 2.6.11 (Mor functor)

For any objects 𝑋,𝑌,𝑍∈ob(𝒞︀), there is a canonical covariant functor

Mor(𝑋,−):𝒞︀⟶𝐒𝐞𝐭𝑌⟶Mor(𝑋,𝑌)

which acts on a morphism 𝑓:𝑌→𝑍 by

Mor(𝑋,𝑓):Mor(𝑋,𝑌)→Mor(𝑋,𝑍)𝑔→𝑓∘𝑔

It’s a functor precisely because composition of functions is associative. Similarly there’s a canonical contravariant functor Mor(−,𝑌).

Definition 2.6.12 (Natural Transformation)

Let 𝐹,𝐺:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ be covariant functors. A natural transformation 𝜂:𝐹⇒𝐺 consists of a family of morphisms

𝜂𝑍:𝐹(𝑍)→𝐺(𝑍)𝑍∈ob(𝒞︀)

such that the following diagram commutes for all 𝑓:𝑍→𝑍′

Definition 2.6.13 (Natural isomorphism)
A natural transformation 𝜂:𝐹⇒𝐺 is a natural isomorphism if 𝜂𝑍 is an isomorphism for all 𝑍∈𝒞︀.
Definition 2.6.14 (Functor Category)

Let 𝐼 be a small category and 𝒟︀ a category. The functor category 𝒟︀𝐼 has

  • objects: functors 𝐹:𝐼→𝒟︀;
  • morphisms 𝐹→𝐺: natural transformations 𝜂:𝐹⇒𝐺 (2.6.12);

  • composition: for 𝜂:𝐹⇒𝐺 and 𝜃:𝐺⇒𝐻, (𝜃∘𝜂)𝑍≔𝜃𝑍∘𝜂𝑍 for 𝑍∈ob(𝐼) – again a natural transformation, since for 𝑓:𝑍→𝑍′ in 𝐼, using naturality of 𝜃 then of 𝜂,

    𝐻(𝑓)∘𝜃𝑍∘𝜂𝑍=𝜃𝑍′∘𝐺(𝑓)∘𝜂𝑍=𝜃𝑍′∘𝜂𝑍′∘𝐹(𝑓);
  • identities: 1𝐹, with (1𝐹)𝑍≔1𝐹(𝑍) (trivially natural).

Associativity and the identity laws hold pointwise at each 𝑍∈ob(𝐼), being inherited from those of 𝒟︀; so 𝒟︀𝐼 is indeed a category.

Definition 2.6.15

We say 𝒞︀′⊂𝒞︀ is a subcategory if

  • ob(𝒞︀′)⊆ob(𝒞︀)
  • Mor𝒞︀′(𝑍,𝑊)⊆Mor𝒞︀(𝑍,𝑊)
  • Composition agrees when it is well-defined

We say 𝒞︀′ is a full subcategory if additionally Mor𝒞︀′(𝑍,𝑊)=Mor𝒞︀(𝑍,𝑊).

2.6.2 Comma and Slice Categories

Definition 2.6.16 (Comma Category)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→ℰ︀ and 𝐺:𝒟︀→ℰ︀ be functors. The comma category (𝐹↓𝐺) is the category with

  • objects: triples (𝐶,𝐷,𝑓) where 𝐶∈𝒞︀, 𝐷∈𝒟︀, and 𝑓:𝐹(𝐶)→𝐺(𝐷) is a morphism in ℰ︀

  • morphisms: a morphism (𝐶,𝐷,𝑓)→(𝐶′,𝐷′,𝑓′) is a pair (𝑔,ℎ) where 𝑔:𝐶→𝐶′ is a morphism in 𝒞︀ and ℎ:𝐷→𝐷′ is a morphism in 𝒟︀, such that

    𝐺(ℎ)∘𝑓=𝑓′∘𝐹(𝑔)

with composition (𝑔′,ℎ′)∘(𝑔,ℎ)≔(𝑔′∘𝑔,ℎ′∘ℎ) and identities 1(𝐶,𝐷,𝑓)≔(1𝐶,1𝐷), inherited from 𝒞︀ and 𝒟︀.

Definition 2.6.17 (Slice Category)

Let 𝒞︀ be a category and 𝑋∈𝒞︀, and let 𝑋:𝟏→𝒞︀ be the functor with 𝑋(⋆)=𝑋. The slice category 𝒞︀/𝑋 (also denoted 𝒞︀↓𝑋) is the comma category (id𝒞︀↓𝑋) (2.6.16).

Explicitly its objects are pairs (𝑌,𝑓) where 𝑌∈ob(𝒞︀) and 𝑓:𝑌→𝑋 is a morphism in 𝒞︀, and a morphism (𝑌,𝑓)→(𝑌′,𝑓′) is a morphism 𝑔:𝑌→𝑌′ in 𝒞︀ such that 𝑓′∘𝑔=𝑓.

Dually the coslice category 𝑋/𝒞︀ (also denoted 𝑋↓𝒞︀) is the comma category (𝑋↓id𝒞︀), with objects pairs (𝑌,𝑓) where 𝑌∈ob(𝒞︀) and 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 is a morphism in 𝒞︀, and a morphism (𝑌,𝑓)→(𝑌′,𝑓′) is a morphism 𝑔:𝑌→𝑌′ in 𝒞︀ such that 𝑔∘𝑓=𝑓′.

2.6.3 Product Categories and Bifunctors

Definition 2.6.18 (Product Category)

Given two categories 𝒞︀, 𝒟︀ we may construct the product category 𝒞︀×𝒟︀ as follows

  • The objects are given by pairs

    ob(𝒞︀×𝒟︀)≔ob(𝒞︀)×ob(𝒟︀)

  • The morphisms are given by pairs

    Mor((𝐶,𝐶′),(𝐷,𝐷′))≔Mor(𝐶,𝐶′)×Mor(𝐷,𝐷′)

    Concretely given 𝑓:𝐶→𝐶′ and 𝑔:𝐷→𝐷′ write (𝑓,𝑔):(𝐶,𝐷)→(𝐶′,𝐷′)

  • The law of composition is determined by

    (𝑓,𝑔)∘(ℎ,𝑘)≔(𝑓∘ℎ,𝑔∘𝑘)

It’s clear that the law of composition is associative and the identity morphism for (𝐶,𝐷) is (1𝐶,1𝐷). Furthermore we observe the following property

Definition 2.6.19 (Bifunctor)

A functor on a product category, 𝐹:𝒞︀×𝒟︀→ℰ︀ is termed a bifunctor. 𝐹 induces a family of functors

  • 𝐹(𝐶,−):𝒟︀→ℰ︀ given by

    𝐹(𝐶,𝑔)≔𝐹(1𝐶,𝑔)

  • 𝐹(−,𝐷):𝒞︀→ℰ︀ given by

    𝐹(𝑓,𝐷)≔𝐹(𝑓,1𝐷)

which satisfy the compatibility conditions

by applying 𝐹 to (*).

Proposition 2.6.20 (Reconstruct Bifunctor)

Consider a family of functors {𝐹𝐿(𝐶):𝒟︀→ℰ︀}𝐶∈ob(𝒞︀) and {𝐹𝑅(𝐷):𝒞︀→ℰ︀}𝐷∈ob(𝒟︀). Suppose the following conditions hold

  • 𝐹𝐿(𝐶)(𝐷)=𝐹𝑅(𝐷)(𝐶)
  • 𝐹𝐿(𝐶′)(𝑔)∘𝐹𝑅(𝐷)(𝑓)=𝐹𝑅(𝐷′)(𝑓)∘𝐹𝐿(𝐶)(𝑔)

then these determine a well-defined bifunctor given by

𝐹(𝑓×𝑔)≔𝐹𝐿(𝐶′)(𝑔)∘𝐹𝑅(𝐷)(𝑓)
Proposition 2.6.21

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀×𝒟︀→ℰ︀ be a bifunctor. For 𝑓:𝐶→𝐶′ then there is a natural transformation

𝐹(𝑓,−):𝐹(𝐶,−)⇒𝐹(𝐶′,−)

given by 𝐹(𝑓,−)𝐷≔𝐹(𝑓,1𝐷). Similarly for 𝑔:𝐷→𝐷′ then there is a natural transformation

𝐹(−,𝑔):𝐹(−,𝐷)⇒𝐹(−,𝐷′)
Proof. The naturality condition is immediate from (*) and the commutative diagram in (2.6.19). ∎
Proposition 2.6.22 (Criteria for Natural Transformation)

Let 𝐹,𝐺:𝒞︀×𝒟︀→ℰ︀ be two bifunctors and suppose we have a family of natural transformations

𝜂𝐶:𝐹(𝐶,−)⇒𝐺(𝐶,−)

for all 𝐶∈𝒞︀. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝜂:𝐹(−,−)⇒𝐺(−,−) is a natural transformation

  2. The following diagram commutes for all 𝐷∈𝒟︀ and 𝑓:𝐶→𝐶′

Proof. a) ⟹ b) This diagram is a special case of the naturality condition.

b) ⟹ a) Suppose 𝑓:𝐶→𝐶′ and 𝑔:𝐷→𝐷′ then we require to show that

𝐺(𝑓,𝑔)(𝜂𝐶,𝐷(𝜙))=𝜂𝐶′,𝐷′(𝐹(𝑓,𝑔)(𝜙))

However

𝐺(𝑓,𝑔)(𝜂𝐶,𝐷(𝜙))=𝐺(𝑓,1𝐷′)(𝐺(1𝐶,𝑔)(𝜂𝐶,𝐷(𝜙)))=𝐺(𝑓,1𝐷′)𝜂𝐶,𝐷′(𝐹(1𝐶,𝑔)(𝜙))=𝜂𝐶′,𝐷′(𝐹(𝑓,1𝐷′)(𝐹(1𝐶,𝑔)(𝜙)))=𝜂𝐶′,𝐷′(𝐹(𝑓,𝑔)(𝜙))

where we have used that 𝜂𝐶,𝐷 is natural in 𝐷 and 𝐶 individually. ∎

Example 2.6.23 (Mor is a bifunctor)

The canonical example is the following, given any locally small category 𝒞︀, we have a bifunctor

Mor:𝒞︀op×𝒞︀→𝐒𝐞𝐭

given by the set of morphisms. The action on morphisms is given by

Mor(𝑓,𝑔)(𝜙)=𝑔∘𝜙∘𝑓

and we verify by associativity of 𝒞︀ that

Mor((𝑓,𝑔)∘(ℎ,𝑘))=Mor(𝑓,𝑔)∘Mor(ℎ,𝑘)

and it’s clear that the commutativity condition in (*) is satisfied.

Example 2.6.24 (Concrete bifunctors)

Let 𝒞︀, 𝒟︀ be concrete categories and consider the following bifunctor

𝐹:𝒟︀op×𝒞︀→𝐒𝐞𝐭𝐹(𝐷,𝐶)≔{𝜙:𝐷→𝐶|𝑃(𝜙)}

where 𝑃(−) is some predicate such that 𝑃(𝜙)⟹𝑃(𝑔∘𝜙∘𝑓).

2.6.4 Equivalence of categories

Definition 2.6.25 (Equivalence of categories)

Let 𝒞︀, 𝒟︀ be categories. An equivalence of categories consists of a pair of functors (either both covariant or both contravariant)

𝒞︀⇌𝐺𝐹𝒟︀

together with natural isomorphisms

𝜂:id𝒞︀⇒𝐺𝐹𝜖:𝐹𝐺⇒id𝒟︀

We say 𝐹 is an equivalence of categories if there exists some 𝐺 satisfying these conditions.

Definition 2.6.26
We say a functor 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ is essentially surjective if for all 𝐷∈𝒟︀ there exists 𝐶∈𝒞︀ such that 𝐹(𝐶) is isomorphic to 𝐷.
Lemma 2.6.27

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀, 𝐺:𝒟︀→𝒞︀ be functors.

If there exists a natural isomorphism 𝜂:id𝒞︀⇒𝐺𝐹 then 𝐹 is faithful. Explicitly 𝐹(−) has a left-inverse given by

𝑔→𝜂𝐶′−1∘𝐺(𝑔)∘𝜂𝐶

Furthermore 𝐺𝐹(𝜂𝐶)=𝜂𝐺𝐹(𝐶).

Proof. Consider the sequence of maps

Mor(𝐶,𝐶′)⟶𝐹(−)Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐹(𝐶′))⟶𝐺(−)Mor(𝐺𝐹(𝐶),𝐺𝐹(𝐶′))⟶Mor(𝜂𝐶,𝜂𝐶′−1)Mor(𝐶,𝐶′)

Note that the composite of this map is given by

𝑓→𝜂𝐶′−1∘𝐺𝐹(𝑓)∘𝜂𝐶=𝜂𝐶′−1∘𝜂𝐶′∘𝑓=𝑓

in other words 𝐹(−) has a left inverse and therefore 𝐹 is faithful.

Note by naturality we have 𝐺𝐹(𝜂𝐶)∘𝜂𝐶=𝜂𝐺𝐹(𝐶)∘𝜂𝐶. Since 𝜂𝐶 is an isomorphism we may cancel to find 𝐺𝐹(𝜂𝐶)=𝜂𝐺𝐹(𝐶). ∎

Proposition 2.6.28 (Equivalence is full and faithful)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ be a functor then the following are equivalent

  • 𝐹 is full, faithful and essentially surjective (2.6.26)
  • 𝐹 is an equivalence of categories (2.6.25)

In other words 𝐹(−) is bijective and hence has a two-sided inverse. Explicitly it is given by

Mor(𝐶,𝐶′)⟷Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐹(𝐶′))𝑓→𝐹(𝑓)𝜂𝐶′−1∘𝐺(𝑔)∘𝜂𝐶←𝑔

Proof. We prove only the second implies the first. By assumption there is an equivalence with 𝐺 and by the previous Lemma both 𝐹 and 𝐺 are faithful by considering 𝜂 and 𝜖−1 in turn. Further the given map is already shown to be a left inverse. We claim it’s also a right inverse, for consider

𝑔′≔𝐹(𝜂𝐶′−1)∘𝐹𝐺(𝑔)∘𝐹(𝜂𝐶).

We claim that 𝐺(𝑔′)=𝐺(𝑔). As 𝐺 is faithful this would imply 𝑔′=𝑔 and the given map is a right inverse as required. Observe

𝐺(𝑔′)=𝐺𝐹(𝜂𝐶′−1)∘𝐺𝐹𝐺(𝑔)∘𝐺𝐹(𝜂𝐶)=𝜂𝐺𝐹(𝐶′)−1∘𝐺𝐹𝐺(𝑔)∘𝜂𝐺𝐹(𝐶)=𝜂𝐺𝐹(𝐶′)−1∘𝜂𝐺𝐹(𝐶′)∘𝐺(𝑔)=𝐺(𝑔)

where we have used the result that 𝐺𝐹(𝜂𝐶)=𝜂𝐺𝐹(𝐶). Since the maps are mutual inverses we see that 𝐹 is full and faithful as required.

Given 𝐷∈𝒟︀ then 𝐹(𝐺(𝐷)) is isomorphic to 𝐷 via 𝜖 so 𝐹 is essentially surjective. ∎

Proposition 2.6.29 (Duality)

Let (−)⋆:𝒞︀→𝒞︀ be a contravariant functor such that there is a natural isomorphism

𝜂:id𝒞︀⇒(−)⋆⋆

then (−)⋆ is an equivalence of categories and in particular full and faithful.

Proof. Define 𝜖=𝜂−1 to determine the equivalence of categories. By the previous result then (−)⋆ is full and faithful. ∎

2.6.5 Properties of Morphisms

Definition 2.6.30 (Injective, Surjective and Bijective)

Let (𝒞︀,𝑈) be a concrete category (2.6.9) and 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 a morphism. Then we say

  • 𝑓 is injective if 𝑈(𝑓) is injective
  • 𝑓 is surjective if 𝑈(𝑓) is surjective
Remark 2.6.31
Note if 𝑓 is both surjective and injective it need not be an isomorphism.

The concepts of monic/split-monic, epic/split-epic, iso generalize the notion of injective, surjective and bijective to general categories as we shall see.

Definition 2.6.32 (Monomorphism / Epimorphism)

A morphism 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 is said to be a monomorphism (or monic) if

𝑓∘𝑔1=𝑓∘𝑔2⟹𝑔1=𝑔2

for all 𝑔1,𝑔2:𝑍→𝑋.

Dually, 𝑓 is said to be an epimorphism (or epic) if

𝑔1∘𝑓=𝑔2∘𝑓⟹𝑔1=𝑔2

for all 𝑔1,𝑔2:𝑌→𝑍.

Remark 2.6.33 (Monic/Epic Duality)
A morphism 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 of 𝒞︀ is monic if and only if 𝑓op:𝑌→𝑋 is epic in 𝒞︀op, and dually 𝑓 is epic if and only if 𝑓op is monic in 𝒞︀op (2.6.4): composition in 𝒞︀op reverses the order of composition in 𝒞︀, so the defining cancellation property of monic in 𝒞︀ is precisely the defining cancellation property of epic in 𝒞︀op, and vice versa.
Definition 2.6.34 (Split-monic / Split-epic)

A morphism 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 is split-monic if it has a left inverse, 𝑔:𝑌→𝑋

𝑔∘𝑓=1𝑋

We say 𝑔 is a section of 𝑓.

Dually, 𝑓 is split-epic if it has a right inverse, 𝑔:𝑌→𝑋

𝑓∘𝑔=1𝑌

We say 𝑔 is a retraction of 𝑓.

Proposition 2.6.35 (Split Monic⇒Monic)

For a general category 𝒞︀ we have

  • split-monic ⟹ monic
  • split-epic ⟹ epic

We say an isomorphism is a morphism with a two-sided inverse. We can refine the criteria for 𝑓 to be an isomorphism using the notions just defined

Proposition 2.6.36 (Isomorphism Criteria)

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑓 is an isomorphism
  2. 𝑓 is both split-epic and split-monic
  3. 𝑓 is split-epic and monic
  4. 𝑓 is split-monic and epic

In this case a morphism 𝑔 is a retraction if and only if it is a section. And such a 𝑔 is unique, so we denote it by 𝑓−1

Proof. This is mostly formal

a) ⟹ b) Clear.

b) ⟹ c,d) This follows from (2.6.35).

c) ⟹ b) Suppose 𝑔 is a retraction of 𝑓, that is 𝑓𝑔=1𝑌. Then 𝑓(𝑔𝑓)=(𝑓𝑔)𝑓=1𝑌∘𝑓=𝑓=𝑓∘1𝑋. As 𝑓 is monic we conclude that 𝑔𝑓=1𝑋 and 𝑔 is a section of 𝑓.

d) ⟹ b) Analogous

b) ⟹ a) We’ve shown that any retraction is a section and vice-versa. Furthermore by monic/epic-ness a retraction or section is unique. ∎

Lemma 2.6.37 (Factors of an Isomorphism)

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be an isomorphism.

  1. If 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑔 for some monomorphism 𝑚, then 𝑚 and 𝑔 are both isomorphisms.
  2. If 𝑓=ℎ∘𝑒 for some epimorphism 𝑒, then ℎ and 𝑒 are both isomorphisms.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

a) Since 𝑓 is an isomorphism, 𝑚∘(𝑔∘𝑓−1)=𝑓∘𝑓−1=1𝑌, so 𝑚 is split-epic. As 𝑚 is also monic, (2.6.36) gives that 𝑚 is an isomorphism, and so 𝑔=𝑚−1∘𝑓 is also an isomorphism, being a composite of isomorphisms.

b) Dually, since 𝑓 is an isomorphism, (𝑓−1∘ℎ)∘𝑒=𝑓−1∘𝑓=1𝑋, so 𝑒 is split-monic. As 𝑒 is also epic, (2.6.36) gives that 𝑒 is an isomorphism, and so ℎ=𝑓∘𝑒−1 is also an isomorphism. ∎

Proposition 2.6.38

For the category 𝐒𝐞𝐭 we have

  • split-monic ⟺ monic ⟺ injective
  • split-epic ⟺ epic ⟺ surjective
  • isomorphism ⟺ bijective
Definition 2.6.39 (Balanced Category)
A category 𝒞︀ is balanced if every morphism which is both monic and epic is an isomorphism.
Example 2.6.40

𝐒𝐞𝐭 is balanced: by (2.6.38), the monic and epic morphisms are precisely the injective and surjective ones, so a morphism which is both is bijective, hence an isomorphism. The category of groups is balanced for the same reason, a bijective group homomorphism has a group homomorphism as its (set-theoretic) inverse.

Not every category is balanced. In 𝐓𝐨𝐩 the map [0,2𝜋)→𝑆1, 𝑡↦𝑒𝑖𝑡 is continuous and bijective, hence monic and epic, but its inverse is not continuous, so it is not an isomorphism. Likewise in 𝐑𝐧𝐠 the inclusion ℤ↪︎ℚ is monic and epic (any two ring homomorphisms out of ℚ agreeing on ℤ agree everywhere) but is not an isomorphism.

Definition 2.6.41 (Preserves/Reflects)

Let 𝒫︀ be a property of morphisms and 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ be a functor then we say

  • 𝐹 preserves 𝒫︀ if (𝑓 satisfies 𝒫︀⟹𝐹(𝑓) satisfies 𝒫︀)
  • 𝐹 reflects 𝒫︀ if (𝐹(𝑓) satisfies 𝒫︀⟹𝑓 satisfies 𝒫︀)
Proposition 2.6.42

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ be a covariant functor then

  • 𝐹 preserves split-monic, split-epic and iso morphisms.

If in addition 𝐹 is faithful then

  • 𝐹 reflects monic and epic morphisms.

and if 𝐹 is full and faithful then

  • 𝐹 reflects split-epic, split-monic and isomorphisms.

Similar statements apply when 𝐹 is contravariant.

Proof. The first statement is easy, for example if 𝑔𝑓=1𝑋 then 𝐹(𝑔)∘𝐹(𝑓)=1𝐹(𝑋).

Suppose 𝐹 is faithful, 𝐹(𝑓) is monic and 𝑓𝑔1=𝑓𝑔2. Then 𝐹(𝑓)𝐹(𝑔1)=𝐹(𝑓)𝐹(𝑔2)⟹𝐹(𝑔1)=𝐹(𝑔2) by assumption. As 𝐹 is faithful 𝑔1=𝑔2 as required. The other statement is similar.

Suppose 𝐹 is full and faithful and 𝐹(𝑓) is split-monic. Then ℎ𝐹(𝑓)=1𝐹(𝑋). As 𝐹 is full ℎ=𝐹(𝑔) and 1𝐹(𝑋)=𝐹(𝑔𝑓). As 𝐹 is faithful then 𝑔𝑓=1𝑋. the other statements are similar. ∎

Proposition 2.6.43

Let (𝒞︀,𝑈) be a concrete category (2.6.9) then

  • 𝑓 split-monic ⟹𝑓 injective ⟹𝑓 monic
  • 𝑓 split-epic ⟹𝑓 surjective ⟹𝑓 epic
  • 𝑓 isomorphism ⟹𝑓 bijective

Proof. Suppose 𝑓 is split-monic, then 𝑈(𝑓) is split-monic by (2.6.42) and so by (2.6.38) 𝑈(𝑓) is injective.

Suppose 𝑈(𝑓) injective, then by (2.6.38) 𝑈(𝑓) is monic. By (2.6.42) 𝑈 reflects monics and so 𝑓 is monic.

The other statements are similar. ∎

We can restate the criteria for split-epic/split-monic

Proposition 2.6.44

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism then

  • 𝑓 is split-monic if and only if Mor(𝑓,𝑍) is surjective for all 𝑍∈𝒞︀
  • 𝑓 is epic if and only if Mor(𝑓,𝑍) is injective for all 𝑍∈𝒞︀

dually

  • 𝑓 is split-epic if and only if Mor(𝑍,𝑓) is surjective for all 𝑍∈𝒞︀
  • 𝑓 is monic if and only if Mor(𝑍,𝑓) is injective for all 𝑍∈𝒞︀

Proof. 𝑓 is epic (resp. monic) iff Mor(𝑓,𝑍) (resp. Mor(𝑍,𝑓)) is injective precisely by the definitions.

Suppose 𝑓 is split-monic, then 𝑔𝑓=1𝑋⟹(ℎ𝑔)𝑓=ℎ for any ℎ. That is Mor(𝑓,𝑍) is surjective. Conversely if it’s surjective then let 𝑍=𝑋 and choose 𝑔 such that 𝑔𝑓=Mor(𝑓,𝑋)(𝑔)=1𝑋.

A similar statement follows dually for 𝑓 split-epic, and 𝑓 monic. ∎

Corollary 2.6.45 (Isomorphism Criteria)

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism then TFAE

  • 𝑓 is an isomorphism
  • Mor(𝑓,𝑍) is bijective for all 𝑍∈𝒞︀
  • Mor(𝑍,𝑓) is bijective for all 𝑍∈𝒞︀
Proof. This follows from combining (2.6.44) with (2.6.36). ∎
Definition 2.6.46 (Conservative)

We say a functor 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ is conservative if it reflects isomorphisms.

We say a concrete category (𝒞︀,𝑈) is conservative if the functor 𝑈:𝒞︀→𝐒𝐞𝐭 is conservative.

Proposition 2.6.47

Let (𝒞︀,𝑈) be a conservative concrete category which admits directed limits. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑈 preserves directed colimits
  2. 𝑈 reflects directed colimits

2.6.6 Pointed Categories

Definition 2.6.48 (Initial object)

An initial object of a category 𝒞︀ is an object ∅ such that for all objects 𝑋

Mor(∅,𝑋)={𝜂∅𝑋}

consists of a single element.

In this case an initial object is unique up to unique isomorphism (2.6.49).

Proposition 2.6.49 (Criteria to be Initial)

Let ∅ be an initial object and 𝑋∈𝒞︀. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑋 is an initial object
  2. there is an isomorphism 𝜙:𝑋→∼∅
  3. there exists a morphism 𝜙:𝑋→∅ and only one endomorphism 1𝑋:𝑋→𝑋

In this case the isomorphism is unique.

Proof. a) ⟹ c) by definition

c) ⟹ b) By assumption 𝜂∅𝑋∘𝜙=1𝑋, and by definition of initial 𝜙∘𝜂∅𝑋=1∅.

b) ⟹ a) We have a bijection

Mor(∅,𝑌)⟷Mor(𝑋,𝑌)𝑓→𝑓∘𝜙𝑔∘𝜙−1←𝑔

so as ∅ is initial, Mor(∅,𝑌) is a singleton for every 𝑌, hence so is Mor(𝑋,𝑌), that is 𝑋 is initial. This closes the cycle a) ⟹ c) ⟹ b) ⟹ a), so all three are equivalent.

Finally, since 𝑋 is then initial, Mor(𝑋,∅) is a singleton, so there is at most one morphism 𝑋→∅; in particular the isomorphism 𝜙 is unique. ∎

Definition 2.6.50 (Terminal Object)

A terminal object of a category 𝒞︀ is an object ⋆ such that for all objects 𝑋∈𝒞︀ we have

Mor(𝑋,⋆)={!𝑋}

is a singleton.

In this case a terminal object is unique up to unique isomorphism (2.6.51).

Proposition 2.6.51 (Criteria to be Terminal)

Let ⋆ be a terminal object and 𝑋∈𝒞︀. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑋 is a terminal object
  2. there is an isomorphism 𝜙:⋆→∼𝑋
  3. there exists a morphism 𝜙:⋆→𝑋 and only one endomorphism 1𝑋:𝑋→𝑋

In this case the isomorphism is unique.

Proof. By (2.6.4), Mor𝒞︀op(∅,𝑋)=Mor𝒞︀(𝑋,∅) for all 𝑋, so ⋆ is a terminal object of 𝒞︀ if and only if ⋆ is an initial object of 𝒞︀op; likewise a morphism ⋆→𝑋 (resp. isomorphism, resp. endomorphism of 𝑋) in 𝒞︀ is exactly a morphism 𝑋→⋆ (resp. isomorphism, resp. endomorphism of 𝑋) in 𝒞︀op. So applying (2.6.49) in 𝒞︀op, with ∅≔⋆, gives exactly the stated equivalence of a), b), c), together with the uniqueness of the isomorphism. ∎
Lemma 2.6.52 (Equivalences of Categories Preserve Terminal Objects)
Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ be an equivalence of categories, with 𝐺 and natural isomorphisms 𝜂:id𝒞︀⇒𝐺𝐹, 𝜖:𝐹𝐺⇒id𝒟︀ as in (2.6.25). Then 𝑇∈𝒞︀ is a terminal object of 𝒞︀ if and only if 𝐹(𝑇) is a terminal object of 𝒟︀.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Suppose 𝑇 is terminal. By (2.6.28), 𝐹 is full and faithful, so for every 𝐶∈𝒞︀ the map Mor(𝐶,𝑇)→Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐹(𝑇)), 𝑓↦𝐹(𝑓), is a bijection; as 𝑇 is terminal Mor(𝐶,𝑇) is a singleton, so Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐹(𝑇)) is too. Now let 𝑌∈𝒟︀ be arbitrary and set 𝐶≔𝐺(𝑌); the isomorphism 𝜖𝑌:𝐹(𝐶)→𝑌 gives a bijection Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐹(𝑇))→Mor(𝑌,𝐹(𝑇)), 𝑔↦𝑔∘𝜖𝑌−1, so combining with the above, Mor(𝑌,𝐹(𝑇)) is a singleton. As 𝑌∈𝒟︀ was arbitrary, 𝐹(𝑇) is terminal.

Conversely, 𝐺 is itself an equivalence of categories (with 𝐹, 𝜖−1:id𝒟︀⇒𝐹𝐺 and 𝜂−1:𝐺𝐹⇒id𝒞︀ playing the roles of 𝐹, 𝜂, 𝜖 in (2.6.25)), so if 𝐹(𝑇) is terminal then applying the above (with 𝐹,𝐺,𝑇 replaced by 𝐺,𝐹,𝐹(𝑇)) shows 𝐺𝐹(𝑇) is terminal; as 𝜂𝑇:𝑇→𝐺𝐹(𝑇) is an isomorphism, 𝑇 is then terminal too by (2.6.51). ∎

Definition 2.6.53 (Terminal Category)

The terminal category 𝟏 is the category with a single object ⋆ and a single morphism 1⋆.

For any category 𝒞︀ and object 𝑋∈𝒞︀, we write 𝑋:𝟏→𝒞︀ for the functor with 𝑋(⋆)=𝑋.

Definition 2.6.54 (Zero Object / Pointed Category)

A zero object of a category 𝒞︀ is both an initial and terminal object. We denote this by 𝟎 or 𝟎𝒞︀ when we need to emphasise the category 𝒞︀

For two objects 𝑋,𝑌∈𝒞︀ we denote by 0𝑋,𝑌 the composite morphism 𝑋→0→𝑌. This is independent of the choice of zero object.

A category with a zero object is pointed. A category 𝒞︀ is pointed iff 𝒞︀op is pointed. Further 𝟎𝒞︀=𝟎𝒞︀op.

Proposition 2.6.55

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category and 𝑋∈𝒞︀. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑋 is an initial object
  2. 𝑋 is a terminal object
  3. 𝑋 is a zero object
Proposition 2.6.56
Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category. Then the morphism 0→𝑋 is a monomorphism and the morphism 𝑌→0 is an epimorphism.
Proposition 2.6.57 (Functors Preserve Zeros)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ be a functor of pointed categories for which 𝐹(0𝒞︀) is a zero object of 𝒟︀. Then for all objects 𝑋,𝑌 we have

𝐹(0𝑋,𝑌)=0𝐹(𝑋),𝐹(𝑌)

2.6.7 Yoneda Lemma

The motivation for the following result becomes more clear in the next section. Roughly speaking properties of an object, 𝑋, are encoded in the functor Mor(𝑋,−).

Proposition 2.6.58 (Yoneda Lemma)

Suppose 𝑋,𝑋′∈𝒞︀ then there is a bijection between morphisms and natural transformation of functors

Mor(𝑋′,𝑋)⟶∼Nat(Mor(𝑋,−),Mor(𝑋′,−))𝑓⟶Mor(𝑓,−):(𝜙→𝜙∘𝑓)𝛼𝑋(1𝑋)⟵𝛼

Observe that under this correspondence

  • 𝑓=Mor(𝑓,𝑋)(1𝑋)
  • Mor(𝑓∘𝑔,−)=Mor(𝑔,−)∘Mor(𝑓,−)
  • 𝑓 is an isomorphism ⟺Mor(𝑓,−) is a natural isomorphism.

In the latter case Mor(𝑓,−)−1=Mor(𝑓−1,−)

In many cases the set of morphisms Mor(𝑋,𝑋′) has an additional structure (typically an abelian group or module). We encode this with the following definition

Definition 2.6.59 (Enriched Hom Functor)

Let (𝒮︀,𝑈) be a concrete category (2.6.9) for which 𝑈 reflects isomorphisms. We say a bifunctor

Hom:𝒞︀op×𝒞︀→𝒮︀

is an enriched hom functor if we have

  • 𝑈(Hom(𝑋,𝑌))=Mor(𝑋,𝑌)
  • 𝑈(Hom(𝑓,𝑌))=Mor(𝑓,𝑌)
  • 𝑈(Hom(𝑋,𝑔))=Mor(𝑋,𝑔)

and bijections

Write the inverse of 𝑓→Hom(𝑓,−) as 𝒴︀. Then for 𝛼∈Nat(Hom(𝑋,−),Hom(𝑋′,−))

  1. 𝛼 is a natural isomorphism ⟺𝑈𝛼 is a natural isomorphism ⟺𝒴︀(𝛼) is an isomorphism.
  2. 𝒴︀(𝛼)=𝑈(𝛼𝑋)(1𝑋)

Note the right hand arrow is always a bijection by Yoneda’s Lemma (2.6.58) and the diagram always commutes by assumption.

Proof. Suppose 𝛼 is a natural isomorphism then 𝑈𝛼−1∘𝑈𝛼=𝑈(1Hom(𝑋,−))=1Mor(𝑋,−) and similarly 𝑈𝛼∘𝑈𝛼−1=1Mor(𝑋′,−), so 𝑈𝛼 is a natural isomorphism. ∎

Note this trivially includes the usual case 𝒮︀=𝐒𝐞𝐭.

2.6.8 Representable Functors

Many algebraic constructions (e.g. tensor product) may be formalised in terms of “representable” functors (2.6.60). The usual definition involves the set-valued functor Mor(𝑋,−) as defined in (2.6.11).

As a generalisation follows we consider an enriched hom functor (2.6.59) Hom(−,−) taking values in the concrete category (𝒮︀,𝑈) where 𝑈 reflects isomorphisms. This clearly generalises the usual case.

Definition 2.6.60 (Representable Functor)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒮︀ a covariant functor. We say 𝐹 is representable if there is a pair (𝑋,Φ) where 𝑋∈𝒞︀ and Φ is a natural isomorphism

We say 𝐹 is represented by the pair (𝑋,Φ). Note this implies 𝑈∘𝐹 is represented by 𝑈Φ.

It is often useful to have another conception of representable functor in terms of universal properties as this is more intuitive for applications.

Definition 2.6.61 (Universal Element)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒮︀ be a covariant functor, then we say that a pair (𝑋,𝑖), where 𝑋∈𝒞︀,𝑖∈(𝑈∘𝐹)(𝑋), is a universal element for 𝐹 if for all 𝑌∈𝒞︀ there are bijections

Mor(𝑋,𝑌)⟶(𝑈∘𝐹)(𝑌)𝑓→(𝑈∘𝐹)(𝑓)(𝑖)

In this case we may also say 𝐹 is represented by the universal element (𝑋,𝑖).

We show the equivalence of the two notions by some abstract nonsense

Proposition 2.6.62 (Representable Set-Valued Functor = Universal Element)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝐒𝐞𝐭 be a covariant functor then there is a natural correspondence between representations and universal elements

{representations of 𝐹}⟷{universal elements of 𝐹}(𝑋,Φ)⟶(𝑋,Φ(1𝑋))(𝑋,𝑓→𝐹(𝑓)(𝑖))⟵(𝑋,𝑖)

The following may in particular be used to show that representations are unique up to isomorphism.

Proposition 2.6.63 (Morphisms Between Representations)

Suppose (𝑋,Φ) and (𝑋′,Φ′) represent the covariant functors 𝐹,𝐹′:𝒞︀op→𝒮︀ respectively. Then there are bijections

Mor(𝑋,𝑋′)⟶∼Nat(Hom(𝑋′,−),Hom(𝑋,−))⟶∼Nat(𝐹′(−),𝐹(−))𝑓→Hom(𝑓,−)→𝑓̂𝑈(𝜂𝑋′)(1𝑋′)←𝜂𝛼⋆←𝛼

where we define the mutual inverses

𝑓̂=Φ∘Hom(𝑓,−)∘(Φ′)−1𝛼⋆=𝑈(Φ𝑋′−1∘𝛼𝑋′∘Φ𝑋′′)(1𝑋′)

Note this has the following properties

  • 1𝑋̂=id𝐹
  • 𝑔∘𝑓̂=𝑓̂∘𝑔̂ where 𝑔:𝑋′→𝑋″ is morphism and (𝑋″,Φ″) represents 𝐹″
  • 𝑓 is an isomorphism ⟺𝑓̂ is a natural isomorphism and in this case 𝑓−1̂=𝑓̂−1.

Further 𝛼⋆∈Mor(𝑋,𝑋′) is the unique morphism such that the following diagram of natural transformations commutes

and satisfies

  • id𝐹⋆=1𝑋
  • (𝛽∘𝛼)⋆=𝛼⋆∘𝛽⋆
  • 𝛼⋆ is an isomorphism ⟺𝛼 is a natural isomorphism
Proof. The first bijection is simply the Yoneda Lemma and the second bijection is obvious. ∎
Corollary 2.6.64 (Representation is Unique)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒮︀ be a covariant functor which is represented by pairs (𝑋,Φ) and (𝑋′,Φ′). Then they are isomorphic with two-sided inverses

where 𝑖≔(𝑈Φ)(1𝑋) and 𝑖′≔(𝑈Φ′)(1𝑋′).

Proof. We may apply the previous result with 𝐹=𝐹′ and the identity natural transformation id𝐹. ∎

In practice we typically have a family of representations, and we want to show the construction is functorial

Definition 2.6.65 (Representable Bifunctor)

Let 𝐹:𝒟︀op×𝒞︀→𝒮︀ be a bifunctor. We say that it is representable by (𝐺,Φ) where 𝐺:𝒟︀→𝒞︀ is a functor, if Φ is a natural isomorphism of bifunctors

Φ:Hom(𝐺(−),−)⟹∼𝐹(−,−)

The following shows we only need to construct the representation pointwise.

Proposition 2.6.66

Let 𝐹:𝒟︀op×𝒞︀→𝒮︀ be a bifunctor such that 𝐹(𝐷,−) is representable for all 𝐷∈𝒟︀, by (𝐺(𝐷),Φ𝐷). Then 𝐺 can be made into a covariant functor uniquely such that Φ constitutes a natural isomorphism of bifunctors

Φ𝐷,𝐶:Hom(𝐺(𝐷),𝐶)⟹∼𝐹(𝐷,𝐶)

Explicitly for any morphism ℎ:𝐷→𝐷′ we have the identity

𝐺(ℎ)=Φ𝐷,𝐺(𝐷′)−1(Φ𝐷′,𝐺(𝐷′)(1𝐺(𝐷′))∘ℎ)

Proof. It is straightforward to verify that for any covariant functor 𝐺, the mapping Mor(𝐺(−),−) is a bifunctor (contravariant in the first “slot”).

Let ℎ:𝐷→𝐷′ be a morphism then by (2.6.21) 𝐹(ℎ,−):𝐹(𝐷′,−)→𝐹(𝐷,−) is a natural transformation. Therefore we may define

𝐺(ℎ)≔𝐹(ℎ,−)⋆

in the notation of (2.6.63); it is the unique morphism making the following diagram commute

Chasing 1𝐺(𝐷′) gives the identity for 𝐺(ℎ).

Furthermore by uniqueness 𝐺(ℎ∘𝑘)=𝐹(ℎ∘𝑘,−)⋆=(𝐹(𝑘,−)∘𝐹(ℎ,−))⋆=𝐹(ℎ,−)⋆∘𝐹(𝑘,−)⋆=𝐺(ℎ)∘𝐺(𝑘). We conclude by (2.6.22) that Φ is a natural transformation of bifunctors. ∎

Example 2.6.67 (Concrete Interpretation)

Let 𝒞︀, 𝒟︀ be concrete categories and consider the following bifunctor

𝐹:𝒟︀op×𝒞︀→𝐒𝐞𝐭𝐹(𝐷,𝐶)≔{𝜙:𝐷→𝐶|𝑃(𝜙)}

where 𝑃(−) is some predicate such that 𝑃(𝜙)⟹𝑃(𝑔∘𝜙∘𝑓). Then the universal element is simply an object 𝐺(𝐷)∈𝒞︀ together with a mapping

𝑖𝐷:𝐷→𝐺(𝐷)

satisfying 𝑃 such that there is a bijection

Mor(𝐺(𝐷),𝐶)⟷∼𝐹(𝐷,𝐶)≔{𝑓:𝐷→𝐶|𝑃(𝑓)}𝜙⟶𝜙∘𝑖𝐷

The functoriality of 𝐺 corresponds to a commutative diagram

where 𝐺(𝑓) is the unique morphism making the diagram commute.

Proposition 2.6.68 (Functorial Yoneda Lemma)

Let 𝐺,𝐺′:𝒟︀→𝒞︀ be functors. Then there is a bijection

Nat(𝐺(−),𝐺′(−))⟶∼Nat(Hom(𝐺′(−),−),Hom(𝐺(−),−))𝑓𝐷→Hom(𝑓𝐷,1𝐶)𝑈(𝜂𝐷,𝐺′(𝐷))(1𝐺′(𝐷))←𝜂𝐷,𝐶

We have the following properties

  • id𝐺̂=id
  • 𝑔∘𝑓̂=𝑓̂∘𝑔̂
  • 𝑓 is a natural isomorphism iff Hom(𝑓,−) is a natural isomorphism

Proof. In order to demonstrate that Hom(𝑓𝐷,1𝐶) is a natural transformation of bifunctors it’s enough by (2.6.21) to show the following diagram commutes for ℎ:𝐷′→𝐷

However 𝑓𝐷∘𝐺(ℎ)=𝐺′(ℎ)∘𝑓𝐷′ by definition of natural transformation, from which it follows immediately. The map is a pointwise bijection (for every 𝐷∈𝒟︀) with the inverse given by the usual Yoneda Lemma.

The first two properties are straightforward. From these it follows that if 𝑓 is a natural isomorphism then so is Hom(𝑓,−). Conversely if Hom(𝑓,−) is a natural isomorphism then it has a two-sided inverse which is of the form Hom(𝑔,−). It’s then straightforward to argue that 𝑔 is a two-sided inverse of 𝑓. ∎

2.6.9 Adjoint Functors

Some universal constructions may be expressed as an adjoint pair of functors. My view is the most illustrative are the module Tensor-Hom adjunction and the sheafification construction. Using this concept we can simplify the verification of universal properties by appealing to general criteria for adjoint functors as below.

Definition 2.6.69 (Adjoint Pair)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ and 𝐺:𝒟︀→𝒞︀ be functors. We say that 𝐹 is left adjoint to 𝐺 if there is a bijection

𝜓𝐶,𝐷:Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐷)⟶Mor(𝐶,𝐺(𝐷))

which is natural in 𝐶 and 𝐷 in the following sense. Let 𝛼:𝐶′→𝐶, 𝛽:𝐷→𝐷′, then for all 𝑓:𝐹(𝐶)→𝐷 we have

𝜓𝐶′,𝐷′(𝛽∘𝑓∘𝐹(𝛼))=𝐺(𝛽)∘𝜓𝐶,𝐷(𝑓)∘𝛼(1)

or equivalently for all 𝑔:𝐶→𝐺(𝐷)

𝛽∘𝜓𝐶,𝐷−1(𝑔)∘𝐹(𝛼)=𝜓𝐶′,𝐷′−1(𝐺(𝛽)∘𝑔∘𝛼)(2)

Equivalently 𝐹(−) represents the bifunctor Mor(−,𝐺(−)) (2.6.65).

Proposition 2.6.70 (Adjoint⇒unit, counit)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ and 𝐺:𝒟︀→𝒞︀ be adjoint functors with relationship

𝜓𝐶,𝐷:Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐷)⟶∼Mor(𝐶,𝐺(𝐷))

Then we have two natural transformations (unit and counit respectively)

𝜂:id𝒞︀⇒𝐺∘𝐹𝜖:𝐹∘𝐺⇒id𝒟︀

defined by

𝜂𝐶=𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶)(1𝐹(𝐶))𝜖𝐷=𝜓𝐺(𝐷),𝐷−1(1𝐺(𝐷))

Furthermore we may recover the adjoint relationship via

𝜓𝐶,𝐷(𝑓)=𝐺(𝑓)∘𝜂𝐶𝜓𝐶,𝐷−1(𝑔)=𝜖𝐷∘𝐹(𝑔)

Proof. We show that the transformations given are natural. Suppose 𝛼:𝐶→𝐶′ then

𝐺(𝐹(𝛼))∘𝜂𝐶=𝐺(𝐹(𝛼))∘𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶)(1𝐹(𝐶))=𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶′)(𝐹(𝛼)∘1𝐹(𝐶))(1)=𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶′)(1𝐹(𝐶′)∘𝐹(𝛼))=𝜓𝐶′,𝐹(𝐶′)(1𝐹(𝐶′))∘𝛼(1)=𝜂𝐶′∘𝛼

so 𝜂 is a natural transformation. Furthermore

𝜓𝐶,𝐷(𝑓)=𝜓𝐶,𝐷(𝑓∘1𝐹(𝐶))=𝐺(𝑓)∘𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶)(1)=𝐺(𝑓)∘𝜂𝐶

as required. Similarly for 𝛽:𝐷→𝐷′

𝛽∘𝜖𝐷=𝛽∘𝜓𝐺(𝐷),𝐷−1(1𝐺(𝐷))=𝜓𝐺(𝐷),𝐷′−1(𝐺(𝛽)∘1𝐺(𝐷))(2)=𝜓𝐺(𝐷),𝐷′−1(1𝐺(𝐷′)∘𝐺(𝛽))=𝜓𝐺(𝐷′),𝐷′−1(1𝐺(𝐷′))∘𝐹(𝐺(𝛽))(2)=𝜖𝐷′∘𝐹(𝐺(𝛽))

 ∎

Given two natural transformations we may recover a corresponding adjoint

Proposition 2.6.71 (Adjoint from unit and counit)

Let 𝐹:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ and 𝐺:𝒟︀→𝒞︀ be functors with two natural transformations

𝜂:id𝒞︀⇒𝐺∘𝐹𝜖:𝐹∘𝐺⇒id𝒟︀

Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝐹 is left adjoint to 𝐺 with unit and counit 𝜂, 𝜖, and

  2. the so-called triangular identities are satisfied

    1𝐺(𝐷):𝐺(𝐷)⟶𝜂𝐺(𝐷)𝐺𝐹𝐺(𝐷)⟶𝐺(𝜖𝐷)𝐺(𝐷)1𝐹(𝐶):𝐹(𝐶)⟶𝐹(𝜂𝐶)𝐹𝐺𝐹(𝐶)⟶𝜖𝐹(𝐶)𝐹(𝐶)

More precisely the adjunction is given by

Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐷)⇌𝜙𝜓Mor(𝐶,𝐺(𝐷))𝑓⟶𝐺(𝑓)∘𝜂𝐶𝜖𝐷∘𝐹(𝑔)⟵𝑔

Proof. Let 𝜓,𝜙 denote the proposed adjunction maps. We will use the triangular identities to show that these are mutually inverse. First observe by naturality of 𝜂 and 𝜖 that

𝜓𝜙(𝑔)=𝐺(𝜖𝐷∘𝐹(𝑔))∘𝜂𝐶=𝐺(𝜖𝐷)∘𝜂𝐺(𝐷)∘𝑔(3)𝜙𝜓(𝑓)=𝜖𝐷∘𝐹(𝐺(𝑓)∘𝜂𝐶)=𝑓∘𝜖𝐹(𝐶)∘𝐹(𝜂𝐶)

It’s then immediate that these are mutually inverse maps if and only if the triangular identities are satisfied (one way is obvious, the other way consider 𝑓=1𝐹(𝐶) and 𝑔=1𝐺(𝐷)).

Further one may easily verify that 𝜓,𝜙 so-defined are natural in 𝐶 and 𝐷

𝜓(𝛽∘𝑓∘𝐹(𝛼))=𝐺(𝛽)∘𝐺(𝑓)∘𝐺𝐹(𝛼)∘𝜂𝐶=𝐺(𝛽)∘𝐺(𝑓)∘𝜂𝐶′∘𝛼=𝐺(𝛽)∘𝜓(𝑓)∘𝛼

 ∎

Proposition 2.6.72 (Criteria for right adjoint to be full and faithful)

Let 𝒞︀⇌𝐺𝐹𝒟︀ be adjoint functors with 𝜂,𝜖 unit and counit transformations. Then

  • 𝐺 is faithful if and only if 𝜖 is pointwise epic
  • 𝐺 is full if and only if 𝜖 is pointwise split-monic
  • 𝐺 is full and faithful if and only if 𝜖 is a pointwise isomorphism

Proof. Consider the composite map

Mor(𝐷′,𝐷)⟶Mor(𝜖𝐷′,𝐷)Mor(𝐹(𝐺(𝐷′)),𝐷)→𝜓𝐺(𝐷′),𝐷Mor(𝐺(𝐷′),𝐺(𝐷))

which is natural in 𝐷 and 𝐷′. Note that image of 𝛼∈Mor(𝐷′,𝐷) is

𝜓𝐺(𝐷′),𝐷(𝛼∘𝜖𝐷′)=𝐺(𝛼)∘𝜓𝐺(𝐷′),𝐷′(𝜖𝐷′)=𝐺(𝛼)

so the composite is just 𝐺(−). The second map is bijective by the adjoint assumption. Therefore the first map is injective (resp. surjective) if and only if 𝐺 is faithful (resp. full).

By (2.6.44) Mor(𝜖𝐷′,𝐷) is injective (resp. surjective) for all 𝐷,𝐷′ if and only if 𝜖𝐷′ is epic (resp. split-monic) for all 𝐷′.

Then the first two statements follow easily. The last statement follows from the previous two, combined with (2.6.36). ∎

Proposition 2.6.73 (Reflective Sub-Category)

Let 𝒞︀⇌𝐺𝐹𝒟︀ be adjoint functors such that 𝐺 is fully faithful. Then for 𝐶∈𝒞︀ we have 𝜂𝐶 is an isomorphism iff 𝐶 is in the essential image of 𝐺 (i.e. is isomorphic to 𝐺(𝐷) for some 𝐷).

In particular let 𝒞︀′ denote the essential image of 𝒟︀ under 𝐺. Then this restricts to an equivalence of categories 𝒞︀′⇌𝐺𝐹𝒟︀

Proof. If 𝜂𝐶:𝐶→𝐺𝐹(𝐶) is an isomorphism define 𝐷≔𝐹(𝐶), and we are done.

Conversely we first show that 𝜂𝐺(𝐷) is an isomorphism. By the triangular identities (2.6.71) we have

𝐺(𝜖𝐷)∘𝜂𝐺(𝐷)=1𝐺(𝐷)

so 𝜂𝐺(𝐷) has a left inverse. Recall by (2.6.72) 𝜖𝐷 is an isomorphism, whence so is 𝐺(𝜖𝐷) (2.6.42). Therefore we may show directly that it is also a right inverse, and therefore 𝜂𝐺(𝐷) is an isomorphism.

Now assume that we have an isomorphism 𝜓:𝐶→∼𝐺(𝐷) for some 𝐷∈𝒟︀. Then by naturality we have a commutative diagram

observing that 𝐺𝐹(𝜓) is also an isomorphism. Then we conclude 𝜂𝐶 is an isomorphism as required. ∎

The following criteria will be useful

Proposition 2.6.74 (Adjoints can be constructed pointwise)

Let 𝐺:𝒟︀→𝒞︀ be a functor. Suppose that for all 𝐶∈ob(𝒞︀) there exists 𝐹(𝐶)∈ob(𝒟︀) such that there is a bijection natural in 𝐷

𝜓𝐶,𝐷:Mor(𝐹(𝐶),𝐷)→∼Mor(𝐶,𝐺(𝐷))

Then there exists a unique functor 𝐹 which ensures this is natural in 𝐶, more precisely for 𝑔:𝐶→𝐶′ this is given by

𝐹(𝑔)=𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶′)−1(𝜂𝐶′∘𝑔)𝜂𝐶≔𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶)(1𝐹(𝐶))

This is also the unique functor which ensures 𝜂𝐶 is a natural transformation.

Proof. The hypothesis is precisely that, for each 𝐶∈𝒞︀, (𝐹(𝐶),𝜓𝐶,−) represents the functor Mor(𝐶,𝐺(−)):𝒟︀→𝒮︀; equivalently, this is the hypothesis of (2.6.66) applied to the (already well-defined, since 𝐺 is a functor) bifunctor Mor(−,𝐺(−)):𝒞︀op×𝒟︀→𝒮︀, with the roles of the two categories there swapped so that 𝐹(𝐶) plays the role of the representing object varying over 𝒞︀. That proposition’s conclusion is precisely that 𝐹 can be made into a functor uniquely such that 𝜓 is a natural isomorphism of bifunctors, giving the first uniqueness; its explicit formula for 𝑔:𝐶→𝐶′ reads

𝐹(𝑔)=𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶′)−1(𝜓𝐶′,𝐹(𝐶′)(1𝐹(𝐶′))∘𝑔)=𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶′)−1(𝜂𝐶′∘𝑔)

using the definition of 𝜂𝐶′ for the second equality.

We have already shown that if 𝜓𝐶,𝐷 is natural in 𝐶 then 𝜂𝐶 is a natural transformation (2.6.70). Conversely suppose that 𝜂𝐶 is a natural transformation. Since we have assumed that 𝜓𝐶,𝐷 is natural in 𝐷, applying this to 𝛽≔𝐹(𝑔) and 𝑓≔1𝐹(𝐶) gives

𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶′)(𝐹(𝑔))=𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶′)(𝐹(𝑔)∘1𝐹(𝐶))=𝐺(𝐹(𝑔))∘𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶)(1𝐹(𝐶))=𝐺𝐹(𝑔)∘𝜂𝐶=𝜂𝐶′∘𝑔

using naturality of 𝜂 for the last equality, whence 𝐹(𝑔)=𝜓𝐶,𝐹(𝐶′)−1(𝜂𝐶′∘𝑔). ∎

Proposition 2.6.75

Let 𝒞︀⇌𝐺𝐹𝒟︀ be a pair of adjoint functors. Then 𝐹 preserves initial objects and 𝐺 preserves terminal objects.

If 𝒞︀,𝒟︀ are pointed categories then 𝐹 and 𝐺 also preserve zero objects and zero morphisms.

Proof. We only prove that 𝐹 preserves initial objects, as the second statement follows dually. By hypothesis there is a bijection natural in 𝐷

Mor(𝐹(∅),𝐷)⟶∼Mor(∅,𝐺(𝐷))

Therefore if ∅ is initial, then so is 𝐹(∅).

The last statement follows from (2.6.55) and (2.6.57). ∎

2.6.10 Limits

Definition 2.6.76
A functor 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ where 𝐼 is a small category is referred to as a diagram
Definition 2.6.77 (Cones)

Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram. We say that the pair (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖:𝐿→𝐹(𝑖)}𝑖∈𝐼) is a cone over 𝐹 if

𝐹(𝛼)∘𝜆𝑖=𝜆𝑗for all morphisms𝛼:𝑖→𝑗

The cones for 𝐹 constitute a cone category (Δ↓𝐹) where a morphism 𝛼:(𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼)→(𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) is just a morphism 𝛼:𝐿→𝐿′ such that 𝜆𝑖′∘𝛼=𝜆𝑖 for all 𝑖∈𝐼

Definition 2.6.78 (Small Limit)

Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram. A cone (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) over 𝐹 is a limit for 𝐹 if it is a terminal object (2.6.50) in the cone category.

Explicitly for every cone (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) there is a unique morphism 𝛼:𝐿′→𝐿 such that 𝜆𝑖∘𝛼=𝜆𝑖′.

We may denote this as lim𝐹.

Proposition 2.6.79

Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram, (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) a limit of 𝐹 and (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) a cone. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝐿′ is a limit for 𝐹
  2. there is an isomorphism of cones 𝐿′→∼𝐿
  3. there is a morphism of cones 𝐿′→𝐿 and precisely one (cone) endomorphism of 𝐿′.

In this case the (cone) isomorphism is the unique cone morphism.

Proof. By definition (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a terminal object of the cone category (Δ↓𝐹), so this is precisely (2.6.51) applied with ⋆≔(𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) and 𝑋≔(𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼). ∎
Proposition 2.6.80 (Uniqueness of Limits)
Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram and (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) and (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) limits of 𝐹. Then there is a unique morphism 𝜓:𝐿→𝐿′ satisfying 𝜆𝑖′∘𝜓=𝜆𝑖, which is an isomorphism.
Proof. Since (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) is a limit for 𝐹, (2.6.79) gives a unique isomorphism of cones 𝜓:𝐿→𝐿′, that is, a unique isomorphism 𝜓 with 𝜆𝑖′∘𝜓=𝜆𝑖 for all 𝑖∈𝐼. ∎
Proposition 2.6.81 (Product)

Let 𝐼 be a discrete small category and {𝑋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 be a family of objects in 𝒞︀. Then there is a unique functor 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ such that 𝐹(𝑖)=𝑋𝑖.

Consider an object 𝑋∈𝒞︀ and family of morphisms 𝜋𝑖:𝑋→𝑋𝑖, then the following are equivalent

  1. The cone (𝑋,{𝜋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a limit for 𝐹
  2. For any family of morphisms 𝜆𝑖:𝑋′→𝑋𝑖 there exists a unique 𝜆:𝑋′→𝑋 such that 𝜋𝑖∘𝜆=𝜆𝑖

  3. For all objects 𝑋′ the map

    Φ:Mor(𝑋′,𝑋)⟶∏𝑖∈𝐼Mor(𝑋′,𝑋𝑖)𝑓→𝜋𝑖∘𝑓

    is a bijection, i.e. (𝑋,Φ) represents the contravariant functor ∏𝑖∈𝐼Mor(−,𝑋𝑗).

In this case we say that (𝑋,{𝜋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a product for {𝑋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 and denote this by ∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖.

For any family of morphisms 𝜆𝑖:𝑋′→𝑋𝑖 we write the induced morphism 𝜆:𝑋′→∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 as (𝜆𝑖)𝑖∈𝐼.

Proposition 2.6.82 (Functoriality of Product)

Let 𝐼 be a discrete small category and suppose that 𝒞︀ has 𝐼-shaped limits. Then we may define a map on objects

∏𝑖∈𝐼(−):𝒞︀𝐼→𝒞︀

Recall that a morphism ∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖→∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 in 𝒞︀𝐼 is simply a family of morphisms (𝑓𝑖:𝑋𝑖→𝑌𝑖)𝑖∈𝐼 in 𝒞︀. Then we define

∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑓𝑖≔(𝑓𝑖∘𝜋𝑖)𝑖∈𝐼

which is the unique morphism satisfying

𝜋𝑖∘∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑓𝑖=𝑓𝑖∘𝜋𝑖

This makes ∏𝑖∈𝐼(−) into a functor.

Proposition 2.6.83 (Products of Monomorphisms)
Let 𝐼 be a discrete small category and {𝑓𝑖:𝑋𝑖→𝑌𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 a family of monomorphisms such that ∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 and ∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 exist. Then ∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑓𝑖:∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖→∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 is a monomorphism.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Suppose 𝑎,𝑏:𝑍→∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 satisfy (∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑓𝑖)∘𝑎=(∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑓𝑖)∘𝑏. For each 𝑖∈𝐼, composing with the projection 𝜋𝑖:∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖→𝑌𝑖 and using 𝜋𝑖∘∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑓𝑖=𝑓𝑖∘𝜋𝑖 gives

𝑓𝑖∘(𝜋𝑖∘𝑎)=𝑓𝑖∘(𝜋𝑖∘𝑏)

and since 𝑓𝑖 is monic, 𝜋𝑖∘𝑎=𝜋𝑖∘𝑏. As this holds for every 𝑖∈𝐼, by the uniqueness clause of the universal property of the product ∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 (2.6.81) we conclude 𝑎=𝑏. ∎

Proposition 2.6.84 (Functoriality of Binary Product)

Let 𝑋,𝑋′,𝑌,𝑌′∈𝒞︀ be such that 𝑋×𝑌 and 𝑋′×𝑌′ exists. For 𝑓:𝑋→𝑋′ and 𝑔:𝑌→𝑌′ there exists a unique morphism

𝑓×𝑔:𝑋×𝑌→𝑋′×𝑌′

such that

𝜋𝑋′∘(𝑓×𝑔)=𝑓∘𝜋𝑋

and

𝜋𝑌′∘(𝑓×𝑔)=𝑔∘𝜋𝑌

If 𝒞︀ has all binary products then this determines a bifunctor

×:𝒞︀×𝒞︀→𝒞︀
Proposition 2.6.85 (Limits exist in Set)

Limits exist in 𝐒𝐞𝐭 more precisely for a diagram 𝐹:𝐼→𝐒𝐞𝐭

lim𝐹={(𝑥𝑖)𝑖∈𝐼∈∏𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)|𝐹(𝛼)(𝑥𝑖)=𝑥𝑗for all𝛼:𝑖→𝑗}
Definition 2.6.86

Let 𝑈:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ be a functor and 𝐼 a small category.

We say that 𝑈 creates limits of shape 𝐼 if for all diagrams 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ such that lim𝑈∘𝐹 exists then lim𝐹 exists and is the unique cone such that 𝑈(lim𝐹)=lim(𝑈∘𝐹).

We say that 𝑈 preserves limits of shape 𝐼 if whenever lim𝐹 exists in 𝒞︀ we have lim𝑈∘𝐹 exists in 𝒟︀ and is equal to 𝑈(lim𝐹).

If we restrict to the case 𝐼 is discrete (resp. 𝐼=𝟐) then we say that 𝑈 creates/preserves products (resp. equalisers).

Proposition 2.6.87 (Creates⇒Preserves)

Let 𝑈:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ which creates limits of shape 𝐼 and 𝒟︀ has all limits of shape 𝐼. Then 𝑈 preserves limits of shape 𝐼.

In particular this holds unconditionally for 𝒟︀=𝐒𝐞𝐭 since this has all limits.

2.6.11 Colimit

Definition 2.6.88 (Co-cones)

Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram. We say that the pair (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖:𝐹(𝑖)→𝐿}𝑖∈𝐼) is a co-cone over 𝐹 if

𝜆𝑗∘𝐹(𝛼)=𝜆𝑖for all morphisms𝛼:𝑖→𝑗

The cones for 𝐹 constitute a co-cone category (𝐹↓Δ) where a morphism 𝛼:(𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼)→(𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) is just a morphism 𝛼:𝐿→𝐿′ such that 𝛼∘𝜆𝑖=𝜆𝑖′ for all 𝑖∈𝐼

Definition 2.6.89 (Small Colimit)

Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram. A co-cone (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) over 𝐹 is a colimit for 𝐹 if it is an initial object (2.6.48) in the co-cone category.

Explicitly for every co-cone (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) there is a unique morphism 𝛼:𝐿→𝐿′ such that 𝜆𝑖′∘𝛼=𝜆𝑖.

We may denote this as colim𝐹.

Proposition 2.6.90

Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram, (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) a colimit of 𝐹 and (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) a co-cone. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝐿′ is a colimit for 𝐹
  2. there is an isomorphism of co-cones 𝐿′→∼𝐿
  3. there is a morphism of co-cones 𝐿′→𝐿 and precisely one (co-cone) endomorphism of 𝐿′.

In this case the (co-cone) isomorphism is unique.

Proof. By definition (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is an initial object of the co-cone category (𝐹↓Δ), so this is precisely (2.6.49) applied with ∅≔(𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) and 𝑋≔(𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼). ∎
Proposition 2.6.91 (Uniqueness of Colimits)
Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram and (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) and (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) colimits of 𝐹. Then there is a unique morphism 𝜓:𝐿→𝐿′ satisfying 𝜓∘𝜆𝑖=𝜆𝑖′, which is an isomorphism.
Proof. Since (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) is a colimit for 𝐹, (2.6.90) gives a unique isomorphism of co-cones 𝜙:𝐿′→𝐿, that is, a unique isomorphism 𝜙 with 𝜙∘𝜆𝑖′=𝜆𝑖. Setting 𝜓≔𝜙−1:𝐿→𝐿′ gives the required unique isomorphism with 𝜓∘𝜆𝑖=𝜆𝑖′. ∎
Proposition 2.6.92 (Limits and Colimits swap under 𝒞︀op)

Let 𝐼 be a small category and 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ a diagram. Write 𝐹op:𝐼op→𝒞︀op for the diagram with 𝐹op(𝑖)≔𝐹(𝑖) on objects and 𝐹op(𝛼op)≔𝐹(𝛼)op for 𝛼op:𝑗→𝑖 the morphism of 𝐼op corresponding to 𝛼:𝑖→𝑗 of 𝐼. Then, regarding each 𝜆𝑖:𝐿→𝐹(𝑖) as a morphism 𝜆𝑖op:𝐹(𝑖)→𝐿 of 𝒞︀op, (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a limit for 𝐹 in 𝒞︀ if and only if (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖op}𝑖∈𝐼) is a colimit for 𝐹op in 𝒞︀op.

Dually, (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a colimit for 𝐹 in 𝒞︀ if and only if (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖op}𝑖∈𝐼) is a limit for 𝐹op in 𝒞︀op.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

We only prove the first statement, the second following by applying it to 𝒞︀op in place of 𝒞︀, using (𝒞︀op)op=𝒞︀.

Define Σ:(Δ↓𝐹)→(𝐹op↓Δ)op, (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼)↦(𝐿,{𝜆𝑖op}𝑖∈𝐼), acting on a cone morphism 𝜇:(𝐿,𝜆)→(𝐿′,𝜆′) (i.e. 𝜇:𝐿→𝐿′ with 𝜆𝑖′∘𝜇=𝜆𝑖 for all 𝑖) by Σ(𝜇)≔𝜇op. This is well-defined: upon reversing every arrow (using Mor𝒞︀op(𝑋,𝑌)=Mor𝒞︀(𝑌,𝑋) and that composition in 𝒞︀op reverses that of 𝒞︀ (2.6.4)), the cone condition 𝐹(𝛼)∘𝜆𝑖=𝜆𝑗 for 𝛼:𝑖→𝑗 of 𝐼 becomes exactly the co-cone condition 𝜆𝑖op∘𝐹op(𝛼op)=𝜆𝑗op for 𝛼op:𝑗→𝑖 of 𝐼op, so {𝜆𝑖op} is a co-cone over 𝐹op; and the cone morphism condition 𝜆𝑖′∘𝜇=𝜆𝑖 becomes 𝜇op∘(𝜆𝑖′)op=𝜆𝑖op, so 𝜇op is a morphism (𝐿′,𝜆′op)→(𝐿,𝜆op) of (𝐹op↓Δ), that is, a morphism (𝐿,𝜆op)→(𝐿′,𝜆′op) of (𝐹op↓Δ)op. Thus Σ is well-defined, and is manifestly functorial.

Dually define Σ−1:(𝐹op↓Δ)op→(Δ↓𝐹), (𝐿,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼)↦(𝐿,{𝜇𝑖op}𝑖∈𝐼), acting on morphisms by 𝜈↦𝜈op. Since (−)op is an involution on morphisms, Σ−1Σ=1 and ΣΣ−1=1, so Σ is an isomorphism of categories, in particular an equivalence of categories (2.6.25).

By (2.6.4), a category 𝒟︀ has 𝑇 as a terminal object if and only if 𝒟︀op has 𝑇 as an initial object (since Mor𝒟︀op(𝑋,𝑇)=Mor𝒟︀(𝑇,𝑋) for all 𝑋). So (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}) is a limit for 𝐹, i.e. terminal in (Δ↓𝐹) (2.6.78), iff, by (2.6.52), Σ(𝐿,{𝜆𝑖})=(𝐿,{𝜆𝑖op}) is terminal in (𝐹op↓Δ)op, iff (applying the noted equivalence to 𝒟︀≔(𝐹op↓Δ)) (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖op}) is initial in (𝐹op↓Δ), that is, a colimit for 𝐹op (2.6.89). ∎

Proposition 2.6.93 (Co-product)

Let 𝐼 be a discrete small category and {𝑋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 be a family of objects in 𝒞︀. Then there is a unique functor 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ such that 𝐹(𝑖)=𝑋𝑖.

Consider an object 𝑋∈𝒞︀ and family of morphisms 𝑠𝑖:𝑋𝑖→𝑋, then the following are equivalent

  1. The co-cone (𝑋,{𝑠𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a colimit for 𝐹
  2. For any family of morphisms 𝜆𝑖:𝑋𝑖→𝑋′ there exists a unique 𝜆:𝑋→𝑋′ such that 𝜆∘𝑠𝑖=𝜆𝑖

  3. For all objects 𝑋′ the map

    Φ:Mor(𝑋,𝑋′)⟶∏𝑖∈𝐼Mor(𝑋𝑖,𝑋′)𝜆→(𝜆∘𝑠𝑖)𝑖∈𝐼

    is a bijection, i.e. (𝑋,Φ) represents the covariant functor ∏𝑖∈𝐼Mor(𝑋𝑖,−).

In this case we say that (𝑋,{𝑠𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a co-product for {𝑋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 and denote this by ∐𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖.

For any family of morphisms 𝜆𝑖:𝑋𝑖→𝑋′ we write the induced morphism 𝜆:∐𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖→𝑋′ as [𝜆𝑖]𝑖∈𝐼.

Definition 2.6.94

Let 𝑈:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ be a functor and 𝐼 a small category.

We say that 𝑈 creates co-limits of shape 𝐼 if for all diagrams 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ such that lim𝑈∘𝐹 exists then colim𝐹 exists and is the unique cone such that 𝑈(colim𝐹)=colim(𝑈∘𝐹).

We say that 𝑈 preserves co-limits of shape 𝐼 if whenever colim𝐹 exists in 𝒞︀ we have colim𝑈∘𝐹 exists in 𝒟︀ and is equal to 𝑈(colim𝐹).

If we restrict to the case 𝐼 is discrete (resp. 𝐼=𝟐) then we say that 𝑈 creates/preserves coproducts (resp. co-equalisers).

Proposition 2.6.95 (Creates⇒Preserves)

Let 𝑈:𝒞︀→𝒟︀ which creates colimits of shape 𝐼 and 𝒟︀ has all colimits of shape 𝐼. Then 𝑈 preserves colimits of shape 𝐼.

In particular this holds unconditionally for 𝒟︀=𝐒𝐞𝐭 since this has all colimits.

2.6.12 Functorial Limits

Having fixed a single diagram at a time so far, we now let the diagram vary. By (2.6.96), taking the limit in one variable of a bifunctor is functorial in the other – so a family of limits indexed by 𝒞︀ assembles into a genuine functor 𝒞︀→ℰ︀. Specialising this to the evaluation bifunctor recovers the more familiar statement, (2.6.97): the limit lim𝐽(−) is itself a functor out of (a subcategory of) the functor category 𝒞︀𝐽, so a natural transformation of diagrams induces a morphism of their limits, compatibly with composition and identities – and in particular carries isomorphisms of diagrams to isomorphisms of limits. We also record that limits are invariant under isomorphism of the indexing category, that a limit over a product of two index categories may be computed either simultaneously or iteratively one variable at a time (2.6.99), with the two iterated orders agreeing whenever both make sense (2.6.100), and dual statements for colimits, together with a comparison morphism relating a colimit of limits to a limit of colimits, which need not be an isomorphism in general.

Proposition 2.6.96 (Pointwise Limits are Functorial)

Let 𝐽 be a small category and 𝐹:𝒞︀×𝐽→ℰ︀ a bifunctor.

Suppose that for every 𝑋∈𝒞︀ there is a limit (lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(𝑋,𝑗),{𝜆𝑋,𝑗}𝑗∈𝐽) for 𝐹(𝑋,−).

Then lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(−,𝑗) is functorial in the sense there is a unique morphism making the following diagram commute

for all 𝑓:𝑋→𝑋′ and 𝛽:𝑗→𝑗′.

Therefore this determines a functor lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(−,𝑗):𝒞︀→ℰ︀.

Proof. Recall that (lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(𝑋,𝑗),{𝜆𝑋,𝑗}𝑗∈𝐽) is a terminal object in the category of cones (Δ↓𝐹(𝑋,−)). Suppose 𝑓:𝑋→𝑋′ is a morphism. Since 𝐹 is a bifunctor (2.6.19), for every 𝛽:𝑗→𝑗′ in 𝐽

𝐹(𝑋′,𝛽)∘𝐹(𝑓,1𝑗)∘𝜆𝑋,𝑗=𝐹(𝑓,𝛽)∘𝜆𝑋,𝑗=𝐹(𝑓,1𝑗′)∘𝐹(𝑋,𝛽)∘𝜆𝑋,𝑗=𝐹(𝑓,1𝑗′)∘𝜆𝑋,𝑗′

so (lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(𝑋,𝑗),{𝐹(𝑓,1𝑗)∘𝜆𝑋,𝑗}𝑗∈𝐽) is a cone over 𝐹(𝑋′,−).

Therefore there is a unique morphism ℎ:lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(𝑋,𝑗)→lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(𝑋′,𝑗) into the terminal object of (Δ↓𝐹(𝑋′,−)) with 𝜆𝑋′,𝑗∘ℎ=𝐹(𝑓,1𝑗)∘𝜆𝑋,𝑗 for every 𝑗∈𝐽. For general 𝛽:𝑗→𝑗′, the target cone condition and the bifunctoriality identity above give

𝜆𝑋′,𝑗′∘ℎ=𝐹(𝑋′,𝛽)∘𝜆𝑋′,𝑗∘ℎ=𝐹(𝑋′,𝛽)∘𝐹(𝑓,1𝑗)∘𝜆𝑋,𝑗=𝐹(𝑓,𝛽)∘𝜆𝑋,𝑗

as required.

Writing lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(𝑓,𝑗)≔ℎ, the identity and composition laws needed for functoriality of lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(−,𝑗) follow directly from this uniqueness: for 𝑓=1𝑋, ℎ=1lim𝑗𝐹(𝑋,𝑗) has the defining property of lim𝑗𝐹(1𝑋,𝑗), so equals it by uniqueness; and for 𝑓:𝑋→𝑋′, 𝑓′:𝑋′→𝑋″, the morphism lim𝑗𝐹(𝑓′,𝑗)∘lim𝑗𝐹(𝑓,𝑗) satisfies the same defining property (compatibility with the 𝜆𝑋″,𝑗) as lim𝑗𝐹(𝑓′𝑓,𝑗), so the two agree by uniqueness (this is the same pattern used for image factorisations, see later). ∎

Corollary 2.6.97 (Limits are Functorial in the Diagram)

Let 𝐽 be a small category and 𝒞︀ a category, and let 𝒞︀lim𝐽 be the full subcategory of the functor category 𝒞︀𝐽 (2.6.14) spanned by those diagrams 𝐷:𝐽→𝒞︀ for which lim𝐽𝐷 exists. Then

lim𝐽(−):𝒞︀lim𝐽→𝒞︀,𝐷↦lim𝐽𝐷

is a functor. Consequently, a natural transformation 𝜂:𝐷⇒𝐷′ of 𝒞︀lim𝐽 induces lim𝐽𝜂:lim𝐽𝐷→lim𝐽𝐷′, satisfying the composition and identity laws of a functor; and if 𝜂 is a natural isomorphism, lim𝐽𝜂 is an isomorphism, with inverse lim𝐽(𝜂−1).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Define the evaluation bifunctor ev:𝒞︀lim𝐽×𝐽→𝒞︀ by ev(𝐷,𝑗)≔𝐷(𝑗) on objects and, for a morphism (𝜂,𝛽):(𝐷,𝑗)→(𝐷′,𝑗′) of 𝒞︀lim𝐽×𝐽 (so 𝜂:𝐷⇒𝐷′ a natural transformation and 𝛽:𝑗→𝑗′ in 𝐽), ev(𝜂,𝛽)≔𝐷′(𝛽)∘𝜂𝑗 (=𝜂𝑗′∘𝐷(𝛽), by naturality of 𝜂 at 𝛽). This preserves identities (ev(1𝐷,1𝑗)=𝐷(1𝑗)∘(1𝐷)𝑗=1𝐷(𝑗)) and composition: for a further morphism (𝜂′,𝛽′):(𝐷′,𝑗′)→(𝐷″,𝑗″),

ev(𝜂′,𝛽′)∘ev(𝜂,𝛽)=𝐷″(𝛽′)∘𝜂𝑗′′∘𝐷′(𝛽)∘𝜂𝑗=𝐷″(𝛽′)∘𝐷″(𝛽)∘𝜂𝑗′∘𝜂𝑗=ev((𝜂′𝜂,𝛽′𝛽)),

using naturality of 𝜂′ at 𝛽 (i.e. 𝜂𝑗′′∘𝐷′(𝛽)=𝐷″(𝛽)∘𝜂𝑗′) and functoriality of 𝐷″; so ev is a bifunctor.

By definition of 𝒞︀lim𝐽, lim𝑗∈𝐽ev(𝐷,𝑗)=lim𝐽𝐷 exists for every 𝐷∈𝒞︀lim𝐽, so (2.6.96) applies to ev (with 𝒞︀lim𝐽 in the role of the first factor), giving that lim𝑗∈𝐽ev(−,𝑗)=lim𝐽(−):𝒞︀lim𝐽→𝒞︀ is a functor, with lim𝐽𝜂 its action on a morphism 𝜂, satisfying the composition and identity laws by functoriality. If 𝜂 is a natural isomorphism, i.e. an isomorphism of 𝒞︀lim𝐽, then lim𝐽𝜂 is an isomorphism with inverse lim𝐽(𝜂−1) by (2.6.42). ∎

Proposition 2.6.98 (Limits are Invariant under Isomorphism of the Indexing Category)
Let 𝜎:𝐽→𝐼 be an isomorphism of categories with inverse 𝜎−1, and 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ a diagram. Then (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a limit for 𝐹 if and only if (𝐿,{𝜆𝜎(𝑗)}𝑗∈𝐽) is a limit for 𝐹𝜎:𝐽→𝒞︀.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Define Σ:(Δ↓𝐹)→(Δ↓𝐹𝜎), (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼)↦(𝐿,{𝜆𝜎(𝑗)}𝑗∈𝐽), acting as the identity on the underlying morphism of apexes; this is well-defined since {𝜆𝜎(𝑗)}𝑗∈𝐽 is a cone over 𝐹𝜎 whenever {𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 is a cone over 𝐹 (the cone condition for 𝐹𝜎 at a morphism 𝛽 of 𝐽 is exactly the cone condition for 𝐹 at 𝜎(𝛽)), and Σ is manifestly functorial.

Dually define Σ−1:(Δ↓𝐹𝜎)→(Δ↓𝐹), (𝐿,{𝜇𝑗}𝑗∈𝐽)↦(𝐿,{𝜇𝜎−1(𝑖)}𝑖∈𝐼). Since 𝜎−1𝜎=1𝐽 and 𝜎𝜎−1=1𝐼, we have Σ−1Σ=1 and ΣΣ−1=1 on the nose, so Σ is an isomorphism of categories, in particular an equivalence of categories (2.6.25) (with identity natural isomorphisms).

By (2.6.52), (Δ↓𝐹) has a terminal object iff (Δ↓𝐹𝜎) does, and Σ carries a terminal object of (Δ↓𝐹), i.e. a limit of 𝐹, to a terminal object of (Δ↓𝐹𝜎), i.e. a limit of 𝐹𝜎, as required. ∎

Proposition 2.6.99 (Iterated Limits)

Let 𝐼,𝐽 be small categories and 𝐹:𝐼×𝐽→𝒞︀ a bifunctor. Suppose that for every 𝑖∈𝐼 there is a limit (𝐿(𝑖),{𝜆𝑖,𝑗}𝑗∈𝐽) for 𝐹(𝑖,−), so that by (2.6.96) this determines a functor 𝐿:𝐼→𝒞︀.

Then lim(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽𝐹(𝑖,𝑗) exists if and only if lim𝑖∈𝐼𝐿(𝑖) exists, and in this case

  1. given a limit (𝑀,{𝜈𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) for 𝐿, the cone (𝑀,{𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜈𝑖}(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽) is a limit for 𝐹;
  2. conversely, given a limit (𝑁,{𝜋𝑖,𝑗}(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽) for 𝐹, for each 𝑖∈𝐼 there is a unique morphism 𝜎𝑖:𝑁→𝐿(𝑖) such that 𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜎𝑖=𝜋𝑖,𝑗 for all 𝑗∈𝐽, and (𝑁,{𝜎𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a limit for 𝐿.

Symmetrically, suppose that for every 𝑗∈𝐽 there is a limit (𝑅(𝑗),{𝜇𝑖,𝑗}𝑖∈𝐼) for 𝐹(−,𝑗), so that by (2.6.96) this determines a functor 𝑅:𝐽→𝒞︀. Then lim(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽𝐹(𝑖,𝑗) exists if and only if lim𝑗∈𝐽𝑅(𝑗) exists, and in this case

  1. given a limit (𝑀′,{𝜉𝑗}𝑗∈𝐽) for 𝑅, the cone (𝑀′,{𝜇𝑖,𝑗∘𝜉𝑗}(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽) is a limit for 𝐹;
  2. conversely, given a limit (𝑁,{𝜋𝑖,𝑗}(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽) for 𝐹, for each 𝑗∈𝐽 there is a unique morphism 𝜏𝑗:𝑁→𝑅(𝑗) such that 𝜇𝑖,𝑗∘𝜏𝑗=𝜋𝑖,𝑗 for all 𝑖∈𝐼, and (𝑁,{𝜏𝑗}𝑗∈𝐽) is a limit for 𝑅.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

We construct mutually inverse functors Ξ:(Δ↓𝐿)→(Δ↓𝐹) and Θ:(Δ↓𝐹)→(Δ↓𝐿); as Θ∘Ξ=1, Ξ∘Θ=1, Ξ is in particular an equivalence of categories (2.6.25) (with identity natural isomorphisms), so by (2.6.52), (Δ↓𝐹) has a terminal object iff (Δ↓𝐿) does, and Ξ carries a terminal object of (Δ↓𝐿), i.e. a limit of 𝐿, to a terminal object of (Δ↓𝐹), i.e. a limit of 𝐹, as required.

The functor Ξ. Given a cone (𝑋,{𝜂𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) over 𝐿, define Ξ(𝑋,{𝜂𝑖})≔(𝑋,{𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜂𝑖}(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽). This is a cone over 𝐹: for (𝛼,𝛽):(𝑖,𝑗)→(𝑖′,𝑗′), writing (𝛼,𝛽)=(𝛼,1𝑗′)∘(1𝑖,𝛽),

𝐹(𝛼,𝛽)∘𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜂𝑖=𝐹(𝛼,1𝑗′)∘𝐹(1𝑖,𝛽)∘𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜂𝑖=𝐹(𝛼,1𝑗′)∘𝜆𝑖,𝑗′∘𝜂𝑖=𝜆𝑖′,𝑗′∘𝐿(𝛼)∘𝜂𝑖=𝜆𝑖′,𝑗′∘𝜂𝑖′

using in turn that 𝜆𝑖,− is a cone over 𝐹(𝑖,−), the defining property of 𝐿(𝛼) (2.6.96), and that 𝜂 is a cone over 𝐿. On morphisms Ξ is the identity on the underlying morphism of apexes, which is trivially functorial.

The functor Θ. Given a cone (𝑋,{𝜌𝑖,𝑗}(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽) over 𝐹, for each 𝑖∈𝐼 the family {𝜌𝑖,𝑗}𝑗∈𝐽 is a cone over 𝐹(𝑖,−), so by the universal property of (𝐿(𝑖),{𝜆𝑖,𝑗}𝑗) there is a unique morphism 𝜃𝑖:𝑋→𝐿(𝑖) such that 𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜃𝑖=𝜌𝑖,𝑗 for all 𝑗∈𝐽. Define Θ(𝑋,{𝜌𝑖,𝑗})≔(𝑋,{𝜃𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼).

We check {𝜃𝑖} is a cone over 𝐿. Fix 𝛼:𝑖→𝑖′ in 𝐼; then for every 𝑗′∈𝐽

𝜆𝑖′,𝑗′∘𝐿(𝛼)∘𝜃𝑖=𝐹(𝛼,1𝑗′)∘𝜆𝑖,𝑗′∘𝜃𝑖=𝐹(𝛼,1𝑗′)∘𝜌𝑖,𝑗′=𝜌𝑖′,𝑗′=𝜆𝑖′,𝑗′∘𝜃𝑖′

using the defining property of 𝐿(𝛼), the defining property of 𝜃𝑖, that 𝜌 is a cone over 𝐹 applied to (𝛼,1𝑗′):(𝑖,𝑗′)→(𝑖′,𝑗′), and the defining property of 𝜃𝑖′. As this holds for all 𝑗′∈𝐽, the universal property of (𝐿(𝑖′),{𝜆𝑖′,𝑗′}𝑗′) gives 𝐿(𝛼)∘𝜃𝑖=𝜃𝑖′.

On morphisms Θ again acts as the identity on apexes: if 𝜙:(𝑋,{𝜌𝑖,𝑗})→(𝑋′,{𝜌𝑖,𝑗′}) is a morphism of cones, then 𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜃𝑖′∘𝜙=𝜌𝑖,𝑗′∘𝜙=𝜌𝑖,𝑗=𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜃𝑖 for all 𝑗, so by uniqueness in the universal property of 𝐿(𝑖), 𝜃𝑖′∘𝜙=𝜃𝑖, i.e. 𝜙 is also a morphism of cones (𝑋,{𝜃𝑖})→(𝑋′,{𝜃𝑖′}).

Mutually inverse. Given a cone (𝑋,{𝜂𝑖}) over 𝐿, applying Ξ then Θ recovers, for each 𝑖, the unique morphism 𝑋→𝐿(𝑖) factoring (𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜂𝑖)𝑗 through {𝜆𝑖,𝑗}𝑗; since 𝜂𝑖 already satisfies this by definition, uniqueness gives Θ(Ξ(𝑋,{𝜂𝑖}))=(𝑋,{𝜂𝑖}). Conversely, given a cone (𝑋,{𝜌𝑖,𝑗}) over 𝐹, applying Θ then Ξ gives (𝑋,{𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜃𝑖})=(𝑋,{𝜌𝑖,𝑗}) directly from the defining property of 𝜃𝑖. Both functors act as the identity on the underlying morphism of apexes, so Ξ and Θ are mutually inverse isomorphisms of categories.

Finally, the symmetric statement follows by applying the above to the bifunctor 𝐹𝑇:𝐽×𝐼→𝒞︀, 𝐹𝑇(𝑗,𝑖)≔𝐹(𝑖,𝑗) (swapping the roles of 𝐼,𝐽, with 𝑅 playing the role of 𝐿), and reindexing via (2.6.98) along the swap isomorphism 𝐼×𝐽≅𝐽×𝐼. ∎

Corollary 2.6.100 (Comparison of Iterated Limits)

Let 𝐼,𝐽 be small categories and 𝐹:𝐼×𝐽→𝒞︀ a bifunctor, and suppose (as in (2.6.99)) that 𝐿(𝑖)≔lim𝑗∈𝐽𝐹(𝑖,𝑗) exists for every 𝑖∈𝐼 and 𝑅(𝑗)≔lim𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖,𝑗) exists for every 𝑗∈𝐽. If any one of lim(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽𝐹(𝑖,𝑗), lim𝑖∈𝐼𝐿(𝑖), lim𝑗∈𝐽𝑅(𝑗) exists, then all three exist, and there is a unique isomorphism Φ such that the following diagram commutes

for all 𝑖′∈𝐼, 𝑗′∈𝐽, where 𝜈𝑖′:lim𝑖∈𝐼𝐿(𝑖)→𝐿(𝑖′) and 𝜉𝑗′:lim𝑗∈𝐽𝑅(𝑗)→𝑅(𝑗′) are the respective limit cones.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

By (2.6.99), lim(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽𝐹(𝑖,𝑗) exists if and only if lim𝑖∈𝐼𝐿(𝑖) exists, and if and only if lim𝑗∈𝐽𝑅(𝑗) exists; so if any one of the three exists, all three do. In this case, taking (𝑀,{𝜈𝑖})≔(lim𝑖∈𝐼𝐿(𝑖),{𝜈𝑖}) in part a), the cone (lim𝑖∈𝐼𝐿(𝑖),{𝜆𝑖,𝑗∘𝜈𝑖}(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽) is a limit for 𝐹; likewise, taking (𝑀′,{𝜉𝑗})≔(lim𝑗∈𝐽𝑅(𝑗),{𝜉𝑗}) in part c), the cone (lim𝑗∈𝐽𝑅(𝑗),{𝜇𝑖,𝑗∘𝜉𝑗}(𝑖,𝑗)∈𝐼×𝐽) is also a limit for 𝐹. By (2.6.80) there is therefore a unique isomorphism Φ as required. ∎

Proposition 2.6.101 (Pointwise Colimits are Functorial)

Let 𝐼 be a small category and 𝐹:𝐼×𝒟︀→ℰ︀ a bifunctor.

Suppose that for every 𝑋∈𝒟︀ there is a colimit (colim𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖,𝑋),{𝜇𝑖,𝑋}𝑖∈𝐼) for 𝐹(−,𝑋)

Then colim𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖,−) is functorial in the sense there is a unique morphism making the following diagram commute

for all 𝑔:𝑋→𝑋′ and 𝛼:𝑖→𝑖′.

Suppose that there exists

Then by functoriality of limit (2.6.96) and definition of the cocone 𝜇−,𝑗′ we have a commutative diagram for all 𝛼:𝑖′→𝑖″

so that for all 𝑗′∈𝐽
