2.6.13 Biproduct

In 𝐀𝐛𝐆𝐫𝐩 and 𝐴-𝐌𝐨𝐝 coproducts and products coincide, so we formalise this property.

Definition 2.6.103 (Finite Biproduct)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category, 𝐼 a finite set and {𝑋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 be a family of objects. We say a triple (⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖,{𝑠𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼,{𝜋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a biproduct for the family {𝑋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 if the following holds

  1. (⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖,{𝜋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a product
  2. (⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖,{𝑠𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a coproduct

  3. The morphisms 𝜋𝑖,𝑠𝑗 satisfy the orthogonality conditions

    𝜋𝑖∘𝑠𝑗=𝛿𝑖𝑗≔{1𝑋𝑖𝑖=𝑗0𝑖≠𝑗
Proposition 2.6.104 (Criteria for Existence of Biproduct)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category, 𝐼 a finite set and {𝑋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 be a family of objects. Suppose both the product ∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 and coproduct ∐𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 exists. Then there is a unique comparison morphism

𝜓:∐𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖⟶∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖

such that

𝜋𝑖∘𝜓∘𝑠𝑗=𝛿𝑖𝑗

Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝜓 is an isomorphism
  2. (∐𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖,{𝑠𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼,{𝜋𝑖∘𝜓}𝑖∈𝐼) is a biproduct
  3. (∏𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖,{𝜓∘𝑠𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼,{𝜋𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a biproduct
  4. a biproduct ⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 exists

Proof. We may write 𝜓=[(𝛿𝑖𝑗)𝑖∈𝐼]𝑗∈𝐼 then 𝜓 is the unique map such that 𝜓∘𝑠𝑗=(𝛿𝑖𝑗)𝑖∈𝐼, which is the unique map such that 𝜋𝑖∘𝜓∘𝑠𝑗=𝛿𝑖𝑗. Suppose 𝜓′ is another such map then 𝜓′∘𝑠𝑗=𝜓∘𝑠𝑗 whence 𝜓′=𝜓.

a) ⟹ b) We show that 𝜓 is a morphism of cones, and the result follows from (2.6.79).

a) ⟹ c) We show that 𝜓−1 is a morphism of co-cones, and the result follows from (2.6.90).

b) ⟹ a) By (2.6.80) 𝜓 is uniquely determined as the isomorphism of limits.

c) ⟹ a) Similarly.

b) ⟹ d) immediate

d) ⟹ a) Let 𝜋𝑖′,𝑠𝑗′ be the biproduct maps for ⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖. Then by (2.6.80) (2.6.91) there is a diagram

where 𝛼 is the unique morphism satisfying 𝛼∘𝑠𝑖=𝑠𝑖′, 𝛽 is the unique morphism satisfying 𝜋𝑖∘𝛽=𝜋𝑖′, and both 𝛼 and 𝛽 are isomorphisms. Therefore 𝜋𝑖∘𝛽∘𝛼∘𝑠𝑗=𝜋𝑖′∘𝑠𝑗′=𝛿𝑖𝑗. Therefore by uniqueness 𝜓=𝛽∘𝛼 and is an isomorphism as required. ∎

Proposition 2.6.105 (Binary biproducts are enough)
Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category. Then it has all (finite) biproducts iff it has all binary biproducts (i.e. the case #𝐼=2).

Proof. We prove that ⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 exists for 𝐼={1,…,𝑛} by induction on 𝑛, where 𝑛=1 is immediate and 𝑛=2 is the base case. Consider a biproduct (⨁𝑖=1𝑛𝑋𝑖,{𝑠𝑖},{𝜋𝑖}) which we denote by 𝑌, and the binary biproduct (𝑌⊕𝑋𝑛+1,{𝑓,𝑔},{𝑝,𝑞}). Then we claim that

𝑍≔(𝑌⊕𝑋𝑛+1,{𝑓∘𝑠1,…,𝑓∘𝑠𝑛,𝑔},{𝜋1∘𝑝,…,𝜋𝑛∘𝑝,𝑞})

is a biproduct. There is a natural isomorphism

Mor(𝑍,−)→∼Mor(𝑌,−)×Mor(𝑋𝑛+1,−)→∼∏𝑖=1𝑛+1Mor(𝑋𝑖,−)

which shows that 𝑍 is a product with the given projection maps. Similarly we may show that 𝑍 is a coproduct. Finally

𝜋𝑖∘𝑝∘𝑓∘𝑠𝑗=𝜋𝑖∘1𝑌∘𝑠𝑗=𝛿𝑖𝑗𝜋𝑖∘𝑝∘𝑔=𝜋𝑖∘0=0𝑞∘𝑓∘𝑠𝑗=0∘𝑠𝑗=0

so that the cone and co-cone morphisms satisfy the required orthogonality conditions. ∎

In 𝐀𝐛𝐆𝐫𝐩 and 𝐴-𝐌𝐨𝐝, a homomorphism between direct sums ⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗→⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 is determined by, and can be recovered from, a matrix of homomorphisms 𝑋𝑗→𝑌𝑖; we record this categorically.

Definition 2.6.106 (Matrix of a Morphism)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category with biproducts ⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗 (injections 𝑠𝑗, projections 𝜋𝑗𝑋) and ⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 (injections 𝑠𝑖𝑌, projections 𝜋𝑖𝑌), and 𝑓:⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗→⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 a morphism. The matrix of 𝑓 is the family (𝑓𝑖𝑗)𝑖∈𝐼,𝑗∈𝐽 of morphisms

𝑓𝑖𝑗≔𝜋𝑖𝑌∘𝑓∘𝑠𝑗:𝑋𝑗→𝑌𝑖

When 𝐼={1,…,𝑚} and 𝐽={1,…,𝑛} we display this as an 𝑚×𝑛 array (𝑓𝑖𝑗), as for ordinary matrices.

Remark 2.6.107
Calling (𝑓𝑖𝑗) a matrix is not yet fully justified: for this notation to behave like ordinary matrix notation, composition should correspond to matrix multiplication, (𝑓∘𝑔)𝑖𝑘=∑𝑗𝑓𝑖𝑗∘𝑔𝑗𝑘, but this formula presupposes an addition on Mor(𝑋𝑘,𝑌𝑖), which is no part of the data of a pointed category with biproducts. We can nonetheless justify composition whenever it requires no addition, namely when each row of 𝑓 (or column of 𝑔) has at most one nonzero entry (2.6.114); addition on hom-sets is only introduced once biproducts are used to construct such an addition (2.6.118), after which the general composition formula above is recovered in full (2.6.122).
Proposition 2.6.108 (Matrix Notation for Biproducts)

In the setting of (2.6.106), the assignment 𝑓↦(𝑓𝑖𝑗)𝑖∈𝐼,𝑗∈𝐽 is a bijection

Mor(⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗,⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖)⟶∼∏𝑖∈𝐼,𝑗∈𝐽Mor(𝑋𝑗,𝑌𝑖)

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Given a family (𝑔𝑖𝑗)𝑖∈𝐼,𝑗∈𝐽 of morphisms 𝑔𝑖𝑗:𝑋𝑗→𝑌𝑖, for each 𝑗∈𝐽 the family (𝑔𝑖𝑗)𝑖∈𝐼 determines, by the universal property of the product ⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 (2.6.81), a unique morphism 𝑐𝑗:𝑋𝑗→⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 with 𝜋𝑖𝑌∘𝑐𝑗=𝑔𝑖𝑗 for every 𝑖∈𝐼. In turn, the family (𝑐𝑗)𝑗∈𝐽 determines, by the universal property of the coproduct ⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗 (2.6.93), a unique morphism 𝑔:⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗→⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 with 𝑔∘𝑠𝑗=𝑐𝑗 for every 𝑗∈𝐽. We show 𝑓↦(𝑓𝑖𝑗) and (𝑔𝑖𝑗)↦𝑔 are mutually inverse.

Starting from 𝑓, form its matrix (𝑓𝑖𝑗) and then 𝑐𝑗,𝑔 as above. Since 𝜋𝑖𝑌∘(𝑓∘𝑠𝑗)=𝑓𝑖𝑗 for every 𝑖, 𝑓∘𝑠𝑗 satisfies the defining property of 𝑐𝑗, so 𝑐𝑗=𝑓∘𝑠𝑗 by uniqueness; then 𝑓 itself satisfies 𝑓∘𝑠𝑗=𝑐𝑗 for every 𝑗, so 𝑔=𝑓 by uniqueness.

Starting from a family (𝑔𝑖𝑗), form 𝑐𝑗,𝑔 as above and then the matrix of 𝑔: for every 𝑖,𝑗, the (𝑖,𝑗) entry of the matrix of 𝑔 is 𝜋𝑖𝑌∘𝑔∘𝑠𝑗=𝜋𝑖𝑌∘𝑐𝑗=𝑔𝑖𝑗, using 𝑔∘𝑠𝑗=𝑐𝑗 and then the defining property of 𝑐𝑗. So the matrix of 𝑔 is again (𝑔𝑖𝑗). ∎

Remark 2.6.109
The matrix of 1⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖 is the identity matrix (𝛿𝑖𝑗1𝑋𝑖)𝑖,𝑗∈𝐼, immediate from the orthogonality conditions 𝜋𝑖∘𝑠𝑗=𝛿𝑖𝑗 (2.6.103).
Remark 2.6.110
Any object 𝑋 is trivially a biproduct of the one-element family {𝑋}, via (𝑋,{1𝑋},{1𝑋}) (the orthogonality condition reduces to 1𝑋∘1𝑋=1𝑋). This lets us apply (2.6.108) whenever one side of a morphism is a single object rather than a genuine biproduct, by regarding it as such.
Remark 2.6.111 (Injections and Projections as Matrices)

For the binary biproduct 𝑋1⊕𝑋2, the injections and projections are themselves matrices in the sense of (2.6.106), namely the columns and rows of the identity matrix

𝑠1=(1𝑋10)𝑠2=(01𝑋2)𝜋1=(1𝑋10)𝜋2=(01𝑋2)

immediate from 𝜋𝑖∘𝑠𝑗=𝛿𝑖𝑗 (2.6.103). More generally, for ⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖, regarding 𝑋𝑖0 as the trivial biproduct of {𝑋𝑖0}, 𝑠𝑖0 is the 𝑖0-th column and 𝜋𝑖0 the 𝑖0-th row of the identity matrix (𝛿𝑖𝑗1𝑋𝑖)𝑖,𝑗∈𝐼.

Lemma 2.6.112 (A Matrix is a Row of Columns and a Column of Rows)

Let 𝑀:𝑋1⊕𝑋2→𝑌1⊕𝑌2 have matrix (𝑀11𝑀12𝑀21𝑀22). Then

𝑀=((𝑀11𝑀21)(𝑀12𝑀22))=((𝑀11𝑀12)(𝑀21𝑀22))

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Write 𝑐1≔𝑀∘𝑠1, 𝑐2≔𝑀∘𝑠2 for the columns of 𝑀. The morphism (𝑐1𝑐2):𝑋1⊕𝑋2→𝑌1⊕𝑌2 is, by definition of the coproduct-induced notation (2.6.93), the unique morphism satisfying (𝑐1𝑐2)∘𝑠1=𝑐1 and (𝑐1𝑐2)∘𝑠2=𝑐2. Since 𝑀 itself satisfies 𝑀∘𝑠1=𝑐1 and 𝑀∘𝑠2=𝑐2 by definition of 𝑐1,𝑐2, uniqueness gives 𝑀=(𝑐1𝑐2).

Dually, writing 𝑟1≔𝜋1∘𝑀, 𝑟2≔𝜋2∘𝑀 for the rows of 𝑀, (𝑟1𝑟2) is the unique morphism with 𝜋1∘(𝑟1𝑟2)=𝑟1 and 𝜋2∘(𝑟1𝑟2)=𝑟2 (2.6.81), and 𝑀 satisfies these by definition of 𝑟1,𝑟2, so 𝑀=(𝑟1𝑟2). ∎

Lemma 2.6.113 (Composing a Column or Row on the Outside)

This is a general fact about products and coproducts, not requiring biproducts: let 𝑝:𝑍→𝑌1, 𝑞:𝑍→𝑌2 and 𝑁:𝑊→𝑍. Then

(𝑝𝑞)∘𝑁=(𝑝∘𝑁𝑞∘𝑁)

Dually, for 𝑎:𝑋1→𝑍, 𝑏:𝑋2→𝑍 and 𝑁:𝑍→𝑊

𝑁∘(𝑎𝑏)=(𝑁∘𝑎𝑁∘𝑏)

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Write 𝜋1,𝜋2 for the projections of 𝑌1⊕𝑌2. Since 𝜋1∘(𝑝𝑞)=𝑝 and 𝜋2∘(𝑝𝑞)=𝑞 (2.6.106), for any 𝑁:𝑊→𝑍, by associativity of composition

𝜋1∘((𝑝𝑞)∘𝑁)=𝑝∘𝑁𝜋2∘((𝑝𝑞)∘𝑁)=𝑞∘𝑁

so (𝑝𝑞)∘𝑁 satisfies the defining property of (𝑝∘𝑁𝑞∘𝑁), and the two are equal by the uniqueness clause of (2.6.81).

Dually, writing 𝑠1,𝑠2 for the injections of 𝑋1⊕𝑋2, since (𝑎𝑏)∘𝑠1=𝑎 and (𝑎𝑏)∘𝑠2=𝑏, for any 𝑁:𝑍→𝑊

(𝑁∘(𝑎𝑏))∘𝑠1=𝑁∘𝑎(𝑁∘(𝑎𝑏))∘𝑠2=𝑁∘𝑏

so 𝑁∘(𝑎𝑏) satisfies the defining property of (𝑁∘𝑎𝑁∘𝑏), and the two are equal by the uniqueness clause of (2.6.93). ∎

2.6.14 Biproduct Additivity

Following [Fre64] [Lan98], our eventual goal is to show that in a pointed category with (binary) biproducts, each hom-set Mor(𝑋,𝑌) carries a canonical addition, making composition bilinear – so that additivity, usually imposed as an axiom, is instead a theorem, derived here purely from the existence of biproducts, via matrix notation.

Proposition 2.6.114 (Composition Without Cross Terms)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category with binary biproducts, hence all finite biproducts (2.6.105), 𝐼,𝐽 finite sets, 𝜎:𝐼→𝐽 a function, and 𝑀:⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗→⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 a morphism whose matrix satisfies 𝑀𝑖𝑗=0 for every 𝑖∈𝐼, 𝑗≠𝜎(𝑖). Then for any 𝑁:⨁𝑘∈𝐾𝑊𝑘→⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗 with matrix (𝑁𝑗𝑘)

(𝑀∘𝑁)𝑖𝑘=𝑀𝑖,𝜎(𝑖)∘𝑁𝜎(𝑖),𝑘for all𝑖∈𝐼,𝑘∈𝐾

Dually, if 𝜏:𝐼→𝐽 and 𝑀′:⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑋𝑖→⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑌𝑗 has matrix satisfying 𝑀𝑗𝑖′=0 for every 𝑖∈𝐼, 𝑗≠𝜏(𝑖), then for any 𝑁:⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑌𝑗→⨁𝑘∈𝐾𝑍𝑘 with matrix (𝑁𝑘𝑗)

(𝑁∘𝑀′)𝑘𝑖=𝑁𝑘,𝜏(𝑖)∘𝑀𝜏(𝑖),𝑖′for all𝑘∈𝐾,𝑖∈𝐼

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

For 𝑖∈𝐼 and any 𝑗∈𝐽, 𝑎𝑖∘𝜋𝜎(𝑖)∘𝑠𝑗=𝑎𝑖∘𝛿𝜎(𝑖),𝑗 (using 𝜋𝜎(𝑖)∘𝑠𝑗=𝛿𝜎(𝑖),𝑗 (2.6.103)), which is 𝑎𝑖=𝑀𝑖,𝜎(𝑖) if 𝑗=𝜎(𝑖) and 0=𝑀𝑖𝑗 otherwise (by hypothesis on 𝑀); this matches 𝜋𝑖∘𝑀∘𝑠𝑗=𝑀𝑖𝑗 for every 𝑗∈𝐽, so by the uniqueness clause of (2.6.93) (applied to maps out of ⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗), 𝜋𝑖∘𝑀=𝑎𝑖∘𝜋𝜎(𝑖).

Hence, for every 𝑖∈𝐼, 𝑘∈𝐾

𝜋𝑖∘𝑀∘𝑁∘𝑠𝑘=𝑎𝑖∘𝜋𝜎(𝑖)∘𝑁∘𝑠𝑘=𝑎𝑖∘𝑁𝜎(𝑖),𝑘

giving the matrix of 𝑀∘𝑁.

Dually, for 𝑖∈𝐼 and any 𝑗∈𝐽, 𝜋𝑗∘𝑠𝜏(𝑖)∘𝑐𝑖=𝛿𝑗,𝜏(𝑖)𝑐𝑖, which matches 𝜋𝑗∘𝑀′∘𝑠𝑖=𝑀𝑗𝑖′ for every 𝑗∈𝐽 (equal to 𝑐𝑖 if 𝑗=𝜏(𝑖) and 0 otherwise, by hypothesis), so by the uniqueness clause of (2.6.81) (applied to maps into ⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑌𝑗), 𝑀′∘𝑠𝑖=𝑠𝜏(𝑖)∘𝑐𝑖; hence, for every 𝑘∈𝐾, 𝑖∈𝐼

𝜋𝑘∘𝑁∘𝑀′∘𝑠𝑖=𝜋𝑘∘𝑁∘𝑠𝜏(𝑖)∘𝑐𝑖=𝑁𝑘,𝜏(𝑖)∘𝑐𝑖

giving the matrix of 𝑁∘𝑀′. ∎

Example 2.6.115

(2.6.114) recovers familiar matrix identities, at various arities, without needing addition, since none of the matrices below have cross terms. For 𝑎:𝑋→𝑌, regarding 𝑋 (resp. 𝑌) as the trivial biproduct of {𝑋} (resp. {𝑌}) (2.6.108)

(𝑎0)=𝑎∘(1𝑋0)(𝑎0)=(1𝑌0)∘𝑎

for 𝑎:𝑋1→𝑌1, 𝑏:𝑋2→𝑌2, 𝑝:𝑊→𝑋1 and 𝑞:𝑊→𝑋2

(𝑎00𝑏)∘(𝑝𝑞)=(𝑎∘𝑝𝑏∘𝑞)

and for 𝑢:𝑋1→𝑍

(𝑢0)∘(𝑝𝑞)=𝑢∘𝑝
Definition 2.6.116 (Diagonal and Codiagonal)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category with binary biproduct 𝑋⊕𝑋, with injections 𝑠1,𝑠2 and projections 𝜋1,𝜋2. Regarding 𝑋 as the trivial biproduct of {𝑋}, (2.6.108) identifies Mor(𝑋,𝑋⊕𝑋) with 2×1 matrices and Mor(𝑋⊕𝑋,𝑋) with 1×2 matrices over Mor(𝑋,𝑋). The diagonal Δ𝑋:𝑋→𝑋⊕𝑋 and codiagonal (or summation map) ∇𝑋:𝑋⊕𝑋→𝑋 are the morphisms with matrices

Δ𝑋=(1𝑋1𝑋)∇𝑋=(1𝑋1𝑋)

that is, the unique morphisms with 𝜋1∘Δ𝑋=𝜋2∘Δ𝑋=1𝑋 and ∇𝑋∘𝑠1=∇𝑋∘𝑠2=1𝑋 respectively.

Remark 2.6.117
In 𝐀𝐛𝐆𝐫𝐩, where 𝑋⊕𝑋 is the direct sum 𝑋×𝑋 with 𝑠1(𝑥)=(𝑥,0), 𝑠2(𝑥)=(0,𝑥), 𝜋1(𝑥,𝑦)=𝑥, 𝜋2(𝑥,𝑦)=𝑦, the codiagonal is exactly the addition map: ∇𝑋(𝑥,0)=𝑥 and ∇𝑋(0,𝑦)=𝑦 force, by additivity of the homomorphism ∇𝑋, ∇𝑋(𝑥,𝑦)=∇𝑋(𝑥,0)+∇𝑋(0,𝑦)=𝑥+𝑦. Dually the diagonal is Δ𝑋(𝑥)=(𝑥,𝑥).
Definition 2.6.118 (Sum of Parallel Morphisms)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category with binary biproducts and 𝑓,𝑔:𝑋→𝑌. We define

𝑓+𝑔≔(𝑓𝑔)∘Δ𝑋=∇𝑌∘(𝑓00𝑔)∘Δ𝑋=∇𝑌∘(𝑓𝑔):𝑋→𝑌

the three expressions agreeing by (2.6.114), since (𝑓00𝑔) has no cross terms.

Proposition 2.6.119 (Interchange Law)
Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category with binary biproducts and 𝑤,𝑥,𝑦,𝑧:𝑋→𝑌. Then (𝑤+𝑥)+(𝑦+𝑧)=(𝑤+𝑦)+(𝑥+𝑧).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino. Following [Fre64] Theorem 2.38.

Let 𝑀≔(𝑤𝑥𝑦𝑧):𝑋⊕𝑋→𝑌⊕𝑌 (2.6.108). Then

𝑀∘Δ𝑋=(2.6.112)((𝑤𝑥)(𝑦𝑧))∘Δ𝑋=(2.6.113)((𝑤𝑥)∘Δ𝑋(𝑦𝑧)∘Δ𝑋)=(2.6.118)(𝑤+𝑥𝑦+𝑧)∇𝑌∘𝑀=(2.6.112)∇𝑌∘((𝑤𝑦)(𝑥𝑧))=(2.6.113)(∇𝑌∘(𝑤𝑦)∇𝑌∘(𝑥𝑧))=(2.6.118)(𝑤+𝑦𝑥+𝑧)

so, applying ∇𝑌∘− to the first display and −∘Δ𝑋 to the second (each a further instance of (2.6.118))

(𝑤+𝑥)+(𝑦+𝑧)=∇𝑌∘(𝑀∘Δ𝑋)=(∇𝑌∘𝑀)∘Δ𝑋=(𝑤+𝑦)+(𝑥+𝑧)

 ∎

Remark 2.6.120 (Eckmann--Hilton Phenomenon)
The Interchange Law is an instance of the classical Eckmann–Hilton argument: whenever a set carries two unital binary operations ∗,· satisfying the interchange law (𝑎∗𝑏)·(𝑐∗𝑑)=(𝑎·𝑐)∗(𝑏·𝑑) and sharing a common unit, the two operations coincide and are commutative and associative. Here the two operations are the row-first and column-first ways of combining the block (𝑤𝑥𝑦𝑧) into a single morphism via Δ𝑋,∇𝑌; (2.6.118) already records that they coincide (as a single well-defined +), and (2.6.119) is exactly the interchange law for it. Commutativity and associativity, proved below, are the usual Eckmann–Hilton consequences, recovered by the substitutions 𝑤=𝑧≔0 and 𝑦≔0 respectively.
Proposition 2.6.121 (Mor(𝑋,𝑌) is a Commutative Monoid, and Composition is Bilinear)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category with binary biproducts. For objects 𝑋,𝑌, (Mor(𝑋,𝑌),+) is a commutative monoid with identity 0. Moreover, for 𝑓,𝑔:𝑋→𝑌, ℎ:𝑌→𝑍 and 𝑘:𝑊→𝑋

ℎ∘(𝑓+𝑔)=ℎ∘𝑓+ℎ∘𝑔(𝑓+𝑔)∘𝑘=𝑓∘𝑘+𝑔∘𝑘

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Identity. Since (𝑓0) and (0𝑓) each have a single nonzero entry, (2.6.114) gives

𝑓+0=(𝑓0)∘(1𝑋1𝑋)=𝑓∘1𝑋=𝑓0+𝑓=(0𝑓)∘(1𝑋1𝑋)=𝑓∘1𝑋=𝑓

Commutativity. By (2.6.119), setting 𝑤≔0, 𝑥≔𝑓, 𝑦≔𝑔, 𝑧≔0 gives (0+𝑓)+(𝑔+0)=(0+𝑔)+(𝑓+0), that is 𝑓+𝑔=𝑔+𝑓 using the identity just proved.

Associativity. For a third morphism ℎ:𝑋→𝑌, setting 𝑤≔𝑓, 𝑥≔𝑔, 𝑦≔0, 𝑧≔ℎ in (2.6.119) gives (𝑓+𝑔)+(0+ℎ)=(𝑓+0)+(𝑔+ℎ), that is (𝑓+𝑔)+ℎ=𝑓+(𝑔+ℎ).

Bilinearity.

ℎ∘(𝑓+𝑔)=(2.6.118)ℎ∘(𝑓𝑔)∘Δ𝑋=(2.6.113)(ℎ∘𝑓ℎ∘𝑔)∘Δ𝑋=(2.6.118)ℎ∘𝑓+ℎ∘𝑔

and dually

(𝑓+𝑔)∘𝑘=(2.6.118)∇𝑌∘(𝑓𝑔)∘𝑘=(2.6.113)∇𝑌∘(𝑓∘𝑘𝑔∘𝑘)=(2.6.118)𝑓∘𝑘+𝑔∘𝑘

 ∎

Proposition 2.6.122 (Composition is Matrix Multiplication)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category with binary biproducts, 𝐼,𝐽,𝐾 finite sets, 𝑀:⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗→⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖 with matrix (𝑀𝑖𝑗) and 𝑁:⨁𝑘∈𝐾𝑊𝑘→⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗 with matrix (𝑁𝑗𝑘). Then

(𝑀∘𝑁)𝑖𝑘=∑𝑗∈𝐽𝑀𝑖𝑗∘𝑁𝑗𝑘for all𝑖∈𝐼,𝑘∈𝐾

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

We first show that any column 𝐶:𝑍→⨁𝑗∈𝐽𝑋𝑗, with entries 𝐶𝑗≔𝜋𝑗∘𝐶, satisfies 𝐶=∑𝑗∈𝐽𝑠𝑗∘𝐶𝑗. Indeed, for each 𝑖∈𝐽, by (2.6.121) (bilinearity, iterated over the finite sum)

𝜋𝑖∘∑𝑗∈𝐽𝑠𝑗∘𝐶𝑗=∑𝑗∈𝐽𝜋𝑖∘𝑠𝑗∘𝐶𝑗=∑𝑗∈𝐽𝛿𝑖𝑗𝐶𝑗=𝐶𝑖

using 𝜋𝑖∘𝑠𝑗=𝛿𝑖𝑗 (2.6.103) and that every term with 𝑗≠𝑖 vanishes (composing with the zero morphism), so this matches the matrix of 𝐶 entrywise, whence ∑𝑗∈𝐽𝑠𝑗∘𝐶𝑗=𝐶 by (2.6.108). Dually, any row 𝑅:⨁𝑖∈𝐼𝑌𝑖→𝑍 satisfies 𝑅=∑𝑖∈𝐼𝑅𝑖∘𝜋𝑖, where 𝑅𝑖≔𝑅∘𝑠𝑖.

Now fix 𝑖∈𝐼, 𝑘∈𝐾. The 𝑘-th column of 𝑁 is 𝑁∘𝑠𝑘, with entries 𝑁𝑗𝑘=𝜋𝑗∘𝑁∘𝑠𝑘, so by the column decomposition, 𝑁∘𝑠𝑘=∑𝑗∈𝐽𝑠𝑗∘𝑁𝑗𝑘. Hence, using bilinearity to distribute 𝑀∘− and then 𝜋𝑖∘− over the finite sum

(𝑀∘𝑁)𝑖𝑘=𝜋𝑖∘𝑀∘𝑁∘𝑠𝑘=𝜋𝑖∘𝑀∘∑𝑗∈𝐽𝑠𝑗∘𝑁𝑗𝑘=∑𝑗∈𝐽𝜋𝑖∘𝑀∘𝑠𝑗∘𝑁𝑗𝑘=∑𝑗∈𝐽𝑀𝑖𝑗∘𝑁𝑗𝑘

 ∎

2.6.15 Direct Limit / Directed Colimit

Here we consider only a certain type of colimit, which is referred to variously as direct limit [AM69], limite inductive [Gro64] or filtered colimit [Lan98]. We also restrict to the case where the indexing category is “thin”, which is more properly refered to as a directed colimit.

Definition 2.6.123 (Directed Preorder)

We say a category 𝐼 is a directed preorder if it is small, thin and filtered, that is for any 𝑖,𝑗∈𝐼

  • there exists at most one morphism 𝑖→𝑗, and
  • there exists 𝑘∈𝐼 and morphisms 𝑖→𝑘 and 𝑗→𝑘

If there exists a morphism 𝑖→𝑗 then we write 𝑖≺𝑗.

Example 2.6.124
A typical example is any family of subsets of a set 𝑋 ordered by reversion inclusion which are closed under finite intersection.
Definition 2.6.125 (Direct limit / Directed colimit)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder and 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ a diagram.

A cocone over 𝐹 is a pair (𝐿,{𝜇:𝐹(𝑖)→𝐿}𝑖∈𝐼) such that

𝑖≺𝑗⟹𝜇𝑗∘𝐹(𝑖→𝑗)=𝜇𝑖

The cocones over 𝐹 constitute a category (𝐹↓Δ) where morphisms 𝛼:(𝐿,{𝜇𝑖})→(𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖′}) are simply morphisms 𝛼:𝐿→𝐿′ such that 𝛼∘𝜇𝑖=𝜇𝑖′ for all 𝑖∈𝐼.

A cone (𝐿,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) over 𝐹 is a direct limit for 𝐹 if it is an initial object (2.6.48) in the cocone category (𝐹↓Δ).

Explicitly for every cocone (𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼) there is a unique morphism 𝛼:𝐿→𝐿′ such that 𝛼∘𝜇𝑖=𝜇𝑖′ for all 𝑖∈𝐼.

We denote this by lim⟶𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖).

Definition 2.6.126 (Cofinal Subpreorder)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder. Then a full subcategory 𝐼′⊂𝐼 is said to be cofinal if

∀𝑖∈𝐼∃𝑖′∈𝐼′s.t.𝑖≤𝑖′

In this case 𝐼′ is also directed.

Proposition 2.6.127 (Cofinal Direct Limit)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder and 𝐼′ a full subcategory which is also directed. Suppose 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ is a diagram then there is a unique morphism of cocones

lim⟶𝑖∈𝐼′𝐹(𝑖)⟶lim⟶𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)

provided both these exist.

If 𝐼′ is cofinal in 𝐼 then this is an isomorphism.

Proposition 2.6.128 (Direct Limits of Sets)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder and 𝐹:𝐼→𝐒𝐞𝐭 a diagram. Consider

𝐿≔{(𝑖,𝑥)|𝑖∈𝐼,𝑥∈𝐹(𝑖)}/∼

where (𝑖,𝑥)∼(𝑗,𝑦) if for some 𝑘∈𝐼 we have 𝑖≺𝑘,𝑗≺𝑘 and 𝐹(𝑖→𝑘)(𝑥)=𝐹(𝑗→𝑘)(𝑦), and let 𝜇𝑖:𝐹(𝑖)→𝐿, 𝜇𝑖(𝑥)≔[(𝑖,𝑥)].

Then ∼ is an equivalence relation, and (𝐿,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a direct limit for 𝐹 (2.6.125), that is 𝐿=lim⟶𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖). Moreover the 𝜇𝑖 are jointly surjective, that is every element of 𝐿 is of the form 𝜇𝑖(𝑥) for some 𝑖∈𝐼, 𝑥∈𝐹(𝑖).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

∼ is an equivalence relation. Reflexivity and symmetry are immediate, using 𝑖≺𝑖 (via the identity morphism). For transitivity, suppose (𝑖,𝑥)∼(𝑗,𝑦) via 𝑘 (so 𝑖,𝑗≺𝑘, 𝐹(𝑖→𝑘)(𝑥)=𝐹(𝑗→𝑘)(𝑦)) and (𝑗,𝑦)∼(𝑙,𝑧) via 𝑚 (so 𝑗,𝑙≺𝑚, 𝐹(𝑗→𝑚)(𝑦)=𝐹(𝑙→𝑚)(𝑧)). As 𝐼 is directed there is 𝑛 with 𝑘,𝑚≺𝑛, and applying 𝐹(𝑘→𝑛), resp. 𝐹(𝑚→𝑛), to the two witnessing equations and using functoriality of 𝐹,

𝐹(𝑖→𝑛)(𝑥)=𝐹(𝑘→𝑛)(𝐹(𝑖→𝑘)(𝑥))=𝐹(𝑘→𝑛)(𝐹(𝑗→𝑘)(𝑦))=𝐹(𝑗→𝑛)(𝑦)𝐹(𝑗→𝑛)(𝑦)=𝐹(𝑚→𝑛)(𝐹(𝑗→𝑚)(𝑦))=𝐹(𝑚→𝑛)(𝐹(𝑙→𝑚)(𝑧))=𝐹(𝑙→𝑛)(𝑧)

so 𝐹(𝑖→𝑛)(𝑥)=𝐹(𝑙→𝑛)(𝑧), that is (𝑖,𝑥)∼(𝑙,𝑧) via 𝑛.

Joint surjectivity. Immediate, as every element of 𝐿 is by construction the class [(𝑖,𝑥)]=𝜇𝑖(𝑥) of some pair.

(𝐿,{𝜇𝑖}) is a cocone. For 𝑖≺𝑗, taking 𝑘≔𝑗 in the equivalence relation (using 𝐹(𝑗→𝑗)=1𝐹(𝑗)) gives (𝑖,𝑥)∼(𝑗,𝐹(𝑖→𝑗)(𝑥)), that is 𝜇𝑗(𝐹(𝑖→𝑗)(𝑥))=𝜇𝑖(𝑥), as required by (2.6.125).

(𝐿,{𝜇𝑖}) is initial. Let (𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖′}) be any cocone over 𝐹. Define 𝛼:𝐿→𝐿′ by 𝛼([(𝑖,𝑥)])≔𝜇𝑖′(𝑥); this is well-defined, for if (𝑖,𝑥)∼(𝑗,𝑦) via 𝑘 then, using the cocone condition for 𝜇′,

𝜇𝑖′(𝑥)=𝜇𝑘′(𝐹(𝑖→𝑘)(𝑥))=𝜇𝑘′(𝐹(𝑗→𝑘)(𝑦))=𝜇𝑗′(𝑦)

and by construction 𝛼∘𝜇𝑖=𝜇𝑖′ for all 𝑖. Any morphism of cocones 𝛽:𝐿→𝐿′ satisfies 𝛽(𝜇𝑖(𝑥))=𝜇𝑖′(𝑥) for all 𝑖,𝑥, so 𝛽=𝛼 by joint surjectivity of the 𝜇𝑖; hence 𝛼 is the unique such morphism, and (𝐿,{𝜇𝑖}) is initial in (𝐹↓Δ), that is a direct limit for 𝐹. ∎

2.6.16 Inverse Limit

Definition 2.6.129 (Inverse Limit / Directed Limit)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder and 𝐹:𝐼op→𝒞︀ a diagram – equivalently, an inverse system indexed by 𝐼: for 𝑖≺𝑗 in 𝐼, a restriction morphism 𝜌𝑖𝑗:𝐹(𝑗)→𝐹(𝑖) in 𝒞︀, with 𝜌𝑖𝑖=1𝐹(𝑖) and 𝜌𝑖𝑘=𝜌𝑖𝑗∘𝜌𝑗𝑘 whenever 𝑖≺𝑗≺𝑘.

A limit for 𝐹 in the sense of (2.6.78) (applied to the small category 𝐼op) is called an inverse limit for the system, denoted lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖): explicitly, a cone (𝐿,{𝜆𝑖:𝐿→𝐹(𝑖)}𝑖∈𝐼) with 𝜌𝑖𝑗∘𝜆𝑗=𝜆𝑖 for every 𝑖≺𝑗, terminal among such cones.

Proposition 2.6.130 (Inverse Limits of Sets)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder and 𝐹:𝐼op→𝐒𝐞𝐭 an inverse system, with restriction maps 𝜌𝑖𝑗:𝐹(𝑗)→𝐹(𝑖) (𝑖≺𝑗). Then

lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)={(𝑥𝑖)𝑖∈𝐼∈∏𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)|𝜌𝑖𝑗(𝑥𝑗)=𝑥𝑖for all𝑖≺𝑗},

with projections 𝜆𝑖((𝑥𝑗)𝑗)≔𝑥𝑖.

Proof. This is (2.6.85) applied to the diagram 𝐹:𝐼op→𝐒𝐞𝐭 (𝐼op a small category, as 𝐼 is). ∎
Proposition 2.6.131 (Cofinal Inverse Limit)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder, 𝐼′⊂𝐼 a full subcategory which is also directed, and 𝐹:𝐼op→𝒞︀ an inverse system, with restriction maps 𝜌𝑖𝑗 (𝑖≺𝑗 in 𝐼). Then, provided both exist, there is a unique morphism of cones

lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)⟶lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼′𝐹(𝑖)

(restricting the limit cone over 𝐼 to the subcategory 𝐼′).

If 𝐼′ is cofinal in 𝐼 (2.6.126) then this is an isomorphism.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Write 𝐿′≔lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼′𝐹(𝑖), with projections 𝜆𝑖′:𝐿′→𝐹(𝑖) (𝑖∈𝐼′). The cone (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼′) over 𝐹|𝐼′op is in particular a cone over all of 𝐹 restricted along the inclusion 𝐼′op⊂𝐼op, so composing with the (terminal, by definition of lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)) limit cone’s universal property in the other direction gives nothing yet – rather, the stated morphism is simply the unique one afforded by terminality of 𝐿′ among cones over 𝐹|𝐼′op, applied to the cone (lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖),{𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼′) (the limit cone over 𝐼, restricted in its indexing set to 𝐼′ – still a cone over 𝐹|𝐼′op, by the cone condition on 𝐼 restricted to 𝑖≺𝑗 both in 𝐼′): this gives the unique morphism lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)→𝐿′ of the statement.

Now suppose 𝐼′ is cofinal. For 𝑖∈𝐼, choose (by cofinality) 𝑖′∈𝐼′ with 𝑖≺𝑖′, and define 𝜇𝑖≔𝜌𝑖,𝑖′∘𝜆𝑖′′:𝐿′→𝐹(𝑖).

𝜇𝑖 is independent of the choice of 𝑖′. If 𝑖≺𝑖1′,𝑖2′ with 𝑖1′,𝑖2′∈𝐼′, directedness of 𝐼′ gives 𝑖3′∈𝐼′ with 𝑖1′,𝑖2′≺𝑖3′; then, using the cone condition for 𝜆′ (within 𝐼′, at 𝑖1′≺𝑖3′) and the restriction composition law of (2.6.129) (at 𝑖≺𝑖1′≺𝑖3′),

𝜌𝑖,𝑖1′∘𝜆𝑖1′′=𝜌𝑖,𝑖1′∘𝜌𝑖1′,𝑖3′∘𝜆𝑖3′′=𝜌𝑖,𝑖3′∘𝜆𝑖3′′,

and symmetrically 𝜌𝑖,𝑖2′∘𝜆𝑖2′′=𝜌𝑖,𝑖3′∘𝜆𝑖3′′; so both choices agree.

(𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is a cone over 𝐹. Let 𝑖≺𝑗 in 𝐼. Choose 𝑗′∈𝐼′ with 𝑗≺𝑗′; then also 𝑖≺𝑗′, so 𝑗′ may be used to compute both 𝜇𝑖 and 𝜇𝑗:

𝜌𝑖𝑗∘𝜇𝑗=𝜌𝑖𝑗∘𝜌𝑗,𝑗′∘𝜆𝑗′′=𝜌𝑖,𝑗′∘𝜆𝑗′′=𝜇𝑖,

using the restriction composition law at 𝑖≺𝑗≺𝑗′. Moreover for 𝑖∈𝐼′ itself, taking 𝑖′≔𝑖 (with 𝜌𝑖𝑖=1𝐹(𝑖)) gives 𝜇𝑖=𝜆𝑖′: the cone (𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) restricts, on 𝐼′, to the original cone (𝐿′,{𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼′).

(𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is terminal. Let (𝑁,{𝜈𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) be any cone over 𝐹. Restricting to 𝐼′ gives a cone over 𝐹|𝐼′op, so by terminality of 𝐿′ there is a unique morphism 𝛾:𝑁→𝐿′ with 𝜆𝑖′∘𝛾=𝜈𝑖 for all 𝑖∈𝐼′. For general 𝑖∈𝐼, choosing 𝑖′∈𝐼′ with 𝑖≺𝑖′,

𝜇𝑖∘𝛾=𝜌𝑖,𝑖′∘𝜆𝑖′′∘𝛾=𝜌𝑖,𝑖′∘𝜈𝑖′=𝜈𝑖

using the cone condition for 𝜈 (over all of 𝐼) at 𝑖≺𝑖′; so 𝛾 is a morphism of cones (𝑁,{𝜈𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼)→(𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼). Any such morphism 𝛿 satisfies, in particular for 𝑖∈𝐼′ (where 𝜇𝑖=𝜆𝑖′), 𝜆𝑖′∘𝛿=𝜈𝑖, so 𝛿=𝛾 by the uniqueness already established for 𝛾. Hence (𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is terminal among cones over 𝐹 on all of 𝐼, that is, (𝐿′,{𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼) is lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖).

By uniqueness of limits up to unique isomorphism of cones (2.6.78), there is a (unique) isomorphism lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)→∼𝐿′ compatible with the projections {𝜇𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 (on the 𝐿′ side) and {𝜆𝑖}𝑖∈𝐼 (on the lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖) side); restricting this compatibility to 𝑖∈𝐼′ (where 𝜇𝑖=𝜆𝑖′) shows it is compatible with {𝜆𝑖′}𝑖∈𝐼′ too, so by the uniqueness clause established in the first paragraph, this isomorphism is exactly the morphism of cones lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼𝐹(𝑖)→lim⟵𝑖∈𝐼′𝐹(𝑖)=𝐿′ of the statement. ∎

Corollary 2.6.132 (Functoriality of the Inverse Limit)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder, and let 𝒞︀lim𝐼op denote the full subcategory of the functor category 𝒞︀𝐼op (2.6.14) spanned by those inverse systems 𝐹:𝐼op→𝒞︀ for which lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖) exists. Then

lim⟵𝑖(−):𝒞︀lim𝐼op⟶𝒞︀,𝐹↦lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖)

is a functor.

More precisely: for a natural transformation 𝜎=(𝜎𝑖:𝐹(𝑖)→𝐺(𝑖))𝑖∈𝐼 there is a unique morphism

lim⟵𝑖𝜎𝑖:lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖)⟶lim⟵𝑖𝐺(𝑖)

compatible with the projections; and

  1. for a further natural transformation 𝜏=(𝜏𝑖:𝐺(𝑖)→𝐾(𝑖))𝑖 (so 𝜏𝜎≔(𝜏𝑖𝜎𝑖)𝑖, itself a natural transformation 𝐹⇒𝐾),

    lim⟵𝑖(𝜏𝑖𝜎𝑖)=lim⟵𝑖𝜏𝑖∘lim⟵𝑖𝜎𝑖;
  2. lim⟵𝑖1𝐹(𝑖)=1lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖).

Consequently, if every 𝜎𝑖 is an isomorphism, so is lim⟵𝑖𝜎𝑖 (2.6.42).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

A natural transformation 𝜎=(𝜎𝑖)𝑖 satisfying 𝜎𝑖∘𝜌𝑖𝑗𝐹=𝜌𝑖𝑗𝐺∘𝜎𝑗 for all 𝑖≺𝑗 is exactly a morphism 𝐹⇒𝐺 of the functor category 𝒞︀𝐼op (2.6.14) (the naturality square for 𝜎 at the morphism 𝑗→𝑖 of 𝐼op corresponding to 𝑖≺𝑗), invertible in 𝒞︀𝐼op exactly when every 𝜎𝑖 is an isomorphism (with inverse (𝜎𝑖−1)𝑖). So this is precisely the case 𝐽≔𝐼op of (2.6.97). ∎

Corollary 2.6.133 (Inverse Limits Commute with Products)

Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder, 𝐾 a set, and (𝐹𝑘)𝑘∈𝐾 inverse systems 𝐹𝑘:𝐼op→𝒞︀, with limit-cone projections 𝜆𝑘,𝑖:lim⟵𝑖𝐹𝑘(𝑖)→𝐹𝑘(𝑖), such that lim⟵𝑖𝐹𝑘(𝑖) exists for every 𝑘∈𝐾; and suppose ∏𝑘∈𝐾𝐹𝑘(𝑖) exists for every 𝑖∈𝐼, with product projections 𝜋𝑘,𝑖:∏𝑘′∈𝐾𝐹𝑘′(𝑖)→𝐹𝑘(𝑖). If ∏𝑘∈𝐾lim⟵𝑖𝐹𝑘(𝑖) exists, with product projections 𝑝𝑘, then lim⟵𝑖(∏𝑘∈𝐾𝐹𝑘(𝑖)) exists too, with limit-cone projections Λ𝑖, and there is a unique morphism

Φ:∏𝑘∈𝐾lim⟵𝑖𝐹𝑘(𝑖)⟶lim⟵𝑖(∏𝑘∈𝐾𝐹𝑘(𝑖))

such that the following commutes for every 𝑘∈𝐾, 𝑖∈𝐼

and Φ is an isomorphism.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Regard 𝐾 as a discrete small category and define a bifunctor 𝐻:𝐾×𝐼op→𝒞︀ by 𝐻(𝑘,𝑖)≔𝐹𝑘(𝑖) (a morphism of 𝐾×𝐼op is a pair (1𝑘,𝛼) for 𝛼 a morphism of 𝐼op, since 𝐾 is discrete, and 𝐻(1𝑘,𝛼)≔𝐹𝑘(𝛼); this is a bifunctor as each 𝐹𝑘 is a functor). By (2.6.81) (limits over a discrete category are products), (∏𝑘∈𝐾𝐹𝑘(𝑖),{𝜋𝑘,𝑖}𝑘) is lim𝑘∈𝐾𝐻(𝑘,𝑖) for every 𝑖∈𝐼op, and by (2.6.129), (lim⟵𝑖𝐹𝑘(𝑖),{𝜆𝑘,𝑖}𝑖) is lim𝑖∈𝐼op𝐻(𝑘,𝑖) for every 𝑘∈𝐾; both exist by hypothesis, so (writing 𝐿(𝑘)≔lim⟵𝑖𝐹𝑘(𝑖), 𝑅(𝑖)≔∏𝑘∈𝐾𝐹𝑘(𝑖)) (2.6.100) applies to 𝐻.

As (∏𝑘∈𝐾lim⟵𝑖𝐹𝑘(𝑖),{𝑝𝑘}𝑘)=(lim𝑘∈𝐾𝐿(𝑘),{𝑝𝑘}𝑘) exists by hypothesis, (2.6.100) gives that lim𝑖∈𝐼op𝑅(𝑖)=lim⟵𝑖(∏𝑘∈𝐾𝐹𝑘(𝑖)) also exists, with limit-cone projections Λ𝑖 say, together with a unique isomorphism Φ making the stated diagram commute for every 𝑘,𝑖 (that proposition’s diagram, with 𝜈𝑘≔𝑝𝑘, 𝜉𝑖≔Λ𝑖, 𝜆𝑘,𝑖 as here, and 𝜇𝑘,𝑖≔𝜋𝑘,𝑖). ∎

2.6.17 Equaliser and Coequaliser

Definition 2.6.134 (Equaliser)

Consider a commutative diagram in a category 𝒞︀

such that 𝛼∘𝑒=𝛽∘𝑒. We say that (𝑋,𝑒) is an equaliser for (𝛼,𝛽) if for all 𝑒′:𝑋′→𝑌 such that 𝛼∘𝑒′=𝛽∘𝑒′ there is a unique factorisation

This is equivalent to (𝑋,𝑒) being a limit for the obvious functor 𝐹:𝟐→𝒞︀ where 𝟐 denotes the category ·⇉·.

Proposition 2.6.135
Every equaliser is a monomorphism, and every coequaliser is an epimorphism.

Proof. Suppose that (𝑋,𝑒) is an equaliser for 𝛼,𝛽:𝑌⇉𝑍, and 𝑒∘𝑓=𝑒∘𝑔=ℎ. Then evidentally 𝛼∘ℎ=𝛽∘ℎ so there is a unique morphism 𝑘 such that 𝑒∘𝑘=ℎ, whence 𝑘=𝑓=𝑔.

The second statement follows by duality. ∎

Proposition 2.6.136
Suppose (𝑋,𝑒)=eq(𝛼,𝛽). Then 𝛼=𝛽 if and only if 𝑒 is an isomorphism.

Proof. By hypothesis 𝛼∘𝑒=𝛽∘𝑒 so if 𝑒 is an isomorphism 𝛼=𝛼∘𝑒∘𝑒−1=𝛽∘𝑒∘𝑒−1=𝛽 as required.

Conversely if 𝛼=𝛽, then 𝛼∘1𝑌=𝛽∘1𝑌 so there is a morphism 𝑖:𝑌→𝑋 such that 𝑒∘𝑖=1𝑌. Therefore 𝑒 is split-epic and monic (2.6.135) and therefore an isomorphism (2.6.36). ∎

Proposition 2.6.137
Let (𝑋,𝑒) be an equaliser for 𝛼,𝛽:𝑌⇉𝑍. Suppose 𝜙:𝑋′→∼𝑋 be an isomorphism. Then (𝑋′,𝑒∘𝜙) is also an equaliser for (𝛼,𝛽).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

By definition of Equaliser, (𝑋,𝑒) is a limit for the diagram 𝐹:𝟐→𝒞︀ determined by (𝛼,𝛽), and since 𝛼∘𝑒=𝛽∘𝑒, (𝑋′,𝑒∘𝜙) is a cone for 𝐹. As 𝑒∘𝜙=𝑒∘𝜙, the isomorphism 𝜙:𝑋′→𝑋 is (tautologically) an isomorphism of cones (𝑋′,𝑒∘𝜙)→(𝑋,𝑒), so by (2.6.79) (𝑋′,𝑒∘𝜙) is also a limit for 𝐹, that is, an equaliser for (𝛼,𝛽). ∎

Proposition 2.6.138
Let (𝑋,𝑒) be a coequaliser for 𝛼,𝛽:𝑌⇉𝑍. Suppose 𝜙:𝑋→∼𝑋′ is an isomorphism. Then (𝑋′,𝜙∘𝑒) is also a coequaliser for (𝛼,𝛽).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

By definition of Coequaliser, (𝑋,𝑒) is a colimit for the diagram 𝐹:𝟐→𝒞︀ determined by (𝛼,𝛽), and since 𝑒∘𝛼=𝑒∘𝛽, (𝑋′,𝜙∘𝑒) is a co-cone for 𝐹. As 𝜙∘𝑒=𝜙∘𝑒, the isomorphism 𝜙:𝑋→𝑋′ is (tautologically) an isomorphism of co-cones (𝑋,𝑒)→(𝑋′,𝜙∘𝑒), so by (2.6.90) (𝑋′,𝜙∘𝑒) is also a colimit for 𝐹, that is, a coequaliser for (𝛼,𝛽). ∎

Proposition 2.6.139

A diagram in 𝐒𝐞𝐭

is an equaliser if and only if 𝑖 is injective and

Im(𝑖)={𝑦∈𝑌|𝛼(𝑦)=𝛽(𝑦)}
Definition 2.6.140 (Coequaliser)

Consider a commutative diagram in a category 𝒞︀

such that 𝜋∘𝛼=𝜋∘𝛽. We say that 𝜋 is a co-equaliser for (𝛼,𝛽) if for all 𝜋′:𝑌→𝑍′ such that 𝜋′∘𝛼=𝜋′∘𝛽 there is a unique factorisation

This is equivalent to (𝑍,𝜋) being a colimit for the obvious functor 𝐹:𝟐→𝒞︀ where 𝟐 denotes the category ·⇉·.

Proposition 2.6.141

The following diagram is a coequaliser

if and only if the following is an equaliser in 𝐒𝐞𝐭 for all 𝑊∈𝒞︀

Proof. We see from the definition that 𝜋 is a coequaliser for (𝛼,𝛽) if and only if Mor(𝜋,𝑊) is injective and

Im(Mor(𝜋,𝑊))={𝜋′:𝑌→𝑊|𝜋′∘𝛼=𝜋′∘𝛽}

which is exactly the criteria (2.6.139) for an equaliser in 𝐒𝐞𝐭. ∎

Proposition 2.6.142 (Left Adjoints Preserve Coequalisers)
Let 𝒞︀⇌𝐺𝐹𝒟︀ a pair of adjoint functors. Then 𝐹 preserves coequalisers and 𝐺 preserves equalisers.

Proof. Consider a coequaliser

By the adjoint relationship we have a commutative diagram for all 𝐷∈𝒟︀

By (2.6.141) the bottom row is an equaliser, and so by the isomorphisms so is the top row. Therefore we conclude by the same result that the following is an equaliser as required

 ∎

Proposition 2.6.143 (Coequalisers in a Reflective Subcategory)

Let 𝒞︀⇌𝐺𝐹𝒟︀ be adjoint functors with 𝐺 fully faithful and unit 𝜂; by (2.6.73) we may regard 𝒟︀ as a full subcategory of 𝒞︀ via 𝐺. Let 𝛼,𝛽:𝑋⇉𝑌 be morphisms of 𝒟︀ and suppose 𝜋:𝑌→𝑍 is a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽) in 𝒞︀. Then 𝜂𝑍∘𝜋:𝑌→𝐹(𝑍) is a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽) in 𝒟︀.

In particular if every pair of morphisms of 𝒟︀ has a coequaliser in 𝒞︀ then 𝒟︀ has all coequalisers.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Write 𝑞≔𝜂𝑍∘𝜋. Since 𝜋∘𝛼=𝜋∘𝛽 we have 𝑞∘𝛼=𝜂𝑍∘𝜋∘𝛼=𝜂𝑍∘𝜋∘𝛽=𝑞∘𝛽.

Suppose 𝑞′:𝑌→𝐻 is a morphism of 𝒟︀ with 𝑞′∘𝛼=𝑞′∘𝛽. Regarding 𝑞′ as a morphism of 𝒞︀ (as 𝒟︀ is a subcategory), the universal property of the coequaliser 𝜋 gives a unique morphism 𝑞̃:𝑍→𝐻 of 𝒞︀ such that 𝑞̃∘𝜋=𝑞′.

Since 𝐹 is left adjoint to 𝐺 with unit 𝜂 (2.6.71), there is a bijection Mor(𝐹(𝑍),𝐻)→∼Mor(𝑍,𝐻), 𝜙↦𝜙∘𝜂𝑍, so there is a unique morphism 𝑞―:𝐹(𝑍)→𝐻 of 𝒟︀ such that 𝑞―∘𝜂𝑍=𝑞̃. Then

𝑞―∘𝑞=𝑞―∘𝜂𝑍∘𝜋=𝑞̃∘𝜋=𝑞′

so 𝑞― is a factorisation of 𝑞′ through 𝑞.

Suppose 𝑞―′ is another morphism of 𝒟︀ with 𝑞―′∘𝑞=𝑞′, that is (𝑞―′∘𝜂𝑍)∘𝜋=𝑞′=𝑞̃∘𝜋. As 𝜋 is a coequaliser it is an epimorphism (2.6.135), whence 𝑞―′∘𝜂𝑍=𝑞̃, and by the uniqueness of the factorisation above 𝑞―′=𝑞―.

Therefore 𝑞=𝜂𝑍∘𝜋 satisfies the universal property of the coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽) in 𝒟︀.

For the final statement, if every pair of morphisms of 𝒟︀ has a coequaliser in 𝒞︀ then the above applies to every such pair, so 𝒟︀ has all coequalisers. ∎

2.6.18 Pullback and Kernel Pairs

Definition 2.6.144 (Pullback)

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑍, 𝑔:𝑌→𝑍 be morphisms in 𝒞︀. We say (𝑊,𝑝1,𝑝2), with 𝑝1:𝑊→𝑋 and 𝑝2:𝑊→𝑌, is a pullback of (𝑓,𝑔) if 𝑓∘𝑝1=𝑔∘𝑝2, and for every (𝑊′,𝑝1′,𝑝2′) with 𝑓∘𝑝1′=𝑔∘𝑝2′ there is a unique morphism 𝜙:𝑊′→𝑊 such that 𝑝1∘𝜙=𝑝1′ and 𝑝2∘𝜙=𝑝2′

This is equivalent to (𝑊,{𝑝1,𝑝2}) being a limit for the evident diagram 𝐹:𝚲→𝒞︀ determined by (𝑓,𝑔), where 𝚲≔{𝑎→𝑐←𝑏} denotes the category with three objects and, besides identities, two further morphisms 𝑎→𝑐, 𝑏→𝑐. We write 𝑊≕𝑋×𝑍𝑌.

Proposition 2.6.145 (Pullback from Products and Equalisers)
Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑍, 𝑔:𝑌→𝑍 be morphisms such that 𝑋×𝑌 exists with projections 𝜋𝑋,𝜋𝑌, and such that (𝑊,𝑒)≔eq(𝑓∘𝜋𝑋,𝑔∘𝜋𝑌:𝑋×𝑌→𝑍) exists. Then (𝑊,𝜋𝑋∘𝑒,𝜋𝑌∘𝑒) is a pullback of (𝑓,𝑔).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Write 𝑝1≔𝜋𝑋∘𝑒, 𝑝2≔𝜋𝑌∘𝑒. By definition of the equaliser, 𝑓∘𝜋𝑋∘𝑒=𝑔∘𝜋𝑌∘𝑒, that is 𝑓∘𝑝1=𝑔∘𝑝2.

Suppose (𝑊′,𝑝1′,𝑝2′) satisfies 𝑓∘𝑝1′=𝑔∘𝑝2′. By the universal property of the product there is a unique ℎ:𝑊′→𝑋×𝑌 with 𝜋𝑋∘ℎ=𝑝1′, 𝜋𝑌∘ℎ=𝑝2′. Then 𝑓∘𝜋𝑋∘ℎ=𝑓∘𝑝1′=𝑔∘𝑝2′=𝑔∘𝜋𝑌∘ℎ, so ℎ equalises (𝑓∘𝜋𝑋,𝑔∘𝜋𝑌), whence by the universal property of the equaliser there is a unique 𝜙:𝑊′→𝑊 with 𝑒∘𝜙=ℎ. Then 𝑝1∘𝜙=𝜋𝑋∘𝑒∘𝜙=𝜋𝑋∘ℎ=𝑝1′, and similarly 𝑝2∘𝜙=𝑝2′.

If 𝜙′ also satisfies 𝑝1∘𝜙′=𝑝1′, 𝑝2∘𝜙′=𝑝2′, then 𝜋𝑋∘(𝑒∘𝜙′)=𝑝1′=𝜋𝑋∘ℎ and 𝜋𝑌∘(𝑒∘𝜙′)=𝑝2′=𝜋𝑌∘ℎ, so by uniqueness in the universal property of the product, 𝑒∘𝜙′=ℎ; as 𝑒 is monic (2.6.135), 𝜙′=𝜙. ∎

Definition 2.6.146 (Kernel Pair)

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism. A kernel pair of 𝑓 is a pullback (𝑍,𝑝1,𝑝2) of (𝑓,𝑓), that is 𝑝1,𝑝2:𝑍→𝑋 with 𝑓∘𝑝1=𝑓∘𝑝2, universal among such pairs

In 𝐒𝐞𝐭, the kernel pair of 𝑓 is precisely the relation {(𝑥,𝑥′)∈𝑋×𝑋|𝑓(𝑥)=𝑓(𝑥′)}⊆𝑋×𝑋, together with its two projections: it records exactly which pairs of elements 𝑓 identifies. So 𝑓 is injective if and only if this relation is trivial, i.e. reduces to the diagonal {(𝑥,𝑥)|𝑥∈𝑋} – this is the picture behind (2.6.147) below, which characterises monomorphisms in general as those morphisms whose kernel pair is trivial.

Proposition 2.6.147 (Monomorphisms via Kernel Pairs)
Let 𝜇:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism with a kernel pair (𝑍,𝑝1,𝑝2). Then 𝜇 is monic if and only if 𝑝1=𝑝2.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

(⇐) Suppose 𝑝1=𝑝2. If 𝑎,𝑏:𝑊→𝑋 satisfy 𝜇∘𝑎=𝜇∘𝑏, then by the universal property of the kernel pair there is a unique 𝜓:𝑊→𝑍 with 𝑝1∘𝜓=𝑎 and 𝑝2∘𝜓=𝑏; since 𝑝1=𝑝2 this gives 𝑎=𝑝1∘𝜓=𝑝2∘𝜓=𝑏. So 𝜇 is monic.

(⇒) Suppose 𝜇 is monic. Since 𝜇∘𝑝1=𝜇∘𝑝2 by definition of the kernel pair (2.6.146), monicity of 𝜇 gives 𝑝1=𝑝2. ∎

Corollary 2.6.148 (Monomorphisms have Trivial Kernel Pair)
Let 𝜇:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism. Then 𝜇 is monic if and only if (𝑋,1𝑋,1𝑋) is a kernel pair of 𝜇.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

(⇐) This is the case 𝑍≔𝑋, 𝑝1=𝑝2≔1𝑋 of (2.6.147) (⇐).

(⇒) Suppose 𝜇 is monic. Given 𝑎,𝑏:𝑊→𝑋 with 𝜇∘𝑎=𝜇∘𝑏, monicity gives 𝑎=𝑏; then 𝜙≔𝑎 satisfies 1𝑋∘𝜙=𝑎 and 1𝑋∘𝜙=𝑏 (as 𝑎=𝑏), and is the unique such morphism, since any 𝜙′ with 1𝑋∘𝜙′=𝑎 must equal 𝑎. So (𝑋,1𝑋,1𝑋) satisfies the universal property of a kernel pair of 𝜇 (2.6.146). ∎

Proposition 2.6.149 (Regular Epimorphism is the Coequaliser of its Kernel Pair)
Let 𝑒:𝑋→𝑌 be a regular epimorphism with kernel pair (𝑍,𝑝1,𝑝2). Then 𝑒 is the coequaliser of (𝑝1,𝑝2).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Since 𝑒 is regular, by (2.6.158) there are morphisms 𝛾,𝛿:𝑊⇉𝑋 such that 𝑒 is the coequaliser of (𝛾,𝛿). Since 𝑒∘𝛾=𝑒∘𝛿, the universal property of the kernel pair (𝑍,𝑝1,𝑝2) gives a unique morphism ℎ:𝑊→𝑍 with 𝑝1∘ℎ=𝛾 and 𝑝2∘ℎ=𝛿.

By definition of the kernel pair, 𝑒∘𝑝1=𝑒∘𝑝2. Suppose 𝑘:𝑋→𝑉 satisfies 𝑘∘𝑝1=𝑘∘𝑝2. Then

𝑘∘𝛾=𝑘∘𝑝1∘ℎ=𝑘∘𝑝2∘ℎ=𝑘∘𝛿

so, as 𝑒 is the coequaliser of (𝛾,𝛿), there is a unique morphism 𝑙:𝑌→𝑉 such that 𝑙∘𝑒=𝑘. Since 𝑒 is (in particular) an epimorphism (2.6.158), this 𝑙 is the unique morphism satisfying 𝑙∘𝑒=𝑘 among all morphisms 𝑌→𝑉, in particular the unique one factoring 𝑘 through 𝑒. So 𝑒 satisfies the universal property of the coequaliser of (𝑝1,𝑝2). ∎

2.6.19 Kernels and Cokernels

Proposition 2.6.150 (Kernel)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category (2.6.54). Suppose we have a sequence

ker(𝛼)⟶𝑖𝑋⟶𝛼𝑌

then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑖 is the equaliser of (𝛼,0)
  2. 𝛼∘𝑖=0 and 𝛼∘𝑖′=0⟹∃!𝑒s.t.𝑖∘𝑒=𝑖′

In this case we say that (𝑖,ker(𝛼)) is the kernel of 𝛼

Lemma 2.6.151 (𝑓 monic ⟹ker(𝑓)=0)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category and 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 monic. Then ker(𝑓)=0.

Dually 𝑓 epic ⟹coker(𝑓)=0.

Proof. Evidentally 𝑓∘0=00,𝑋 and for any object 𝑋′ we have a unique morphism 0𝑋′,0:𝑋′→0, so satisfies the uniqueness property. ∎
Remark 2.6.152
The converse does not hold, for we may define a monoid homomorphism 𝑓:ℕ→ℕ given by 𝑓(𝑛)≔min(𝑛,1). Then 𝑓 is a homomorphism, ker(𝑓)={0} but 𝑓 is not injective.
Proposition 2.6.153 (Cokernel)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category (2.6.54). Suppose we have a sequence

𝑋⟶𝛼𝑌⟶𝜋coker(𝛼)

then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝜋 is the coequaliser of (𝛼,0),
  2. 𝜋∘𝛼=0 and 𝜋′∘𝛼=0⟹∃!ℎs.t.ℎ∘𝜋=𝜋′,

In this case we say that (𝜋,coker(𝛼)) is the cokernel of 𝑓

Lemma 2.6.154 (Kernels and Cokernels swap under 𝒞︀op)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category and 𝛼:𝑋→𝑌 a morphism, with kernel ker(𝛼)⟶𝑖𝑋 and cokernel 𝑌⟶𝜋coker(𝛼). Regarding 𝑖 and 𝜋 as morphisms of 𝒞︀op,

(ker(𝛼),𝑖)is a cokernel of𝛼opin𝒞︀op,(coker(𝛼),𝜋)is a kernel of𝛼opin𝒞︀op.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

The defining property of (ker(𝛼),𝑖) (2.6.150) – namely 𝛼∘𝑖=0, and for every 𝑖′:𝑋′→𝑋 with 𝛼∘𝑖′=0 there is a unique 𝑒:𝑋′→ker(𝛼) with 𝑖∘𝑒=𝑖′ – is, upon reversing every arrow, exactly the defining property (2.6.153) of (ker(𝛼),𝑖) as a cokernel of 𝛼op in 𝒞︀op. The dual statement follows similarly. ∎

Proposition 2.6.155 (Left Adjoints Preserve Cokernels)

Let 𝒞︀,𝒟︀ be pointed categories and 𝒞︀⇌𝐺𝐹𝒟︀ a pair of adjoint functors.

Then 𝐹 preserves cokernels and 𝐺 preserves kernels.

Proof. By (2.6.75) we see that 𝐹 and 𝐺 preserve zero morphisms. Therefore we are done by (2.6.142) since a cokernel of 𝑓 is just the coequaliser of (𝑓,0). ∎

2.6.20 Normal, Regular and Extremal Morphisms

In a category which is not balanced, monic and epic are not always the “right” notions to characterise isomorphisms; the following refinements repair this.

Definition 2.6.156 (Extremal Epimorphism / Monomorphism)

An epimorphism 𝑒:𝑋→𝑌 is extremal if whenever 𝑒=𝑚∘𝑓 for some monomorphism 𝑚, then 𝑚 is an isomorphism.

Dually, a monomorphism 𝑚:𝑋→𝑌 is extremal if whenever 𝑚=𝑓∘𝑒 for some epimorphism 𝑒, then 𝑒 is an isomorphism.

Proposition 2.6.157

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑓 is an isomorphism
  2. 𝑓 is a monomorphism and an extremal epimorphism
  3. 𝑓 is an extremal monomorphism and an epimorphism

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Being an isomorphism is a self-dual notion, and monic/epic swap under passing to 𝒞︀op (2.6.33), so condition c) is precisely condition b) applied in 𝒞︀op. Hence it suffices to prove a) ⟺ b); applying this to 𝒞︀op then gives a) ⟺ c).

a) ⟹ b) An isomorphism is trivially monic and epic; if 𝑓 is an isomorphism and 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑔 then by (2.6.37), 𝑚 is an isomorphism, so 𝑓 is an extremal epimorphism.

b) ⟹ a) Suppose 𝑓 is monic and an extremal epimorphism. The trivial factorisation 𝑓=𝑓∘1𝑋 exhibits 𝑓 as a monomorphism through which 𝑓 factors, so by extremality 𝑓 is an isomorphism. ∎

Definition 2.6.158 (Regular Epimorphism / Monomorphism)

An epimorphism 𝑒:𝑋→𝑌 is regular if there exist morphisms 𝛼,𝛽:𝑊⇉𝑋 such that 𝑒 is the coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽).

Dually, a monomorphism 𝑚:𝑋→𝑌 is regular if there exist morphisms 𝛼,𝛽:𝑌⇉𝑍 such that 𝑚 is the equaliser of (𝛼,𝛽).

Definition 2.6.159 (Normal Epimorphism / Monomorphism)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category (2.6.54). An epimorphism 𝑒:𝑋→𝑌 is conormal if (𝑒,𝑌) is the cokernel of some morphism 𝛼:𝑊→𝑋.

Dually, a monomorphism 𝑚:𝑋→𝑌 is normal if (𝑚,𝑋) is the kernel of some morphism 𝛼:𝑌→𝑍.

Proposition 2.6.160 (Normal, Regular and Extremal Morphisms)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category. Then every normal monomorphism (resp. conormal epimorphism) is regular.

In a general category 𝒞︀ every regular monomorphism (resp. epimorphism) is an extremal monomorphism (resp. epimorphism).

In summary

𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐥 (𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐥) ⟹𝐫𝐞𝐠𝐮𝐥𝐚𝐫⟹𝐞𝐱𝐭𝐫𝐞𝐦𝐚𝐥⟹𝐦𝐨𝐧𝐢𝐜 (𝐞𝐩𝐢𝐜)

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

(Normal ⟹ regular) If 𝑒 is a normal monomorphism, then by (2.6.150) 𝑒 is the equaliser of (𝛼,0) for some 𝛼, so 𝑒 is regular.

(Regular ⟹ extremal) Suppose 𝑚:𝑋→𝑌 is the equaliser of 𝛼,𝛽:𝑌⇉𝑊, and 𝑚=ℎ∘𝑒 for some epimorphism 𝑒:𝑋→𝑍. Since 𝛼∘𝑚=𝛽∘𝑚 we get (𝛼∘ℎ)∘𝑒=(𝛽∘ℎ)∘𝑒, and as 𝑒 is epic, 𝛼∘ℎ=𝛽∘ℎ. Hence ℎ is equalised by (𝛼,𝛽), so by the universal property of the equaliser there is a unique 𝑘:𝑍→𝑋 with 𝑚∘𝑘=ℎ.

Then 𝑚∘(𝑘∘𝑒)=ℎ∘𝑒=𝑚=𝑚∘1𝑋, and since equalisers are monic (2.6.135) we may cancel 𝑚 to get 𝑘∘𝑒=1𝑋, so 𝑒 is split-monic. As 𝑒 is also epic, (2.6.36) gives that 𝑒 is an isomorphism, and 𝑚 is extremal.

Dually, every conormal epimorphism is regular and every regular epimorphism is extremal. ∎

For balanced categories we can reverse the implication

Proposition 2.6.161 (Balanced Categories via Extremal Morphisms)

Let 𝒞︀ be a category. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝒞︀ is balanced
  2. every monomorphism in 𝒞︀ is extremal
  3. every epimorphism in 𝒞︀ is extremal

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Being balanced is a self-dual notion: monic and epic swap under passing to 𝒞︀op (2.6.33) while isomorphisms remain isomorphisms, so 𝒞︀ is balanced iff 𝒞︀op is. Likewise, by the “Dually” clause of (2.6.156), a morphism is an extremal epimorphism in 𝒞︀ iff it is an extremal monomorphism in 𝒞︀op. So it suffices to prove a) ⟺ b); applying this to 𝒞︀op then gives a) ⟺ c).

a) ⟹ b) Suppose 𝒞︀ is balanced and 𝑚:𝑋→𝑌 is monic. If 𝑚=𝑓∘𝑒 for some epimorphism 𝑒:𝑋→𝑊, then 𝑒 is also monic: if 𝑒𝑔1=𝑒𝑔2 for 𝑔1,𝑔2:𝑍→𝑋 then 𝑓∘𝑒∘𝑔1=𝑓∘𝑒∘𝑔2, that is 𝑚𝑔1=𝑚𝑔2, whence 𝑔1=𝑔2 as 𝑚 is monic. As 𝑒 is both monic and epic, balancedness gives that 𝑒 is an isomorphism, so 𝑚 is extremal.

b) ⟹ a) Suppose every monomorphism is extremal and 𝑓 is both monic and epic. Then 𝑓 is an extremal monomorphism, so by (2.6.157) (with 𝑓 extremal monic and epic) 𝑓 is an isomorphism. So 𝒞︀ is balanced. ∎

Lemma 2.6.162

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category and 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 a morphism for which ker(coker(𝑓)) exists. Then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑓 is normal
  2. 𝑓=ker(coker(𝑓))

Dually, suppose coker(ker(𝑓)) exists then the following are equivalent

  1. 𝑓 is conormal
  2. 𝑓=coker(ker(𝑓))

Proof. b) ⟹ a) immediate.

a) ⟹ b) By assumption 𝜋:𝑌→coker(𝑓) and 𝑖:ker(𝜋)→𝑌 exists so we have a commutative diagram.

By definition of the cokernel 𝜋∘𝑓=0 whence there is a unique 𝜙:𝑋→ker(𝜋) such that 𝑖∘𝜙=𝑓.

As 𝑔∘𝑓=0 then by definition there is a unique 𝜃:coker(𝑓)→𝑍 such that 𝜃∘𝜋=𝑔.

Therefore 𝑔∘𝑖=𝜃∘𝜋∘𝑖=0. So by definition there is a unique 𝜓:ker(𝜋)→𝑋 such that 𝑓∘𝜓=𝑖.

Then 𝑖∘𝜙∘𝜓=𝑓∘𝜓=𝑖 and since 𝑖 is a monomorphism (2.6.135) 𝜙∘𝜓=1ker(𝜋). Similarly 𝑓∘𝜓∘𝜙=𝑖∘𝜙=𝑓 and since 𝑓=ker(𝑔) is a monomorphism (2.6.135) 𝜓∘𝜙=1𝑋. Therefore 𝑋 and ker(𝜋) are isomorphic via 𝜙 and 𝜓, and since 𝑖∘𝜙=𝑓, by (2.6.137) 𝑋 is also a kernel for 𝜋 as required.

Dually, 𝒞︀op is again pointed with the same zero object (2.6.54), monic/epic swap under passing to 𝒞︀op (2.6.33), and ker(𝑓), coker(𝑓) computed in 𝒞︀ are precisely coker(𝑓), ker(𝑓) computed in 𝒞︀op (2.6.154). So applying the equivalence just proved to 𝑓 regarded as a morphism of 𝒞︀op shows 𝑓 is conormal iff 𝑓=coker(ker(𝑓)). ∎

Definition 2.6.163

We say a pointed category 𝒞︀ is

  • normal if every monomorphism is normal (i.e. a kernel of some morphism).
  • conormal if every epimorphism is conormal (i.e. the cokernel of some morphism).
  • binormal if it is both normal and conormal.
Corollary 2.6.164
A normal (resp. conormal, binormal) category is balanced.
Example 2.6.165

We will see that the categories 𝐀𝐛𝐆𝐫𝐩 and 𝐴-𝐌𝐨𝐝 are binormal (and therefore every epi and mono is regular), whereas 𝐆𝐫𝐩 is only conormal. All three are balanced.

We also see may verify directly that in 𝐒𝐞𝐭 every monomorphism and epimorphism is regular.

Proposition 2.6.166

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category and 𝑓 a morphism. Then the following are equivalent

  1. ker(𝑓)=0
  2. 𝑓∘𝑔=0⟹𝑔=0

Dually, the following are equivalent

  1. coker(𝑓)=0
  2. 𝑔∘𝑓=0⟹𝑔=0

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Write 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 and 𝑖:ker(𝑓)→𝑋 for the kernel of 𝑓, so by (2.6.150), 𝑓∘𝑖=0 and for every 𝑖′:𝑊→𝑋 with 𝑓∘𝑖′=0 there is a unique 𝑒:𝑊→ker(𝑓) with 𝑖∘𝑒=𝑖′.

a) ⟹ b) Suppose ker(𝑓)=0 and 𝑓∘𝑔=0 for some 𝑔:𝑊→𝑋. By the universal property there is a unique 𝑒:𝑊→0 with 𝑖∘𝑒=𝑔; as 𝑖=00,𝑋 (since ker(𝑓)=0) and 𝑒=0𝑊,0 (since 0 is terminal), 𝑔=𝑖∘𝑒=0𝑊,𝑋=0.

b) ⟹ a) Let 𝜄:0→𝑋 be the canonical morphism. Since 0 is initial, 𝑓∘𝜄=0 automatically. Given any 𝑖′:𝑊→𝑋 with 𝑓∘𝑖′=0, the hypothesis gives 𝑖′=0, that is 𝑖′=𝜄∘0𝑊,0, and 0𝑊,0:𝑊→0 is the unique such morphism since 0 is terminal. So (0,𝜄) satisfies the universal property of ker(𝑓) (2.6.150), whence ker(𝑓)=0.

Dually, 𝒞︀op is again pointed with the same zero object (2.6.54), and ker(𝑓), coker(𝑓) computed in 𝒞︀ are precisely coker(𝑓), ker(𝑓) computed in 𝒞︀op (2.6.154), so applying the above to 𝑓 regarded as a morphism of 𝒞︀op gives the dual equivalence. ∎

2.6.21 Images and Coimages

In order to define exact sequence we need a categorical notion of image. We also define its dual.

Definition 2.6.167 (Image)

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism in 𝒞︀. An image for 𝑓 is a triple (Im(𝑓),𝑒,𝑚) such that 𝑚 is monic, we have a commutative triangle

and for any other factorisation 𝑓=𝑚′∘𝑒′ with 𝑚′ monic there exists a unique morphism 𝑔:Im(𝑓)→𝑇 such that 𝑚′∘𝑔=𝑚.

Note that any such 𝑔 satisfies 𝑔∘𝑒=𝑒′, since 𝑚′∘(𝑔∘𝑒)=𝑚∘𝑒=𝑓=𝑚′∘𝑒′ and 𝑚′ is monic.

The factorisations of 𝑓 through a monomorphism constitute a category SubObjFactors(𝑓), with objects the triples (𝑇,𝑒′,𝑚′) as above and a morphism (𝑇,𝑒′,𝑚′)→(𝑇″,𝑒″,𝑚″) given by a morphism 𝑔:𝑇→𝑇″ such that 𝑚″∘𝑔=𝑚′. So an image for 𝑓 is precisely an initial object (2.6.48) of SubObjFactors(𝑓), and is therefore unique up to unique isomorphism.

There is a dual notion

Definition 2.6.168 (Coimage)

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism in 𝒞︀. A coimage for 𝑓 is a triple (Coim(𝑓),𝑒,𝑚) such that 𝑒 is epic and we have a commutative triangle

and for any other factorisation 𝑓=𝑚′∘𝑒′ with 𝑒′ epic there exists a unique morphism 𝑔:𝑇→Coim(𝑓) such that 𝑔∘𝑒′=𝑒.

Note that any such 𝑔 satisfies 𝑚∘𝑔=𝑚′, since (𝑚∘𝑔)∘𝑒′=𝑚∘𝑒=𝑓=𝑚′∘𝑒′ and 𝑒′ is epic.

Dually, the factorisations of 𝑓 through an epimorphism constitute a category QuotObjFactors(𝑓), with objects the triples (𝑇,𝑒′,𝑚′) as above and a morphism (𝑇,𝑒′,𝑚′)→(𝑇″,𝑒″,𝑚″) given by a morphism 𝑔:𝑇→𝑇″ such that 𝑔∘𝑒′=𝑒″. So a coimage for 𝑓 is precisely a terminal object (2.6.50) of QuotObjFactors(𝑓), and is therefore unique up to unique isomorphism.

Remark 2.6.169
We note that (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) is an image in 𝒞︀ if and only if (𝐼,𝑚op,𝑒op) is a coimage in 𝒞︀op.
Lemma 2.6.170

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism and (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) an image. Suppose 𝒞︀ has equalisers, then 𝑒 is epic.

Dually if (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) is a coimage for 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌, and suppose 𝒞︀ has coequalisers. Then 𝑚 is monic.

Proof. Consider the diagram

and suppose 𝛼∘𝑒=𝛽∘𝑒. Let 𝐾=coeq(𝛼,𝛽), then by definition there is a morphism 𝑔:𝑋→𝐾 such that 𝑖∘𝑔=𝑒. Then (𝑚∘𝑖)∘𝑔=𝑓 is a factorisation with 𝑚∘𝑖 a monomorphism (2.6.135). Then by the universal property of images there is a morphism 𝑗:Im(𝑓)→𝐾 such that (𝑚𝑓∘𝑖)∘𝑗=𝑚. As 𝑚 is monic 𝑖∘𝑗=1Im(𝑓) and so 𝑖 is split-epic and therefore an isomorphism (2.6.36). ∎

Lemma 2.6.171
Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category and 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 a monomorphism. Then the triple (𝑋,1𝑋,𝑓) is an image for 𝑓.

Proof. Denote the morphism by 𝑓 and suppose we have another factorisation 𝑋→𝑓̄𝑊→𝑖𝑌 with 𝑖 monic, then we have a commutative diagram

and we may show by the argument in (2.6.167) that the factorisation is unique. ∎

Lemma 2.6.172 (Images and Coimages are Preserved under Isomorphism)

Let (𝑇,𝑒,𝑚) be an image of 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 and 𝜃:𝑇→∼𝑇′ an isomorphism. Then (𝑇′,𝜃∘𝑒,𝑚∘𝜃−1) is also an image of 𝑓.

Dually, if (𝑇,𝑒,𝑚) is a coimage of 𝑓 and 𝜃:𝑇→∼𝑇′ an isomorphism, then (𝑇′,𝜃∘𝑒,𝑚∘𝜃−1) is also a coimage of 𝑓.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

For the image case 𝜃 determines a well-defined isomorphism in SubObjFactors(𝑓)

(𝑇,𝑒,𝑚)⟶∼(𝑇′,𝜃∘𝑒,𝑚∘𝜃−1)

As isomorphisms preserve initial objects (2.6.49) we see that the right hand side is an image.

Dually, the coimage case follows by applying the image case to 𝑓op in 𝒞︀op (2.6.169). ∎

2.6.22 Epi-Mono Factorisations

We saw that under mild conditions image and coimage yield an epi-mono factorisation. Strengthening this factorisation can ensure functorial properties; concretely, in an algebraic category, upgrading an epimorphism to a regular epimorphism is exactly upgrading from the (possibly too weak) categorical notion of epimorphism to the familiar notion of a surjective homomorphism (2.6.195).

Definition 2.6.173

Let 𝒞︀ be a category and 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 a morphism. We say that 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒 is

  • a regular epi-mono factorisation if 𝑚 is a monomorphism and 𝑒 is a regular epimorphism.
  • an epi-regular mono factorisation if 𝑚 is a regular monomorphism and 𝑒 is an epimorphism

We note that 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒 is a regular epi-mono (resp. epi-regular mono) factorisation if and only if 𝑓op=𝑒op∘𝑚op is an epi-regular mono (resp. regular epi-mono) factorisation.

Proposition 2.6.174 (Regular Epi-Mono Factorisation)

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism with regular epi-mono factorisation 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒. Then (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) is an image and every image is a regular epi-mono factorisation.

Dually, let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism with epi-regular mono factorisation 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒. Then (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) is a coimage and every coimage is an epi-regular mono factorisation.

Proof. Consider the diagram

where 𝑒 is a coequaliser for (𝛼,𝛽), 𝑚′ is a monomorphism and 𝑒′ is a general morphism. Then we need to prove the existence of a unique morphism (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚)→(𝐼′,𝑒′,𝑚′). Since 𝑒 coequalises (𝛼,𝛽), 𝑒∘𝛼=𝑒∘𝛽, so

𝑓∘𝛼=𝑚∘𝑒∘𝛼=𝑚∘𝑒∘𝛽=𝑓∘𝛽

and as 𝑓=𝑚′∘𝑒′ with 𝑚′ monic, 𝑚′∘𝑒′∘𝛼=𝑓∘𝛼=𝑓∘𝛽=𝑚′∘𝑒′∘𝛽 gives 𝑒′∘𝛼=𝑒′∘𝛽. Therefore by definition of the coequaliser there is a unique 𝜓 such that 𝜓∘𝑒=𝑒′. Further

𝑚′∘𝜓∘𝑒=𝑚′∘𝑒′=𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒

and as 𝑒 is an epimorphism (2.6.135) we conclude that 𝑚′∘𝜓=𝑚, as required for a morphism (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚)→(𝐼′,𝑒′,𝑚′) in SubObjFactors(𝑓) (2.6.167). If 𝜓′ also satisfies 𝑚′∘𝜓′=𝑚, then 𝑚′∘𝜓=𝑚=𝑚′∘𝜓′, and since 𝑚′ is monic 𝜓=𝜓′; so 𝜓 is unique.

Let (𝐼′,𝑒′,𝑚′) be an image, so 𝑚′ is in particular monic and the above applies. As images are unique up to isomorphism (2.6.167) there is an isomorphism 𝜃:𝐼→∼𝐼′ such that 𝑚′∘𝜃=𝑚; then

𝑚′∘(𝜃∘𝑒)=(𝑚′∘𝜃)∘𝑒=𝑚∘𝑒=𝑓=𝑚′∘𝑒′

and as 𝑚′ is monic, 𝜃∘𝑒=𝑒′. Since 𝑒 is a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽) and 𝜃 is an isomorphism with 𝜃∘𝑒=𝑒′, post-composing the coequalising cocone for 𝑒 with 𝜃 shows 𝑒′ is again a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽), as colimits are preserved under isomorphisms (2.6.90); hence 𝑒′ is regular (2.6.158), as required. ∎

Proposition 2.6.175 (Regular Epi-Mono)
𝐒𝐞𝐭 has regular epi-mono factorisations.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism in 𝐒𝐞𝐭. Set Im(𝑓)≔{𝑓(𝑥)|𝑥∈𝑋} and let 𝑚:Im(𝑓)↪︎𝑌 denote the inclusion, which is injective and therefore monic by (2.6.38). Let 𝑒:𝑋→Im(𝑓) be the corestriction of 𝑓, so that 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒.

Define 𝑅={(𝑥,𝑥′)∈𝑋×𝑋|𝑓(𝑥)=𝑓(𝑥′)} with projections 𝛼,𝛽:𝑅⇉𝑋, 𝛼(𝑥,𝑥′)=𝑥, 𝛽(𝑥,𝑥′)=𝑥′. We claim 𝑒 is the coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽).

First 𝑒∘𝛼=𝑒∘𝛽: for (𝑥,𝑥′)∈𝑅 we have 𝑓(𝑥)=𝑓(𝑥′) by definition of 𝑅, that is 𝑒(𝑥)=𝑒(𝑥′).

Now let 𝜋′:𝑋→𝑍 satisfy 𝜋′∘𝛼=𝜋′∘𝛽, that is 𝑓(𝑥)=𝑓(𝑥′)⟹𝜋′(𝑥)=𝜋′(𝑥′) for all 𝑥,𝑥′∈𝑋. Since every 𝑦∈Im(𝑓) is of the form 𝑓(𝑥) for some 𝑥∈𝑋, we may define 𝜓:Im(𝑓)→𝑍 by 𝜓(𝑦)=𝜋′(𝑥) for any such 𝑥; this is well-defined precisely because 𝑓(𝑥)=𝑓(𝑥′)=𝑦 implies 𝜋′(𝑥)=𝜋′(𝑥′). By construction 𝜓∘𝑒=𝜋′, and since 𝑒 is surjective onto Im(𝑓) by definition, any 𝜓′ with 𝜓′∘𝑒=𝜋′ agrees with 𝜓 at every point of Im(𝑓), so 𝜓 is the unique such factorisation.

Hence 𝑒 is a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽), so is a regular epimorphism (2.6.158). ∎

Lemma 2.6.176 (Diagonal Fill-In Lemma)

Let 𝑒:𝑋→𝐼 be a regular epimorphism and 𝑚′:𝐼′→𝑌 a monomorphism. Then for every commutative square

there is a unique 𝜃 such that 𝜃∘𝑒=𝑎. Furthermore it satisfies 𝑚′∘𝜃=𝑚.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Since 𝑒 is a regular epimorphism, by (2.6.158) there are morphisms 𝛼,𝛽:𝑊⇉𝑋 such that 𝑒 is the coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽).

We have 𝑒∘𝛼=𝑒∘𝛽, so 𝑚∘𝑒∘𝛼=𝑚∘𝑒∘𝛽, whence by commutativity of the square 𝑚′∘𝑎∘𝛼=𝑚′∘𝑎∘𝛽. As 𝑚′ is monic we may cancel it to get 𝑎∘𝛼=𝑎∘𝛽.

By the universal property of the coequaliser 𝑒 there is therefore a unique morphism 𝜃:𝐼→𝐼′ such that

𝜃∘𝑒=𝑎

We check that 𝜃 also satisfies the remaining identity: 𝑚′∘𝜃∘𝑒=𝑚′∘𝑎=𝑚∘𝑒, and since 𝑒 is an epimorphism (2.6.135) we may cancel it to get

𝑚′∘𝜃=𝑚

 ∎

Proposition 2.6.177 (Regular Epi-Mono Factorisation is Functorial)

Suppose 𝒞︀ has regular epi-mono factorisations 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒:𝑋→𝑌, 𝑓′=𝑚′∘𝑒′:𝑋′→𝑌′ and morphisms 𝑎:𝑋→𝑋′, 𝑏:𝑌→𝑌′ such that 𝑏∘𝑓=𝑓′∘𝑎. Then there is a unique morphism 𝜓𝑎,𝑏:𝐼→𝐼′ which makes the top square commute

Furthermore the whole diagram commutes and the construction is functorial: 𝜓1𝑋,1𝑌=1𝐼 (taking 𝑓′=𝑓, 𝑎=1𝑋, 𝑏=1𝑌), and given a further regular epi-mono factorisation 𝑓″=𝑚″∘𝑒″:𝑋″→𝑌″ and morphisms 𝑐:𝑋′→𝑋″, 𝑑:𝑌′→𝑌″ such that 𝑑∘𝑓′=𝑓″∘𝑐 (with induced comparison morphism 𝜓𝑐,𝑑:𝐼′→𝐼″), we have 𝜓𝑐,𝑑∘𝜓𝑎,𝑏=𝜓𝑐∘𝑎,𝑑∘𝑏.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Since 𝑒 is a regular epimorphism, by (2.6.158) there are morphisms 𝛼,𝛽:𝑊⇉𝑋 such that 𝑒 is the coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽).

We first show 𝑒′∘𝑎 coequalises (𝛼,𝛽). Since 𝑒∘𝛼=𝑒∘𝛽 we have 𝑓∘𝛼=𝑚∘𝑒∘𝛼=𝑚∘𝑒∘𝛽=𝑓∘𝛽, and so by hypothesis 𝑓′∘𝑎∘𝛼=𝑏∘𝑓∘𝛼=𝑏∘𝑓∘𝛽=𝑓′∘𝑎∘𝛽, that is 𝑚′∘𝑒′∘𝑎∘𝛼=𝑚′∘𝑒′∘𝑎∘𝛽. As 𝑚′ is monic we may cancel it to get (𝑒′∘𝑎)∘𝛼=(𝑒′∘𝑎)∘𝛽.

By the universal property of the coequaliser 𝑒 there is therefore a unique morphism 𝜓𝑎,𝑏:𝐼→𝐼′ such that

𝜓𝑎,𝑏∘𝑒=𝑒′∘𝑎

We check that 𝜓𝑎,𝑏 also satisfies the second required identity: 𝑚′∘𝜓𝑎,𝑏∘𝑒=𝑚′∘𝑒′∘𝑎=𝑓′∘𝑎=𝑏∘𝑓=𝑏∘𝑚∘𝑒, and since 𝑒 is an epimorphism (2.6.135) we may cancel it to get

𝑚′∘𝜓𝑎,𝑏=𝑏∘𝑚

so the diagram commutes.

Taking 𝑓′=𝑓, 𝑎=1𝑋, 𝑏=1𝑌 (a valid compatible pair since 1𝑌∘𝑓=𝑓=𝑓∘1𝑋), 1𝐼 satisfies 1𝐼∘𝑒=𝑒=𝑒∘1𝑋 and 𝑚∘1𝐼=𝑚=1𝑌∘𝑚, so by the uniqueness established above 𝜓1𝑋,1𝑌=1𝐼.

For the composition law, let 𝑐:𝑋′→𝑋″, 𝑑:𝑌′→𝑌″ satisfy 𝑑∘𝑓′=𝑓″∘𝑐, with induced comparison morphism 𝜓𝑐,𝑑:𝐼′→𝐼″. Then

(𝜓𝑐,𝑑∘𝜓𝑎,𝑏)∘𝑒=𝜓𝑐,𝑑∘(𝑒′∘𝑎)=(𝜓𝑐,𝑑∘𝑒′)∘𝑎=𝑒″∘𝑐∘𝑎=𝑒″∘(𝑐∘𝑎)

Note 𝑑∘𝑏∘𝑓=𝑑∘𝑓′∘𝑎=𝑓″∘𝑐∘𝑎=𝑓″∘(𝑐∘𝑎), so (𝑐∘𝑎,𝑑∘𝑏) is again a compatible pair, with induced comparison morphism 𝜓𝑐∘𝑎,𝑑∘𝑏:𝐼→𝐼″ satisfying 𝜓𝑐∘𝑎,𝑑∘𝑏∘𝑒=𝑒″∘(𝑐∘𝑎) by definition. Since both 𝜓𝑐,𝑑∘𝜓𝑎,𝑏 and 𝜓𝑐∘𝑎,𝑑∘𝑏 satisfy this same equation, and 𝜓𝑐∘𝑎,𝑑∘𝑏 is, by the uniqueness established above, the unique morphism 𝐼→𝐼″ doing so, we conclude

𝜓𝑐,𝑑∘𝜓𝑎,𝑏=𝜓𝑐∘𝑎,𝑑∘𝑏

 ∎

Proposition 2.6.178 (Regular Epi-Mono Factorisation is Unique)
Let 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒=𝑚′∘𝑒′ be two regular epi-mono factorisations, with 𝑒:𝑋→𝐼, 𝑒′:𝑋→𝐼′. Then there is a unique morphism 𝜃:𝐼→𝐼′ such that 𝑒′=𝜃∘𝑒. Furthermore it is an isomorphism and satisfies 𝑚′∘𝜃=𝑚.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Applying (2.6.177) to the factorisations (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) and (𝐼′,𝑒′,𝑚′) of 𝑓, with 𝑓′=𝑓, 𝑎=1𝑋, 𝑏=1𝑌, gives a unique morphism 𝜃:𝐼→𝐼′ such that 𝜃∘𝑒=𝑒′ and 𝑚′∘𝜃=𝑚.

Symmetrically, applying (2.6.177) to the factorisations (𝐼′,𝑒′,𝑚′) and (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) of 𝑓 (i.e. with the roles of the two factorisations swapped) gives a unique morphism 𝜃′:𝐼′→𝐼 such that 𝜃′∘𝑒′=𝑒 and 𝑚∘𝜃′=𝑚′.

By the composition law of (2.6.177), applied to the chain of factorisations (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚)→(𝐼′,𝑒′,𝑚′)→(𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) (i.e. 𝑓′=𝑓, 𝑓″=𝑓, with 𝑐=1𝑋, 𝑑=1𝑌, and 𝜃, 𝜃′ as the two successive comparison morphisms), 𝜃′∘𝜃 is the comparison morphism from (𝐼,𝑒,𝑚) to itself, and so equals 1𝐼 by the identity law of (2.6.177).

Symmetrically 𝜃∘𝜃′=1𝐼′, so 𝜃 is an isomorphism with inverse 𝜃′. ∎

2.6.23 Algebraic Categories

Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

The categories of groups, rings and modules all share a common shape: their objects are sets equipped with some finitary operations, subject to some equational axioms. The following makes this precise, following the classical treatment of universal algebra [Bir35] [BS81] and its later categorical formulation [ARV10].

Definition 2.6.179 (Signature)
A signature Ω is a set of operation symbols, each 𝜔∈Ω assigned a natural number 𝑛𝜔, its arity.
Definition 2.6.180 (Ω-algebra)

Let Ω be a signature. An 𝛀-algebra is a set 𝑆 together with, for each 𝜔∈Ω, a function 𝜔𝑆:𝑆𝑛𝜔→𝑆 (when 𝑛𝜔=0 this is simply a distinguished element of 𝑆, since 𝑆0 is a singleton).

A homomorphism of Ω-algebras 𝑓:𝑆→𝑇 is a function such that

𝑓(𝜔𝑆(𝑠1,…,𝑠𝑛𝜔))=𝜔𝑇(𝑓(𝑠1),…,𝑓(𝑠𝑛𝜔))∀𝜔∈Ω,𝑠1,…,𝑠𝑛𝜔∈𝑆

This determines a concrete category Ω-𝐀𝐥𝐠 (2.6.9).

Example 2.6.181
Taking Ω={·(2),−1(1),𝑒(0)} (writing the arity of each symbol in brackets), Ω-algebras are exactly sets equipped with a binary, a unary and a nullary operation; the subcategory of those satisfying the group axioms, (2.6.184) below, is the category of groups.
Definition 2.6.182 (Terms)

Let Ω be a signature and 𝑋 a set, whose elements we call variables. The set 𝑇Ω(𝑋) of Ω-terms over 𝑋 is defined recursively by

  • every 𝑥∈𝑋 is a term;
  • if 𝜔∈Ω and 𝑡1,…,𝑡𝑛𝜔∈𝑇Ω(𝑋) then 𝜔(𝑡1,…,𝑡𝑛𝜔)∈𝑇Ω(𝑋).

Given an Ω-algebra 𝑆 and a function 𝜃:𝑋→𝑆, there is a unique evaluation 𝜃―:𝑇Ω(𝑋)→𝑆 such that 𝜃―(𝑥)=𝜃(𝑥) for 𝑥∈𝑋 and

𝜃―(𝜔(𝑡1,…,𝑡𝑛𝜔))=𝜔𝑆(𝜃―(𝑡1),…,𝜃―(𝑡𝑛𝜔))
Remark 2.6.183 (The term algebra)

𝑇Ω(𝑋) is itself an Ω-algebra, via 𝜔𝑇Ω(𝑋)(𝑡1,…,𝑡𝑛𝜔)≔𝜔(𝑡1,…,𝑡𝑛𝜔); with this structure, the defining recursion for 𝜃― is exactly the condition that 𝜃―:𝑇Ω(𝑋)→𝑆 is a homomorphism, and it is the unique homomorphism 𝑇Ω(𝑋)→𝑆 restricting to 𝜃 on 𝑋.

Consequently, for any homomorphism ℎ:𝑆→𝑆′ and 𝜃:𝑋→𝑆, both ℎ∘𝜃― and ℎ∘𝜃― are homomorphisms 𝑇Ω(𝑋)→𝑆′ restricting to ℎ∘𝜃 on 𝑋, so by uniqueness

ℎ∘𝜃―=ℎ∘𝜃―
Definition 2.6.184 (Identity, Algebraic category)

Let Ω be a signature. An Ω-identity is a pair 𝑝,𝑞∈𝑇Ω(𝑋) for some set of variables 𝑋, written 𝑝=𝑞. An Ω-algebra 𝑆 satisfies 𝑝=𝑞 if 𝜃―(𝑝)=𝜃―(𝑞) for every 𝜃:𝑋→𝑆 (2.6.182).

Given a set 𝐸 of Ω-identities, the algebraic category determined by (Ω,𝐸) – also called an equational category or variety in the literature – is the full subcategory of Ω-𝐀𝐥𝐠 of those Ω-algebras satisfying every identity in 𝐸, again concrete over 𝐒𝐞𝐭.

Example 2.6.185
𝐆𝐫𝐩,𝐀𝐛𝐆𝐫𝐩,𝐑𝐧𝐠 are algebraic categories, taking 𝐸 to consist of the usual group, abelian group and ring axioms respectively, each expressed as an identity. By contrast, the category of fields is not an algebraic category: the axiom that every nonzero element has an inverse cannot be expressed as an identity holding at every element, since it fails at 0.
Example 2.6.186 (𝐴-𝐌𝐨𝐝 as an algebraic category)

Fix a ring 𝐴. Take Ω={+,−,0}∪{𝜆𝑎}𝑎∈𝐴, with + binary, − unary, 0 nullary and each 𝜆𝑎 unary; note Ω is infinite (one symbol per element of 𝐴) but every operation remains finitary. Take 𝐸 to consist of the abelian group axioms for (+,−,0) together with, for all 𝑎,𝑎′∈𝐴,

𝜆𝑎(𝑥+𝑦)=𝜆𝑎(𝑥)+𝜆𝑎(𝑦),𝜆1(𝑥)=𝑥,𝜆𝑎+𝑎′(𝑥)=𝜆𝑎(𝑥)+𝜆𝑎′(𝑥),𝜆𝑎𝑎′(𝑥)=𝜆𝑎(𝜆𝑎′(𝑥))

Setting 𝜆𝑎(𝑚)≔𝑎·𝑚, these are exactly the 𝐴-module axioms, so 𝐴-𝐌𝐨𝐝 is the algebraic category determined by (Ω,𝐸).

Example 2.6.187 (𝐀𝐥𝐠𝑘 as an algebraic category)

Fix a commutative ring 𝐴 (so 𝐀𝐥𝐠𝑘 is the case 𝐴=𝑘 a field). Take Ω={+,×,−,0,1}∪{𝜆𝑎}𝑎∈𝐴, with +,× binary, − unary, 0,1 nullary and each 𝜆𝑎 unary, and take 𝐸 to consist of the ring axioms for (+,×,−,0,1) (not imposing commutativity of ×) together with the four identities above and, in addition,

𝜆𝑎(𝑥)=𝜆𝑎(1)×𝑥∀𝑎∈𝐴

Given such an Ω-algebra 𝐵, set 𝑖𝐵(𝑎)≔𝜆𝑎(1). Additivity and unitality of 𝑖𝐵 are immediate from the identities above at 𝑥=1, and multiplicativity follows from the last two identities,

𝑖𝐵(𝑎𝑎′)=𝜆𝑎𝑎′(1)=𝜆𝑎(𝜆𝑎′(1))=𝜆𝑎(1)×𝜆𝑎′(1)=𝑖𝐵(𝑎)𝑖𝐵(𝑎′)

so 𝑖𝐵 is a ring homomorphism, and the final identity reads 𝜆𝑎(𝑏)=𝑖𝐵(𝑎)·𝑏 for all 𝑏∈𝐵: this is exactly an 𝐴-algebra structure on 𝐵. Conversely every 𝐴-algebra satisfies these identities, and a ring homomorphism commutes with every 𝜆𝑎 if and only if it respects the structural morphisms (apply the final identity at 𝑏=1), so 𝐀𝐥𝐠𝐴, and in particular 𝐀𝐥𝐠𝑘, is the algebraic category determined by (Ω,𝐸).

Remark 2.6.188
Birkhoff’s theorem characterises the algebraic (equational) subcategories of Ω-𝐀𝐥𝐠 as exactly those closed under homomorphic images, subalgebras and products [Bir35]; see [BS81] for a modern account, and [ARV10] for the categorical perspective via algebraic theories.
Proposition 2.6.189 (Properties of Algebraic Categories)

Let 𝒞︀ be an algebraic category determined by (Ω,𝐸) (2.6.184), with forgetful functor 𝑈:𝒞︀→𝐒𝐞𝐭. Then

  1. 𝑈 reflects isomorphisms
  2. 𝑈 creates limits and directed colimits
  3. 𝑈 has a left adjoint (i.e. free algebras exist)

In particular 𝑈 also preserves limits and directed colimits by (2.6.87).

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Throughout, for 𝜔∈Ω we write 𝑟=1,…,𝑛𝜔 for the arguments of 𝜔, reserving 𝑖,𝑗,𝑘 for diagram indices.

𝑈 creates limits. Let 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ be a diagram and suppose 𝐿≔lim(𝑈∘𝐹) exists in 𝐒𝐞𝐭, with structure maps 𝜋𝑖:𝐿→𝑈(𝐹(𝑖)); explicitly, by (2.6.85), 𝐿={(𝑥𝑖)𝑖∈𝐼∈∏𝑖𝑈(𝐹(𝑖))|𝑈(𝐹(𝛼))(𝑥𝑖)=𝑥𝑗∀𝛼:𝑖→𝑗}.

For 𝜔∈Ω and 𝑥(1),…,𝑥(𝑛𝜔)∈𝐿, define 𝜔𝐿(𝑥(1),…,𝑥(𝑛𝜔))𝑖≔𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝑥𝑖(1),…,𝑥𝑖(𝑛𝜔)) for each 𝑖∈𝐼. This again lies in 𝐿: for 𝛼:𝑖→𝑗, since 𝐹(𝛼) is a homomorphism, 𝐹(𝛼)(𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝑥𝑖(1),…))=𝜔𝐹(𝑗)(𝐹(𝛼)(𝑥𝑖(1)),…)=𝜔𝐹(𝑗)(𝑥𝑗(1),…), using that each 𝑥(𝑟)∈𝐿. So 𝐿 is an Ω-algebra and each 𝜋𝑖 is, by construction, a homomorphism; this is the unique such structure on 𝐿, since 𝜔𝐿(…) is pinned down coordinatewise by the requirement that every 𝜋𝑖 be a homomorphism, and 𝐿⊆∏𝑖𝑈(𝐹(𝑖)).

Given 𝑝=𝑞∈𝐸 with variables in a set 𝑋, and 𝜃:𝑋→𝐿: for each 𝑖, 𝜋𝑖∘𝜃:𝑋→𝑈(𝐹(𝑖)), and by (2.6.183), 𝜋𝑖(𝜃―(𝑡))=𝜋𝑖∘𝜃―(𝑡) for every term 𝑡. As 𝐹(𝑖)∈𝒞︀ satisfies 𝑝=𝑞, 𝜋𝑖𝜃―(𝑝)=𝜋𝑖𝜃―(𝑞), so 𝜋𝑖(𝜃―(𝑝))=𝜋𝑖(𝜃―(𝑞)) for every 𝑖∈𝐼, hence 𝜃―(𝑝)=𝜃―(𝑞) as elements of 𝐿⊆∏𝑖𝑈(𝐹(𝑖)). So 𝐿∈𝒞︀.

Finally (𝐿,{𝜋𝑖}) is a limit for 𝐹 in 𝒞︀: given a cone (𝑀,{𝜇𝑖}) in 𝒞︀, the unique 𝐒𝐞𝐭-map 𝜑:𝑈(𝑀)→𝐿 with 𝜋𝑖∘𝜑=𝜇𝑖 (afforded by 𝐿=lim(𝑈∘𝐹)) is a homomorphism, since for 𝜔∈Ω, 𝑚(1),…,𝑚(𝑛𝜔)∈𝑈(𝑀) and every 𝑖,

𝜋𝑖(𝜑(𝜔𝑀(𝑚(1),…)))=𝜇𝑖(𝜔𝑀(𝑚(1),…))=𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝜇𝑖(𝑚(1)),…)=𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝜋𝑖𝜑(𝑚(1)),…)=𝜋𝑖(𝜔𝐿(𝜑(𝑚(1)),…))

using that 𝜇𝑖 is a homomorphism, so 𝜑(𝜔𝑀(𝑚(1),…))=𝜔𝐿(𝜑(𝑚(1)),…). As 𝒞︀ is a full subcategory of Ω-𝐀𝐥𝐠, 𝜑 is the unique morphism of 𝒞︀ with 𝜋𝑖∘𝜑=𝜇𝑖, so (𝐿,{𝜋𝑖}) is a limit for 𝐹 in 𝒞︀ with 𝑈(𝐿)=𝐿, as required.

𝑈 creates directed colimits. Let 𝐼 be a directed preorder and 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ a diagram, and suppose 𝐿≔lim⟶(𝑈∘𝐹) exists in 𝐒𝐞𝐭 (2.6.128), with structure maps 𝜇𝑖:𝑈(𝐹(𝑖))→𝐿.

For 𝜔∈Ω and ℓ(1),…,ℓ(𝑛𝜔)∈𝐿: as 𝐼 is directed and 𝑛𝜔 is finite, there is a common 𝑖∈𝐼 and 𝑦(1),…,𝑦(𝑛𝜔)∈𝑈(𝐹(𝑖)) with 𝜇𝑖(𝑦(𝑟))=ℓ(𝑟) for all 𝑟 (each ℓ(𝑟) is represented at some stage, and finitely many stages admit a common upper bound); define 𝜔𝐿(ℓ(1),…,ℓ(𝑛𝜔))≔𝜇𝑖(𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝑦(1),…,𝑦(𝑛𝜔))). This is independent of the choice of 𝑖 and the 𝑦(𝑟): given another such 𝑖′,(𝑦′(𝑟)), for each 𝑟 there is, by (2.6.128), a stage 𝑘𝑟⪰𝑖,𝑖′ with 𝐹(𝑖→𝑘𝑟)(𝑦(𝑟))=𝐹(𝑖′→𝑘𝑟)(𝑦′(𝑟)); as 𝐼 is directed and there are finitely many 𝑟, there is a common 𝑗⪰𝑘1,…,𝑘𝑛𝜔, and applying 𝐹(𝑘𝑟→𝑗) to each equality gives 𝐹(𝑖→𝑗)(𝑦(𝑟))=𝐹(𝑖′→𝑗)(𝑦′(𝑟)) for every 𝑟 simultaneously. As 𝐹(𝑖→𝑗),𝐹(𝑖′→𝑗) are homomorphisms,

𝜇𝑖(𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝑦(1),…))=𝜇𝑗(𝜔𝐹(𝑗)(𝐹(𝑖→𝑗)(𝑦(1)),…))=𝜇𝑗(𝜔𝐹(𝑗)(𝐹(𝑖′→𝑗)(𝑦′(1)),…))=𝜇𝑖′(𝜔𝐹(𝑖′)(𝑦′(1),…))

So 𝐿 is an Ω-algebra and each 𝜇𝑖 is, by construction, a homomorphism; as the 𝜇𝑖 are jointly surjective (2.6.128), this is again the unique such structure.

Given 𝑝=𝑞∈𝐸 with (finitely many) variables 𝑋, and 𝜃:𝑋→𝐿: as 𝑋 is finite and 𝐼 directed, there is 𝑖∈𝐼 and 𝜃𝑖:𝑋→𝑈(𝐹(𝑖)) with 𝜃=𝜇𝑖∘𝜃𝑖 (as above); by (2.6.183), 𝜃―=𝜇𝑖∘𝜃𝑖―, so 𝜃―(𝑝)=𝜇𝑖(𝜃𝑖―(𝑝))=𝜇𝑖(𝜃𝑖―(𝑞))=𝜃―(𝑞), using 𝐹(𝑖)∈𝒞︀. So 𝐿∈𝒞︀.

Finally (𝐿,{𝜇𝑖}) is a colimit for 𝐹 in 𝒞︀: given a cocone (𝑀,{𝜈𝑖}) in 𝒞︀, the unique 𝐒𝐞𝐭-map 𝜓:𝐿→𝑈(𝑀) with 𝜓∘𝜇𝑖=𝜈𝑖 is a homomorphism (for ℓ(𝑟)=𝜇𝑖(𝑦(𝑟)) at a common 𝑖, 𝜓(𝜔𝐿(ℓ(1),…))=𝜓(𝜇𝑖(𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝑦(1),…)))=𝜈𝑖(𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝑦(1),…))=𝜔𝑀(𝜈𝑖(𝑦(1)),…)=𝜔𝑀(𝜓(ℓ(1)),…), using that 𝜈𝑖 is a homomorphism), and is the unique morphism of 𝒞︀ with this property as 𝒞︀ is full in Ω-𝐀𝐥𝐠.

𝑈 reflects isomorphisms. Let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 in 𝒞︀ with 𝑈(𝑓) bijective. For 𝜔∈Ω and 𝑦(1),…,𝑦(𝑛𝜔)∈𝑈(𝑌), writing 𝑥(𝑟)≔𝑈(𝑓)−1(𝑦(𝑟)), since 𝑓 is a homomorphism 𝑓(𝜔𝑋(𝑥(1),…))=𝜔𝑌(𝑓(𝑥(1)),…)=𝜔𝑌(𝑦(1),…), so applying 𝑈(𝑓)−1,

𝑈(𝑓)−1(𝜔𝑌(𝑦(1),…,𝑦(𝑛𝜔)))=𝜔𝑋(𝑈(𝑓)−1(𝑦(1)),…,𝑈(𝑓)−1(𝑦(𝑛𝜔)))

so 𝑈(𝑓)−1 is a homomorphism 𝑌→𝑋, hence a morphism of 𝒞︀ (full subcategory), inverse to 𝑓 on underlying sets; as 𝑈 is faithful, it is a two-sided inverse to 𝑓 in 𝒞︀, so 𝑓 is an isomorphism.

𝑈 has a left adjoint. Fix a set 𝑋. Define a relation ∼ on 𝑇Ω(𝑋) by 𝑡∼𝑡′ if 𝜃―(𝑡)=𝜃―(𝑡′) for every 𝐴∈𝒞︀ and 𝜃:𝑋→𝑈(𝐴); this is manifestly an equivalence relation, and a congruence: if 𝑡(𝑟)∼𝑡′(𝑟) for 𝑟=1,…,𝑛𝜔, then for every 𝐴,𝜃, 𝜃―(𝜔(𝑡(1),…))=𝜔𝐴(𝜃―(𝑡(1)),…)=𝜔𝐴(𝜃―(𝑡′(1)),…)=𝜃―(𝜔(𝑡′(1),…)), so 𝜔(𝑡(1),…,𝑡(𝑛𝜔))∼𝜔(𝑡′(1),…,𝑡′(𝑛𝜔)).

Let Free(𝑋)≔𝑇Ω(𝑋)/∼, with 𝜔Free(𝑋)([𝑡(1)],…,[𝑡(𝑛𝜔)])≔[𝜔(𝑡(1),…,𝑡(𝑛𝜔))] (well-defined as ∼ is a congruence), and let 𝜋:𝑇Ω(𝑋)→Free(𝑋), 𝑡↦[𝑡], an (evidently surjective) homomorphism. Write 𝜄:𝑋→𝑈(Free(𝑋)), 𝜄(𝑥)≔[𝑥].

Free(𝑋)∈𝒞︀: let 𝑝=𝑞∈𝐸 with variable set 𝑌, and 𝜓:𝑌→𝑈(Free(𝑋)); choose 𝜓̃:𝑌→𝑇Ω(𝑋) with 𝜋∘𝜓̃=𝜓 (possible as 𝜋 is surjective). Viewing 𝑇Ω(𝑋) as an Ω-algebra (2.6.183), 𝜓̃―:𝑇Ω(𝑌)→𝑇Ω(𝑋) is a homomorphism, and for every 𝐴∈𝒞︀, 𝜃:𝑋→𝑈(𝐴), (2.6.183) gives 𝜃―∘𝜓̃―=𝜃―∘𝜓̃―; as 𝜃―∘𝜓̃:𝑌→𝑈(𝐴) and 𝐴⊧𝑝=𝑞, 𝜃―𝜓̃―(𝑝)=𝜃―𝜓̃―(𝑞), so 𝜃―(𝜓̃―(𝑝))=𝜃―(𝜓̃―(𝑞)). As 𝐴,𝜃 were arbitrary, 𝜓̃―(𝑝)∼𝜓̃―(𝑞), that is 𝜋(𝜓̃―(𝑝))=𝜋(𝜓̃―(𝑞)). Again by (2.6.183), 𝜋∘𝜓̃―=𝜓― (both extend 𝜋∘𝜓̃=𝜓 on 𝑌), so 𝜓―(𝑝)=𝜓―(𝑞). As 𝜓 was arbitrary, Free(𝑋)⊧𝑝=𝑞; as 𝑝=𝑞∈𝐸 was arbitrary, Free(𝑋)∈𝒞︀.

Universal property: given 𝐴∈𝒞︀ and 𝜃:𝑋→𝑈(𝐴), define 𝜃̂([𝑡])≔𝜃―(𝑡); this is well-defined (𝑡∼𝑡′⟹𝜃―(𝑡)=𝜃―(𝑡′), by definition of ∼) and a homomorphism, since 𝜃̂(𝜔Free(𝑋)([𝑡(1)],…))=𝜃̂([𝜔(𝑡(1),…)])=𝜃―(𝜔(𝑡(1),…))=𝜔𝐴(𝜃―(𝑡(1)),…)=𝜔𝐴(𝜃̂([𝑡(1)]),…), and satisfies 𝑈(𝜃̂)∘𝜄=𝜃. If 𝜑:Free(𝑋)→𝐴 is any morphism of 𝒞︀ with 𝑈(𝜑)∘𝜄=𝜃, then 𝜑∘𝜋 is a homomorphism 𝑇Ω(𝑋)→𝐴 restricting to 𝜃 on 𝑋, so 𝜑∘𝜋=𝜃― by (2.6.183); as 𝜋 is surjective, 𝜑=𝜃̂. So Free(𝑋) is free on 𝑋, and 𝑋↦Free(𝑋) is left adjoint to 𝑈 by (2.6.74). ∎

Remark 2.6.190 (Limits are computed pointwise)
Unwinding the construction in the proof of (2.6.189): for a diagram 𝐹:𝐼→𝒞︀ admitting a limit, 𝑈(lim𝐹)=lim(𝑈∘𝐹) (2.6.85), and each 𝜔∈Ω acts on lim𝐹 coordinatewise, 𝜔lim𝐹(𝑥(1),…)𝑖=𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝑥𝑖(1),…) for 𝑖∈𝐼. In particular this applies to products.
Corollary 2.6.191 (Inverse Limits in Algebraic Categories)

Let 𝒞︀ be an algebraic category determined by (Ω,𝐸) (2.6.184), with forgetful functor 𝑈:𝒞︀→𝐒𝐞𝐭, 𝐼 a directed preorder, and 𝐹:𝐼op→𝒞︀ an inverse system. Then lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖) exists in 𝒞︀, with

𝑈(lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖))=lim⟵𝑖𝑈(𝐹(𝑖))={(𝑥𝑖)𝑖∈𝐼∈∏𝑖𝑈(𝐹(𝑖))|𝑈(𝜌𝑖𝑗)(𝑥𝑗)=𝑥𝑖∀𝑖≺𝑗}

(2.6.130), and each 𝜔∈Ω acts coordinatewise: 𝜔lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖)(𝑥(1),…)𝑖=𝜔𝐹(𝑖)(𝑥𝑖(1),…) for every 𝑖∈𝐼.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

By (2.6.189), 𝑈 creates limits, and lim𝐼op(𝑈∘𝐹)=lim⟵𝑖𝑈(𝐹(𝑖)) exists in 𝐒𝐞𝐭 for every diagram, being computed as in (2.6.130) (a special case of (2.6.85)); so lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖)≔lim𝐼op𝐹 exists in 𝒞︀ too, with 𝑈 carrying it to this set-level description. The coordinatewise formula for 𝜔∈Ω is then the case lim𝐹≔lim⟵𝑖𝐹(𝑖) of (2.6.190). ∎

Definition 2.6.192 (Subalgebra)
Let 𝐴 be an Ω-algebra. A subset 𝑆⊆𝑈(𝐴) is a subalgebra if 𝜔𝐴(𝑠1,…,𝑠𝑛𝜔)∈𝑆 for all 𝜔∈Ω and 𝑠1,…,𝑠𝑛𝜔∈𝑆.
Proposition 2.6.193 (Subalgebra criterion)

Let 𝐴 be an Ω-algebra and 𝑆⊆𝑈(𝐴) a subalgebra (2.6.192). Then 𝑆 carries a unique Ω-algebra structure making the inclusion 𝜄:𝑆↪︎𝐴 a homomorphism, namely 𝜔𝑆≔𝜔𝐴|𝑆𝑛𝜔.

If moreover 𝐴 satisfies an identity 𝑝=𝑞, then so does 𝑆; in particular, if 𝐴 lies in the algebraic category 𝒞︀ determined by (Ω,𝐸), then so does 𝑆.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Existence and uniqueness of 𝜔𝑆 are immediate: 𝑆 being closed under 𝜔𝐴 means 𝜔𝐴|𝑆𝑛𝜔 takes values in 𝑆, and this is forced by the requirement that 𝜄 be a homomorphism.

Let 𝑝=𝑞 be an identity with variables 𝑌, satisfied by 𝐴, and 𝜃:𝑌→𝑆. Writing 𝜄∘𝜃:𝑌→𝑈(𝐴), (2.6.183) gives 𝜄(𝜃―(𝑝))=𝜄𝜃―(𝑝)=𝜄𝜃―(𝑞)=𝜄(𝜃―(𝑞)), using that 𝐴 satisfies 𝑝=𝑞; as 𝜄 is injective, 𝜃―(𝑝)=𝜃―(𝑞), so 𝑆 satisfies 𝑝=𝑞. ∎

Proposition 2.6.194 (Injective ⟺ Monic)
Let 𝒞︀ be an algebraic category. Then a morphism 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 is a monomorphism if and only if 𝑈(𝑓) is injective.

Proof. If 𝑈(𝑓) is injective and 𝑓∘𝑔=𝑓∘ℎ then 𝑈(𝑓)∘𝑈(𝑔)=𝑈(𝑓)∘𝑈(ℎ) whence 𝑈(𝑔)=𝑈(ℎ) and by faithful-ness 𝑔=ℎ as required.

Conversely if 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 is monic, consider the left adjoint 𝐹 to 𝑈 (2.6.189), then by definition we have a natural bijection

Ψ𝑋:Mor(𝐹({⋆}),𝑋)→∼𝑈(𝑋)

Suppose 𝑈(𝑓)(𝑥)=𝑈(𝑓)(𝑦) for 𝑥,𝑦∈𝑈(𝑋). Let 𝑔,ℎ be morphisms corresponding to 𝑥 and 𝑦 under this bijection, that is 𝑥=Ψ𝑋(𝑔) and 𝑦=Ψ𝑋(ℎ).

Then by naturality of Ψ

𝑈(𝑓)(𝑥)=Ψ𝑌(𝑓∘𝑔)

and

𝑈(𝑓)(𝑦)=Ψ𝑌(𝑓∘ℎ)

so by assumption 𝑓∘𝑔=𝑓∘ℎ. As 𝑓 is monic we have 𝑔=ℎ whence 𝑥=𝑦. Therefore 𝑈(𝑓) is injective. ∎

Proposition 2.6.195 (Regular Epimorphism ⟺ Surjective)
Let 𝒞︀ be an algebraic category (2.6.184) and 𝑒:𝑋→𝑌 a morphism of 𝒞︀. Then 𝑒 is a regular epimorphism if and only if 𝑈(𝑒) is surjective.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

(⟹) Since 𝑒 is regular, there are 𝛼,𝛽:𝑊⇉𝑋 such that 𝑒 is the coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽) (2.6.158).

The image is a subalgebra. Let 𝐼≔𝑈(𝑒)(𝑈(𝑋))⊆𝑈(𝑌). For 𝜔∈Ω and 𝑦1,…,𝑦𝑛𝜔∈𝐼, writing 𝑦𝑟=𝑈(𝑒)(𝑥𝑟) for 𝑥𝑟∈𝑈(𝑋), since 𝑒 is a homomorphism 𝜔𝑌(𝑦1,…)=𝜔𝑌(𝑈(𝑒)(𝑥1),…)=𝑈(𝑒)(𝜔𝑋(𝑥1,…))∈𝐼; so 𝐼 is a subalgebra (2.6.192). By (2.6.193), 𝐼 carries an Ω-algebra structure making the inclusion 𝜄:𝐼↪︎𝑌 a homomorphism, and 𝐼∈𝒞︀ (as 𝑌∈𝒞︀); as 𝒞︀ is full in Ω-𝐀𝐥𝐠, 𝜄 is a morphism of 𝒞︀.

Write 𝑒′:𝑋→𝐼 for the corestriction of 𝑒, that is 𝑈(𝑒′)≔𝑈(𝑒) regarded as a map into 𝐼; since 𝜔𝐼 is just 𝜔𝑌 restricted to 𝐼, 𝑒′ is again a homomorphism, hence a morphism of 𝒞︀, with 𝜄∘𝑒′=𝑒 and 𝑈(𝑒′) surjective onto 𝐼 by construction.

(𝐼,𝑒′) is a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽). Since 𝜄∘(𝑒′𝛼)=𝑒𝛼=𝑒𝛽=𝜄∘(𝑒′𝛽) and 𝜄 is monic (2.6.194), 𝑒′𝛼=𝑒′𝛽. Given ℎ:𝑋→𝑍 with ℎ𝛼=ℎ𝛽, the universal property of 𝑒 gives a unique 𝑘:𝑌→𝑍 with 𝑘∘𝑒=ℎ; then 𝑘′≔𝑘∘𝜄 satisfies 𝑘′∘𝑒′=𝑘∘𝜄∘𝑒′=𝑘∘𝑒=ℎ. If 𝑘″ also satisfies 𝑘″∘𝑒′=ℎ, then 𝑈(𝑘′)∘𝑈(𝑒′)=𝑈(ℎ)=𝑈(𝑘″)∘𝑈(𝑒′); as 𝑈(𝑒′) is surjective, 𝑈(𝑘′)=𝑈(𝑘″), so 𝑘′=𝑘″ (𝑈 faithful). So (𝐼,𝑒′) is a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽) (2.6.140), in particular 𝑒′ is epic (2.6.135).

𝜄 is an isomorphism. Applying the universal property of 𝑒 to 𝑒′ (which satisfies 𝑒′𝛼=𝑒′𝛽) gives a unique 𝜓:𝑌→𝐼 with 𝜓∘𝑒=𝑒′. Then (𝜄∘𝜓)∘𝑒=𝜄∘𝑒′=𝑒=1𝑌∘𝑒, and as 𝑒 is epic (2.6.135), 𝜄∘𝜓=1𝑌. Also (𝜓∘𝜄)∘𝑒′=𝜓∘𝑒=𝑒′=1𝐼∘𝑒′, and as 𝑒′ is epic, 𝜓∘𝜄=1𝐼. So 𝜄 is an isomorphism, with inverse 𝜓.

So 𝑈(𝜄) is bijective; but 𝑈(𝜄) is, by construction, the inclusion 𝐼↪︎𝑈(𝑌), so 𝐼=𝑈(𝑌). As 𝐼=𝑈(𝑒)(𝑈(𝑋)) by definition, 𝑈(𝑒) is surjective.

(⟸) Suppose 𝑈(𝑒) is surjective.

Construction of the quotient. Write ∼ for the relation 𝑎∼𝑏:⟺𝑈(𝑒)(𝑎)=𝑈(𝑒)(𝑏) on 𝑈(𝑋), an equivalence relation, and 𝑄≔𝑈(𝑋)/∼ with quotient map 𝜋:𝑈(𝑋)→𝑄, 𝑎↦[𝑎]; 𝜋 is surjective by construction. For 𝜔∈Ω and 𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛𝜔,𝑏1,…,𝑏𝑛𝜔∈𝑈(𝑋) with 𝑎𝑟∼𝑏𝑟 for every 𝑟: since 𝑒 is a homomorphism, 𝑈(𝑒)(𝜔𝑋(𝑎1,…))=𝜔𝑌(𝑈(𝑒)(𝑎1),…)=𝜔𝑌(𝑈(𝑒)(𝑏1),…)=𝑈(𝑒)(𝜔𝑋(𝑏1,…)), that is 𝜔𝑋(𝑎1,…)∼𝜔𝑋(𝑏1,…); so ∼ is a congruence, and 𝜔𝑄([𝑎1],…,[𝑎𝑛𝜔])≔[𝜔𝑋(𝑎1,…,𝑎𝑛𝜔)] is well-defined, making 𝑄 into an Ω-algebra with 𝜋 a homomorphism.

𝑄∈𝒞︀. Let 𝑝=𝑞∈𝐸 with variables 𝑊, and 𝜃:𝑊→𝑄; as 𝜋 is surjective, choose 𝜃̃:𝑊→𝑈(𝑋) with 𝜋∘𝜃̃=𝜃. Since 𝑋∈𝒞︀, 𝑋 satisfies 𝑝=𝑞, that is 𝜃̃―(𝑝)=𝜃̃―(𝑞) in 𝑈(𝑋); applying the homomorphism 𝜋 and (2.6.183) (𝜋∘𝜃̃―=𝜋∘𝜃̃―=𝜃―),

𝜃―(𝑝)=𝜋(𝜃̃―(𝑝))=𝜋(𝜃̃―(𝑞))=𝜃―(𝑞)

As 𝜃 was arbitrary, 𝑄 satisfies 𝑝=𝑞; as 𝑝=𝑞∈𝐸 was arbitrary, 𝑄∈𝒞︀, and 𝜋:𝑋→𝑄 is a morphism of 𝒞︀ (full subcategory of Ω-𝐀𝐥𝐠).

The kernel relation is a subalgebra. Let 𝑅≔{(𝑎,𝑏)∈𝑈(𝑋)2|𝑎∼𝑏}. For 𝜔∈Ω and (𝑎1,𝑏1),…,(𝑎𝑛𝜔,𝑏𝑛𝜔)∈𝑅, since 𝑒 is a homomorphism, 𝑈(𝑒)(𝜔𝑋(𝑎1,…))=𝜔𝑌(𝑈(𝑒)(𝑎1),…)=𝜔𝑌(𝑈(𝑒)(𝑏1),…)=𝑈(𝑒)(𝜔𝑋(𝑏1,…)), so (𝜔𝑋(𝑎1,…),𝜔𝑋(𝑏1,…))∈𝑅; as 𝑈(𝑋×𝑋)=𝑈(𝑋)2 (2.6.190), 𝑅 is a subalgebra of 𝑋×𝑋 (2.6.192). By (2.6.193), 𝑅∈𝒞︀, and 𝛼≔𝜋1|𝑅, 𝛽≔𝜋2|𝑅 (restrictions of the product projections) are morphisms of 𝒞︀.

(𝑄,𝜋) is a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽). For (𝑎,𝑏)∈𝑅, i.e. 𝑎∼𝑏, 𝜋(𝛼(𝑎,𝑏))=𝜋(𝑎)=[𝑎]=[𝑏]=𝜋(𝛽(𝑎,𝑏)); as 𝑈 is faithful, 𝜋∘𝛼=𝜋∘𝛽. Suppose ℎ:𝑋→𝑍 satisfies ℎ∘𝛼=ℎ∘𝛽; then for every (𝑎,𝑏)∈𝑅 (i.e. every 𝑎∼𝑏), 𝑈(ℎ)(𝑎)=𝑈(ℎ)(𝑏), so ℎ―:𝑄→𝑈(𝑍), [𝑎]↦𝑈(ℎ)(𝑎), is a well-defined map, and a homomorphism, since ℎ―(𝜔𝑄([𝑎1],…))=ℎ―([𝜔𝑋(𝑎1,…)])=𝑈(ℎ)(𝜔𝑋(𝑎1,…))=𝜔𝑍(𝑈(ℎ)(𝑎1),…)=𝜔𝑍(ℎ―([𝑎1]),…), using that ℎ is a homomorphism. So ℎ― is a morphism of 𝒞︀ with ℎ―∘𝜋=ℎ (𝑈 faithful). If 𝑘:𝑄→𝑍 also satisfies 𝑘∘𝜋=ℎ, then 𝑈(𝑘)∘𝑈(𝜋)=𝑈(ℎ)=𝑈(ℎ―)∘𝑈(𝜋); as 𝑈(𝜋) is surjective, 𝑈(𝑘)=𝑈(ℎ―), so 𝑘=ℎ― (𝑈 faithful). So (𝑄,𝜋) is a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽) (2.6.140), in particular a regular epimorphism.

Conclusion. Define 𝑒―:𝑄→𝑌, [𝑎]↦𝑈(𝑒)(𝑎); well-defined as 𝑎∼𝑏⟹𝑈(𝑒)(𝑎)=𝑈(𝑒)(𝑏), and a homomorphism by the same computation as for 𝜋, hence a morphism of 𝒞︀, with 𝑒―∘𝜋=𝑒. As 𝑒―([𝑎])=𝑒―([𝑏])⟹𝑈(𝑒)(𝑎)=𝑈(𝑒)(𝑏)⟹𝑎∼𝑏⟹[𝑎]=[𝑏], 𝑈(𝑒―) is injective; as 𝑒=𝑒―∘𝜋 and 𝑈(𝑒) is surjective (hypothesis), 𝑈(𝑒―) is surjective. So 𝑈(𝑒―) is bijective, hence 𝑒― is an isomorphism, as 𝒞︀ is algebraic and 𝑈 reflects isomorphisms (2.6.189).

Since 𝜋 is the coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽) and 𝑒― is an isomorphism, 𝑒=𝑒―∘𝜋 is again a coequaliser of (𝛼,𝛽), as colimits are preserved under isomorphism (2.6.90); hence 𝑒 is a regular epimorphism (2.6.158). ∎

Proposition 2.6.196 (Algebraic Categories have Regular Epi-Mono Factorisations)

Let 𝒞︀ be an algebraic category (2.6.184). Then 𝒞︀ has regular epi-mono factorisations for every morphism (2.6.173).

More precisely, let 𝑓:𝑋→𝑌 be a morphism of 𝒞︀ and 𝐼≔𝑈(𝑓)(𝑈(𝑋))⊆𝑈(𝑌) the (underlying-set) image of 𝑓. Then 𝐼 is a subalgebra of 𝑌, and 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒 is a regular epi-mono factorisation of 𝑓, where 𝑒:𝑋→𝐼 is the corestriction of 𝑓 and 𝑚:𝐼↪︎𝑌 is the inclusion.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

𝐼 is a subalgebra. For 𝜔∈Ω and 𝑦1,…,𝑦𝑛𝜔∈𝐼, writing 𝑦𝑟=𝑈(𝑓)(𝑥𝑟) for 𝑥𝑟∈𝑈(𝑋), since 𝑓 is a homomorphism 𝜔𝑌(𝑦1,…)=𝜔𝑌(𝑈(𝑓)(𝑥1),…)=𝑈(𝑓)(𝜔𝑋(𝑥1,…))∈𝐼; so 𝐼 is a subalgebra (2.6.192). By (2.6.193), 𝐼 carries a (unique) Ω-algebra structure making the inclusion 𝑚:𝐼↪︎𝑌 a homomorphism, with 𝐼∈𝒞︀ (as 𝑌∈𝒞︀); as 𝒞︀ is full in Ω-𝐀𝐥𝐠, 𝑚 is a morphism of 𝒞︀, and monic by (2.6.194) (being injective).

Write 𝑒:𝑋→𝐼 for the corestriction of 𝑓, that is 𝑈(𝑒)≔𝑈(𝑓) regarded as a map into 𝐼; since 𝜔𝐼 is just 𝜔𝑌 restricted to 𝐼, 𝑒 is again a homomorphism, hence a morphism of 𝒞︀, with 𝑚∘𝑒=𝑓 and 𝑈(𝑒) surjective onto 𝐼 by construction. By (2.6.195), 𝑒 is therefore a regular epimorphism, so 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒 is a regular epi-mono factorisation of 𝑓 (2.6.173). ∎

Proposition 2.6.197 (Equalisers in Algebraic Categories)

Consider a commutative diagram in an algebraic category 𝒞︀

Then 𝑒 is an equaliser for (𝑑0,𝑑1) if and only if 𝑈(𝑒) is injective and Im(𝑈(𝑒))={𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝑑0)(𝑦)=𝑈(𝑑1)(𝑦)}.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Write 𝐹:𝟐→𝒞︀ for the diagram 𝑑0,𝑑1:𝑌⇉𝑍, so that 𝑒 being an equaliser for (𝑑0,𝑑1) means precisely that (𝑋,𝑒) is a limit for 𝐹.

(⟹) Suppose (𝑋,𝑒) is a limit for 𝐹. Since 𝒞︀ is algebraic, 𝑈 creates limits (2.6.189), so by (2.6.87), using that 𝐒𝐞𝐭 has all limits, 𝑈 preserves limits. Hence (𝑈(𝑋),𝑈(𝑒)) is a limit for 𝑈∘𝐹 in 𝐒𝐞𝐭, that is, an equaliser for (𝑈(𝑑0),𝑈(𝑑1)). By (2.6.139), 𝑈(𝑒) is injective and Im(𝑈(𝑒))={𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝑑0)(𝑦)=𝑈(𝑑1)(𝑦)}, as required.

(⟸) Suppose 𝑈(𝑒) is injective and Im(𝑈(𝑒))={𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝑑0)(𝑦)=𝑈(𝑑1)(𝑦)}.

By (2.6.139) the diagram 𝑈(𝑌)⇉𝑈(𝑍) has an equaliser in 𝐒𝐞𝐭, that is lim(𝑈∘𝐹) exists. Since 𝑈 creates limits (2.6.189), lim𝐹 exists in 𝒞︀; write (𝑋′,𝑒′) for this limit, so that 𝑒′ is an equaliser for (𝑑0,𝑑1). By the (⟹) direction applied to 𝑒′, 𝑈(𝑒′) is injective and

Im(𝑈(𝑒′))={𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝑑0)(𝑦)=𝑈(𝑑1)(𝑦)}=Im(𝑈(𝑒))

using the hypothesis on 𝑒 for the second equality.

As 𝑑0∘𝑒=𝑑1∘𝑒, the universal property of the equaliser (𝑋′,𝑒′) yields a unique morphism 𝜑:𝑋→𝑋′ with 𝑒′∘𝜑=𝑒.

We claim 𝑈(𝜑) is a bijection. If 𝑈(𝜑)(𝑥)=𝑈(𝜑)(𝑦) then applying 𝑈(𝑒′) gives 𝑈(𝑒)(𝑥)=𝑈(𝑒′)(𝑈(𝜑)(𝑥))=𝑈(𝑒′)(𝑈(𝜑)(𝑦))=𝑈(𝑒)(𝑦), so 𝑥=𝑦 as 𝑈(𝑒) is injective; hence 𝑈(𝜑) is injective. Given 𝑥′∈𝑈(𝑋′), we have 𝑈(𝑒′)(𝑥′)∈Im(𝑈(𝑒′))=Im(𝑈(𝑒)), so 𝑈(𝑒′)(𝑥′)=𝑈(𝑒)(𝑥) for some 𝑥∈𝑈(𝑋), that is 𝑈(𝑒′)(𝑥′)=𝑈(𝑒′)(𝑈(𝜑)(𝑥)), whence 𝑥′=𝑈(𝜑)(𝑥) as 𝑈(𝑒′) is injective; hence 𝑈(𝜑) is surjective.

So 𝑈(𝜑) is a bijection, hence an isomorphism in 𝐒𝐞𝐭. Since 𝒞︀ is algebraic, 𝑈 reflects isomorphisms (2.6.189), so 𝜑 is an isomorphism in 𝒞︀.

Since (𝑋′,𝑒′) is an equaliser for (𝑑0,𝑑1) and 𝜑:𝑋→𝑋′ is an isomorphism with 𝑒′∘𝜑=𝑒, by (2.6.137) (𝑋,𝑒) is also an equaliser for (𝑑0,𝑑1), as required. ∎

Proposition 2.6.198 (Every Object has a Zero Element)

Let 𝒞︀ be an algebraic pointed category. Then a zero object 𝟎 consists of precisely one element, denoted by 0𝟎.

Every object 𝐴 has a unique element 0𝐴 such that 𝑈(0𝟎,𝐴)(0)=0𝐴 for any (resp. all) zero objects 𝟎.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Since 𝒞︀ is an algebraic category, 𝑈 creates limits (2.6.189), so by (2.6.87) 𝑈 preserves limits, and this holds unconditionally as the target category is 𝐒𝐞𝐭. In particular 𝑈 preserves terminal objects, these being the limit over the empty diagram.

As 𝟎 is a zero object it is in particular a terminal object of 𝒞︀ (2.6.55), so 𝑈(𝟎) is a terminal object of 𝐒𝐞𝐭. A terminal object of 𝐒𝐞𝐭 is a singleton, so 𝑈(𝟎) consists of precisely one element, which we denote 0𝟎.

Now fix an object 𝐴 and a zero object 𝟎, and set

0𝐴≔𝑈(0𝟎,𝐴)(0𝟎)∈𝑈(𝐴)

where 0𝟎,𝐴:𝟎→𝐴 is the unique morphism afforded by 𝟎 being an initial object (2.6.48), and 0𝟎∈𝑈(𝟎) is the unique element found above.

It remains to check that 0𝐴 does not depend on the choice of zero object. Let 𝟎′ be another zero object, with associated element 0𝐴′≔𝑈(0𝟎′,𝐴)(0𝟎′). Since 𝟎,𝟎′ are both initial objects (2.6.55), by uniqueness of initial objects (2.6.48) there is a (unique) isomorphism 𝜑:𝟎→𝟎′. As Mor(𝟎,𝐴) is a singleton, being initial, we have

0𝟎′,𝐴∘𝜑=0𝟎,𝐴

so applying 𝑈 and evaluating at 0𝟎

𝑈(0𝟎,𝐴)(0𝟎)=𝑈(0𝟎′,𝐴)(𝑈(𝜑)(0𝟎))

Now 𝑈(𝜑):𝑈(𝟎)→𝑈(𝟎′) is a map between singletons, so it necessarily sends 0𝟎 to the unique element 0𝟎′ of 𝑈(𝟎′). Hence

0𝐴=𝑈(0𝟎,𝐴)(0𝟎)=𝑈(0𝟎′,𝐴)(0𝟎′)=0𝐴′

so 0𝐴 is independent of the choice of zero object, as required. ∎

Proposition 2.6.199 (Kernels in Algebraic Categories)

Let 𝒞︀ be an algebraic pointed category, and consider a diagram

ker(𝛼)⟶𝑖𝑌⟶𝛼𝑍

Then (𝑖,ker(𝛼)) is a kernel for 𝛼 if and only if

  1. 𝑈(𝑖) is injective
  2. Im(𝑈(𝑖))={𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝛼)(𝑦)=0𝑍}

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Since 𝒞︀ is pointed, by (2.6.150) (𝑖,ker(𝛼)) is a kernel for 𝛼 if and only if 𝑖 is an equaliser for (𝛼,0𝑌,𝑍), where 0𝑌,𝑍:𝑌→𝑍 denotes the zero morphism (2.6.54).

As 𝒞︀ is algebraic, (2.6.197) (applied with 𝑑0=𝛼, 𝑑1=0𝑌,𝑍) shows this holds if and only if 𝑈(𝑖) is injective and

Im(𝑈(𝑖))={𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝛼)(𝑦)=𝑈(0𝑌,𝑍)(𝑦)}

It remains to identify 𝑈(0𝑌,𝑍)(𝑦) with 0𝑍 for every 𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌). Write 0𝑌,𝑍=0𝟎,𝑍∘!𝑌, where !𝑌:𝑌→𝟎 and 0𝟎,𝑍:𝟎→𝑍 are the unique morphisms afforded by 𝟎 being terminal, resp. initial (2.6.54). By (2.6.198), 𝑈(𝟎) is a singleton {0𝟎}, so 𝑈(!𝑌)(𝑦)=0𝟎 for every 𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌), and therefore

𝑈(0𝑌,𝑍)(𝑦)=𝑈(0𝟎,𝑍)(𝑈(!𝑌)(𝑦))=𝑈(0𝟎,𝑍)(0𝟎)=0𝑍

using the definition of 0𝑍 from (2.6.198). Hence

{𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝛼)(𝑦)=𝑈(0𝑌,𝑍)(𝑦)}={𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝛼)(𝑦)=0𝑍}

so combining with the above, (𝑖,ker(𝛼)) is a kernel for 𝛼 if and only if 𝑈(𝑖) is injective and Im(𝑈(𝑖))={𝑦∈𝑈(𝑌)|𝑈(𝛼)(𝑦)=0𝑍}, as required. ∎

2.6.24 Exact Sequences

Definition 2.6.200 (Exact Sequence)

Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed category with an image of every morphism (2.6.167) – e.g. a pointed algebraic category (2.6.184), which has regular epi-mono factorisations (2.6.196), hence images (2.6.174).

Let 𝑋⟶𝑓𝑌⟶𝑔𝑍 be a pair of composable morphisms and (Im(𝑓),𝑒,𝑚) an image of 𝑓. We say the pair is exact at 𝑌 if Im(𝑓)=ker(𝑔), that is, (Im(𝑓),𝑚) is (literally) a kernel of 𝑔.

This does not depend on the choice of image of 𝑓: images are unique up to (unique) isomorphism (2.6.167), so given any other image (Im′(𝑓),𝑒′,𝑚′) of 𝑓, there is an isomorphism 𝜃:Im(𝑓)→Im′(𝑓) with 𝑚′∘𝜃=𝑚, and by (2.6.137) (applied to 𝜃 and to 𝜃−1), (Im(𝑓),𝑚) is a kernel of 𝑔 if and only if (Im′(𝑓),𝑚′) is.

Proposition 2.6.201 (Concrete Criterion, Algebraic Case)
Let 𝒞︀ be a pointed algebraic category, and Im(𝑓) the canonical (literal subalgebra) construction. Then the pair is exact at 𝑌 (2.6.200) if and only if 𝑓(𝑋)=𝑔−1({0}), as subsets of 𝑌.

Proof. Drafted by Claude Sonnet 5, reviewed by David Rufino.

Write 𝐼≔𝑓(𝑋)⊆𝑌 for the canonical image of 𝑓 (2.6.196), a subalgebra of 𝑌 with the literal inclusion 𝑚:𝐼↪︎𝑌 as structure map, so 𝑓=𝑚∘𝑒 (with 𝑒 the corestriction of 𝑓) is a regular epi-mono factorisation of 𝑓. By (2.6.200) (independence of representatives), we may use this particular representative: the pair is exact at 𝑌 if and only if (𝐼,𝑚) is a kernel of 𝑔, that is, by (2.6.150), 𝑚 is an equaliser of (𝑔,0). By (2.6.197), since 𝑚 is (already) injective, this holds if and only if Im(𝑚)=𝐼 equals {𝑦∈𝑌|𝑔(𝑦)=0}=𝑔−1({0}). ∎
